structure.title: General information
structure.heading: 1. General information
structure.start_phrase: OTP Bank Plc. has also prepared its CSRD Sustainability Statement (in accordance with the European Sustainability Reporting Standards, ESRS) at the individual level, covering the individual operations of the parent bank (hereinafter “the Bank”, “OTP Bank”), with the same scope as the individual -level financial statement.
structure.summary:
- Scope and basis: OTP Bank Plc. prepared a stand-alone CSRD Sustainability Statement in line with ESRS, covering the parent bank’s individual operations, aligned in scope with its individual financial statements. A separate consolidated report covers the OTP Group.
- Terminology: Clarifies use of “OTP Bank” for the parent company and “OTP Group/Banking Group” for the consolidated group.
- Confidentiality and omissions: No use of exemptions for intellectual property, know-how, innovation, or pending developments; full disclosures provided.
- Regulatory reporting format: Hungarian law requires XHTML (ESEF) and XBRL tagging for sustainability disclosures (including EU Taxonomy Art. 8), but XBRL tagging was not possible because an ESEF sustainability taxonomy has not yet been adopted.
- Value chain and materiality: Group-level double materiality assessment includes upstream and downstream value chain; as the parent, OTP Bank’s individual report reflects the Group’s value chain relevance.
- ESRS 2 BP-2 alignment: Time horizons, value chain estimation, and uncertainty approaches at the individual level are consistent with the Group’s methodology.
- First-time reporting: This is the first individual-level ESRS disclosure; therefore, no prior-period changes or comparative figures. Forward-looking statements carry uncertainty not separately disclosed.
- Error materiality: Defines material error for prior periods as one that could reasonably influence user decisions based on the Sustainability Statement.
- Standards and indicators: No additional reporting standard indicators are presented at the individual level.
- Cross-references: Disclosures incorporated by reference are listed in the ESRS content index (Section 5).
- Phasing-in: The Bank applied ESRS phasing-in options for selected subtopics/items in this first reporting period, detailed in the ESRS index and the Group sustainability report.

nodes.title: Basis for preparation of the report
nodes.heading: 1.1. Basis for preparation of the report
nodes.start_phrase: OTP Bank Plc. has also prepared its CSRD Sustainability Statement (in accordance with the European Sustainability Reporting Standards, ESRS) at the individual level, covering the individual operations of the parent bank (hereinafter “the Bank”, “OTP Bank”), with the same scope as the individual -level financial statement.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and purpose: Stand-alone CSRD/ESRS Sustainability Statement for OTP Bank Plc. at the individual (parent bank) level, aligned with the scope of its individual financial statements; the Group’s consolidated sustainability report is published separately.
- Reporting basis and compliance: Prepared under ESRS (ESRS 2 BP-1 and BP-2). Complies with Hungarian Accounting Law requirements for XHTML/ESEF format; XBRL tagging not applied because an ESEF sustainability taxonomy has not yet been adopted. No omissions for intellectual property or negotiations. First-time ESRS individual reporting, so no prior-period comparatives; definition of material error provided. Forward-looking uncertainty acknowledged but not separately disclosed. No other standards’ indicators presented. Disclosures by reference are listed in the ESRS Index; phasing-in option applied with items identified in the Index.
- Value chain and materiality: Group-level double materiality, covering upstream and downstream value chain, is applied to the Bank at individual level. Time horizons, estimation approaches, and uncertainty handling align with Group methodology.
- Governance structure (ESRS 2 GOV-1): Governance bodies mirror the Group’s—Supervisory Board, Board of Directors, Audit Committee, and other permanent/special committees. Composition, experience, and diversity details are referenced to the Group Sustainability Report and the individual financial report.
- Sustainability governance: An ESG organisation established in 2021 covers the entire Group, including the Bank. ESG Committee and ESG Sub-Committee are permanent; roles, responsibilities, reporting lines, and measures to ensure sustainability expertise are defined.
- Business conduct (ESRS G1 GOV-1): Ethical conduct overseen by the Supervisory Board, Board of Directors, and Ethics Committee. Strong focus on anti–money laundering with a dedicated Money Laundering Prevention Committee. Compliance oversight rests with the Board and Supervisory Board.
- Governance information flows and remuneration (ESRS 2 GOV-2): Sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities are communicated through integrated channels consistent with Group practices. Risk management, strategic decision processes, and executive remuneration follow Group policies.
- Incentives (ESRS 2 GOV-3, E1 GOV-3): Remuneration Policy includes an ESG-CSR indicator encompassing climate considerations; no explicit GHG emissions reduction target is used in incentive benchmarking.

nodes.title: Governance
nodes.heading: 1.2. Governance
nodes.start_phrase: The management, executive and supervisory bodies of OTP Bank Plc. are the Supervisory Board, the Board of Directors and all their committees, including the Audit Committee and the special and permanent committees listed in the Responsible Corporate Governance Report, which are the same as the management bodies of the OTP Group.
nodes.summary:
- Governance structure and oversight: OTP Bank Plc.’s governing bodies comprise the Supervisory Board, Board of Directors, Audit Committee, and permanent/special committees, aligned with OTP Group structures. Composition, diversity, and experience of these bodies are referenced to the OTP Group Sustainability Report.
- Sustainability governance: An ESG organisation established in 2021 operates group-wide, with permanent ESG Committee and ESG Sub-Committee embedded in the Organisational and Operational Rules. Roles, responsibilities, reporting, and measures to ensure sustainability expertise follow group practices.
- Ethical business conduct: The Supervisory Board, Board of Directors, and Ethics Committee oversee ethical conduct and compliance. Anti–money laundering is a key priority, supported by the Money Laundering Prevention Committee. Governance responsibility for compliance rests with the Board and Supervisory Board.
- Information flow to governing bodies: Sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities from materiality assessment are communicated through integrated sectoral channels rather than standalone reports; remuneration policy and executive pay criteria follow OTP Group practices.
- Incentives: The group-level Remuneration Policy includes an ESG-CSR indicator that incorporates sustainability and climate considerations for covered persons; no GHG emission reduction targets are used for benchmarking.
- Due diligence: Elements of due diligence are integrated into group operations, grounded in the Bank’s Compliance Policy.
- Sustainability reporting risk management: The Marketing and Communications Directorate coordinates sustainability reporting, maintains internal controls, collaborates with group functions, and conducts an annual review to identify risks, difficulties, and improvement actions, mirroring consolidated report controls.
- Strategy and business model: OTP Bank is Hungary’s leading credit institution, serving retail, private banking, micro/small, medium/large enterprises, and municipalities via a nationwide branch network and evolving digital/remote channels. It offers deposits and a broad suite of savings and investment products (treasury, government securities, funds, equities, corporate bonds, structured products), aiming for stable liquidity across cycles. The Bank served over 4.3 million customers and employed 10,820 people at end-2024.
- Strategic priorities: Continuous digitalisation, strong emphasis on sustainability to avoid negative and enhance positive impacts, customer-centric products that support financial well-being, commitment to employee well-being, and active roles in financial literacy and cultural development.
- Value chain (upstream): Predominantly services procurement required for operations, especially marketing communications and IT.

nodes.title: Strategy
nodes.heading: 1.3. Strategy
nodes.start_phrase: OTP Bank is the leading credit institution in Hungary.
nodes.summary:
- Governance and due diligence (ESRS 2 GOV-4, GOV-5)
  - Due diligence elements are embedded in group operations and guided by OTP Group’s Compliance Policy.
  - Sustainability reporting is coordinated by OTP Bank’s Marketing and Communications Directorate, which oversees internal controls, collaborates closely with business areas and group members, and provides strategic/functional guidance.
  - After each annual cycle, the Directorate reviews reporting processes, identifies risks and obstacles (technical/administrative/substantive), and defines improvement steps, aligned with the consolidated reporting approach.

- Strategy, business model and value chain (ESRS 2 SBM-1)
  - OTP Bank is Hungary’s leading credit institution, serving retail, private banking, MSME, corporate (mid/large), and municipal clients via branches and evolving digital/remote channels.
  - Offers deposits and a broad suite of savings/investment and treasury products (incl. government securities, funds, equities, corporate bonds, structured investments).
  - Strategic focus on stable liquidity across cycles, continuous digitalisation, accessibility, security, and sustainability (avoiding negative impacts, realising positives, and customer well-being).
  - Workforce and reach: 10,820 employees and over 4.3 million customers in Hungary at end-2024.

- Value chain highlights
  - Upstream: service procurement dominates (marketing communications, IT, telecom); operational real estate includes intra-group and leased properties; company cars typically owned within the group.
  - Downstream: strong agency (third-party) sales, especially mortgage brokerage; 58% of OTP Bank product sales in 2024 via third parties; 477 dependent agents at OTP Financial Point are counted in own workforce per ESRS.
  - Most significant environmental and social impacts arise through customers, mainly via lending.
  - As parent, OTP Bank steers and coordinates group practices (including ESG); group policies extend group-wide while allowing local initiatives.

- ESG strategy
  - OTP Bank leads the group’s four-year ESG strategy (adopted 2021) to be a regional leader in financing a fair, gradual transition to a low-carbon economy and enabling ethical, socially and environmentally sound financial choices.

- Stakeholders (ESRS 2 SBM-2)
  - Corporate and ESG strategies prioritise customers, investors, employees, and broader stakeholders.
  - Code of Ethics mandates ethical conduct for all employees and agents.
  - Ongoing engagement with subsidiaries, clients, investors/analysts, employees, regulators, NGOs/professional bodies, sponsored organisations, education/research institutions, the public, suppliers, and competitors through surveys, meetings, reporting, and consultations.
  - Feedback informs strategy, services, products, and programs; governing bodies receive regular stakeholder-related reports.
  - Note: materiality assessment and due diligence did not specifically examine stakeholder views on the strategy and business model.

- Materiality assessment (ESRS 2; topical E1–E5, G1 IRO-1)
  - OTP Bank’s analysis builds on the Group’s ESRS-aligned double materiality assessment; for individual reporting, it focuses on impacts, risks, and opportunities from financial services.
  - Group identified three activity scopes: financial services (most prominent), real estate, and agriculture; the latter two are not relevant for OTP Bank.
  - Assessment emphasised areas with heightened risk of adverse impacts; no new OTP Bank–specific impacts beyond group-level findings.
  - Stakeholder inputs included ESG ratings/questionnaires (Sustainalytics, MSCI, Moody’s), TRI*M customer surveys, a 2024 employee engagement survey (8,596 responses; 79% response rate), and an online stakeholder questionnaire (NGOs, academia, authorities/regulators, analysts/stock exchanges, media, employee representatives).
  - Based on feedback, “employees: work-life balance” was added as a material topic; financial analysts and market stakeholders informed financial materiality.

nodes.title: Materiality assessment
nodes.heading: 1.4. Materiality assessment
nodes.start_phrase: The purpose of the materiality assessment is to enable OTP Bank to identify material impacts, risks and opportunities arising from its activities.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Describes OTP Bank’s materiality assessment to identify material sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities, using a double materiality approach aligned with ESRS and based on the OTP Group’s group-level methodology.
- Group-to-entity alignment: OTP Bank, as parent, leverages the Group’s top-down double materiality analysis; no new bank-specific impacts were identified beyond group-level. Of the Group’s three activity scopes (financial services, real estate, agriculture), only financial services are material for the Bank’s standalone reporting.
- Methodology references: Points to the OTP Group Sustainability Report for detailed methods on identifying and assessing impacts, risks, and opportunities, including climate-related topics.
- Stakeholder engagement: Incorporates inputs from ESG rating questionnaires (Sustainalytics, MSCI, Moody’s), national retail TRI*M brand/satisfaction surveys, an employee engagement survey (8,596 responses; 79% response rate), and an online stakeholder questionnaire (NGOs, academia, authorities/regulators, analysts, media, employee reps). Work–life balance was added as a material topic based on feedback.
- Financial risks and opportunities identification: Began with ESRS themes, SASB for financials, and ESG assessment topics; workshops and expert consultations prioritized a short list and considered short/medium/long-term horizons; no additional bank-specific risks/opportunities beyond group-level.
- Validation and governance: Internal reviews included near-threshold topics corrected with stakeholder feedback; Hungarian and foreign subsidiaries commented. The ESG Sub-Committee approved the final list (with one modification).
- Key material topics (ESRS 2 SBM-3) and responses:
  - Climate (E1): Mitigation and adaptation are material. Scope 3 portfolio emissions dominate; Scope 1–2 are smaller but significant overall. A loan portfolio decarbonization (transition) plan was prepared by end-2024; Scope 1–2 reduction plans are being developed, with green electricity a key lever. Green lending presents major opportunities; transition and physical risks are managed within ESG risk frameworks and stress testing.
  - Energy: Financing energy-intensive and fossil-fuel users creates credit/reputational risks; opportunities in renewables and energy efficiency through green lending.
  - Water (E3): Exposure via clients in high water-withdrawal sectors; minimum compliance expectations set, with ongoing deeper assessment to inform future expectations; potential financial risks if clients cannot meet evolving requirements.
  - Biodiversity (E4): Potential negative client impacts in certain sectors; current focus on legal compliance and permits, with further understanding to shape expectations; biodiversity not considered financially material for resilience assessment at this stage.
  - Own workforce (S1): Material subtopics include work–life balance, health and safety (noting stress risks), gender equality and equal pay (generally small gaps in same roles; lower female representation at higher levels), training and skills (broad access; room for improvement in consistency), employment of persons with disabilities (low current levels; anti-discrimination in place but limited targeted measures), anti-violence/harassment measures, and wider diversity.
  - Consumers/end-users (S4): Information security, data protection and cyber defense are critical; ongoing system, process, and training enhancements; residual risks remain. Access to quality information and to financial products/services (including digital access and state-supported mortgages) are material, with continuous improvements and remaining gaps.
  - Business conduct (G1): Corporate culture, compliance, and AML/CFT are central, supported by code of ethics, whistleblowing, and mandatory trainings; residual risks of non-compliance exist. Anti-corruption practices include training, clauses for partners, and risk assessments, acknowledging potential for isolated abuse.
- Risk and resilience insights: No provisions or capital buffers were set for ESG-related risks in 2024; ESG-flagging applied in operational loss data collection; no significant ESG-related losses realized in 2024. Climate stress testing conducted; biodiversity/ecosystem resilience not performed due to limited financial materiality. Further financial impact analysis planned for 2025.
- Reporting approach and ESRS coverage: OTP Bank’s standalone disclosures follow group-developed data collection and reporting practices, mapped to ESRS and EFRAG guidance (ID 177/AR16). Entity-specific disclosures are prioritized for information security/data protection, quality information, access to financial products/services, and business conduct/AML; value-chain topics (water withdrawal; direct drivers of biodiversity loss) are material with entity-specific disclosures to be developed. Use of phase-in options and a consolidated ESRS Index are referenced.

nodes.title: List of ESRS requirements covered and general reporting policy
nodes.heading: 1.5. List of ESRS requirements covered and general reporting policy
nodes.start_phrase: In preparing its sustainability statement, OTP Bank has determined the list of disclosure requirements based on the results of the materiality assessment carried out by the Group, which are also relevant at an individual level.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and materiality: OTP Bank’s stand‑alone report aligns with OTP Group’s materiality assessment, focusing on sustainability impacts tied to financial services (primarily lending). Detailed impact mapping is referenced to the Group Sustainability Report (section 1.4).

- ESG risk management: No provisions or capital buffers for ESG-related risks were set in 2024. Operational loss events are ESG-flagged where relevant; no significant ESG-related losses occurred in 2024. The Bank plans to analyze and estimate expected financial impacts in 2025.

- Resilience and stress testing: Existing risk management and planning processes support resilience to sustainability risks and opportunities. A climate change stress test was conducted for regulatory and business reasons. No biodiversity/ecosystem resilience assessment was performed, as these were not considered financially material, though further analyses may be warranted.

- Market and regulatory readiness: The Bank monitors evolving market opportunities and regulatory requirements to respond appropriately.

- Reporting evolution: Previously, OTP Bank reported only at Group level under GRI 2021; this is a stand‑alone report drawing on Group methodologies.

- Entity-specific topics followed from Group ESRS approach: 
  - Water withdrawal (material in value chain; disclosure to be developed)
  - Direct drivers of biodiversity loss (material in value chain; disclosure to be developed)
  - Information security and data protection
  - Quality information
  - Access to financial products and services
  - Corporate culture, compliance, and anti–money laundering

- ESRS reporting policy (ESRS 2 IRO‑2): Disclosures are selected based on Group materiality but applied at Bank level. The parent bank coordinates Group-wide data collection and methodologies, follows EFRAG guidance (ID 177) for linking data points, and uses a structured approach (Data Points, Policy, Action, Target, Metrics, Entity‑specific Disclosures). Where applicable, information is cross‑referenced to the Group report. Phase‑in options and a detailed ESRS Index are provided in chapter 5.

- Environmental information – EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosures:
  - Main KPI (GAR stock):
    - Environmentally sustainable assets: HUF 21,669m (turnover-based) and HUF 66,252m (capex-based)
    - GAR: 0.17% (turnover-based) and 0.51% (capex-based)
    - Coverage over total assets: 68.25%
    - Assets excluded: 33.43% from numerator; 31.75% from denominator (per Annex V rules)
  - Additional KPI (GAR flow):
    - Environmentally sustainable activities: HUF 8,779m (turnover-based) and HUF 33,225m (capex-based)
    - GAR flow: 0.32% (turnover-based) and 1.20% (capex-based)
    - Coverage over total assets: 89.52%
    - Assets excluded: 23.47% from numerator; 10.48% from denominator
  - Financial guarantees and assets under management KPIs reported as 0.
  - Fees/commissions and trading book KPIs to apply from 2026; SME inclusion subject to future assessment.

nodes.title: Disclosure under the EU Taxonomy Regulation
nodes.heading: 2.1.1. Disclosure under the EU Taxonomy Regulation
nodes.start_phrase: • Across the reporting templates: cells shaded in grey should not be reported.
nodes.summary:
- Context and scope: This section of the standalone Management Report (Integrated Annual Report 2024) provides environmental information focused on EU Taxonomy disclosures for a credit institution under Article 8 of the Taxonomy Regulation. It reports as of 31 December 2024.

- KPI summary under the EU Taxonomy:
  - Main KPI – Green Asset Ratio (GAR, stock):
    - Environmentally sustainable assets: HUF 21,669 million (turnover-based) and HUF 66,252 million (capex-based).
    - Reported GAR values: 0.17% (turnover-based) and 0.51% (capex-based).
    - High exclusions: a significant share of assets excluded from GAR numerator and denominator per Article 7 and Annex V.
  - Additional KPIs – GAR (flow):
    - Environmentally sustainable activities: HUF 8,779 million (turnover-based) and HUF 33,225 million (capex-based).
    - Reported values: 0.32% (turnover-based) and 1.20% (capex-based).
    - Exclusions remain high in the numerator (around 90%) and material in the denominator (around 10–23%).
  - Financial guarantees and Assets under Management: reported as zero.
  - Note on scope: Fees/Commissions and Trading Book KPIs will apply starting 2026; SME inclusion subject to a positive impact assessment.

- GAR asset base and coverage – turnover-based:
  - Total assets: HUF 18,925,227 million.
  - Total GAR assets: HUF 12,915,794 million.
  - Assets covered in both numerator and denominator (loans, debt securities, equity not HfT): HUF 6,588,317 million, with taxonomy-eligible and aligned amounts disclosed by environmental objective.
  - Assets excluded from numerator (but in denominator): HUF 6,327,477 million, including:
    - SMEs and NFCs not subject to NFRD: HUF 2,846,798 million.
    - Non-EU counterparties not subject to NFRD: HUF 200,740 million.
    - Derivatives, on-demand interbank, cash and other assets.
  - Assets not covered for GAR calculation: HUF 6,009,433 million (central governments/supranationals, central bank exposures, trading book).
  - Counterparty breakdown includes financial undertakings (notably credit institutions), non-financial undertakings, and households (with details for residential mortgages and building renovation loans).

- GAR asset base and coverage – capex-based:
  - Same total assets and GAR asset base as turnover view.
  - Higher taxonomy-aligned amounts relative to turnover-based view, especially within non-financial undertakings.
  - Detailed split of environmentally sustainable exposures by environmental objective (Climate Change Mitigation and Adaptation dominate; Water, Circular Economy, Pollution, Biodiversity minimal or zero).
  - Households reported similarly (including renovation loans), with no additional taxonomy alignment under capex.

- Environmental objectives detail:
  - Disclosures distinguish taxonomy-eligible vs taxonomy-aligned exposures across six objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), and Biodiversity (BIO).
  - Reported aligned amounts are concentrated in Climate Change Mitigation; minor amounts in Adaptation; negligible in Water, CE, PPC, BIO.

- Household and collateral specifics:
  - Households include loans collateralised by residential property and building renovation loans (with renovation loans explicitly identified).
  - No motor vehicle loans reported as taxonomy-relevant.

- Sectoral (NACE-4) breakdown – turnover-based:
  - Provides a granular mapping of non-financial corporates (subject to NFRD) vs SMEs/other NFCs into CCM/CCA/WTR eligibility and alignment.
  - Sectors represented include energy and utilities (e.g., 3511–3514), transport and logistics (e.g., 4931, 4950), financial and holding activities (6420, 6492, 7010), selected manufacturing codes, real estate (6820), and others, with aligned amounts indicated where applicable.

- Reporting notes and methodology:
  - Uses both counterparty Turnover KPI and CapEx KPI consistent with Delegated Acts; for general lending, turnover KPI is applied.
  - Clarifies treatment of use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities (mostly limited amounts).
  - All figures presented in HUF million with coverage percentages over total assets and specified exclusions aligned to Article 7 and Annex V of the Taxonomy disclosures.

nodes.summary:

- Provides mandatory EU Taxonomy disclosures split by:
  - Basis: Turnover-based GAR and Capex-based GAR.
  - Environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and marine resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution prevention and control (PPC), Biodiversity and ecosystems (BIO).
  - Counterparty types: Non‑financial corporates subject to NFRD vs SMEs and other non‑financial corporates not subject to NFRD.

- For each NACE sector, shows gross carrying amounts (HUF million) and the portion that is environmentally sustainable for each objective, plus a total across all objectives.

- Capex-based table indicates high taxonomy-aligned capex in head offices (7010), holding companies (6420), electricity generation/transmission/distribution (3511–3513), chemicals (2059), urban transport (4931), and others; many sectors have limited or no aligned capex.
- All amounts are disclosed in HUF million and distinguish between taxonomy-eligible exposures and the subset that is environmentally sustainable (aligned), serving as inputs to the institution’s GAR.

nodes.title: GAR Sector information – Capex based
nodes.heading: 2. GAR Sector information – Capex based
nodes.start_phrase: Breakdown by sector -
nodes.summary:
- Presents EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures for 2024 within the Management Report, focusing on:
  - Section 2: Capex-based GAR sector information by NACE 4-digit codes.
    - For each sector, gross carrying amounts (HUF million) are shown for exposures to non-financial corporates subject to NFRD and to SMEs/other NFCs not subject to NFRD.
    - Breakdowns cover the six environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), and Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO), with “of which environmentally sustainable” amounts for each.
    - Data indicate CCM dominates the environmentally sustainable capex; CCA, WTR, PPC, and BIO show minimal values, with CE contributing modest amounts in select sectors.
    - Notable CCM concentrations (by code) include 7010, 6420, 3511, 2059, 1062, 4931, and 3512; several sectors record zeros or very small sustainable amounts.
    - A total column aggregates environmentally sustainable capex across all six objectives for each sector.
  - Section 3: GAR KPI Stock – Turnover-based data (as of 31 December 2024).
    - Reports percentages relative to total covered assets, distinguishing taxonomy-eligible vs. taxonomy-aligned exposures for CCM, CCA, and WTR.
    - Breakdowns by counterparty/instrument class: financial undertakings (incl. credit institutions), non-financial undertakings, households, local governments; and by asset type (loans, debt securities, equity).
    - For CCM, taxonomy-aligned exposures are further split into use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling; for CCA/WTR, into use-of-proceeds and enabling.
    - Key figures: non-financial undertakings show 10.6% taxonomy-eligible and 6.6% taxonomy-aligned under CCM (with 1.8% transitional and 3.7% enabling); households include taxonomy-relevant categories such as residential mortgages (33.5%) and building renovation loans (100%) though aligned shares are 0.0%.
    - Overall total GAR assets reflect low taxonomy exposure on a turnover basis: 0.5% taxonomy-eligible and 0.2% taxonomy-aligned under CCM, with negligible CCA and WTR.

nodes.title: GAR KPI Stock – Turnover based data
nodes.heading: 3. GAR KPI Stock – Turnover based data
nodes.start_phrase: % (compared to total covered assets in the denominator) Disclosure reference date 31 December 2024
nodes.summary:
- Extract from the Integrated Annual Report 2024 (Management Report, Stand‑Alone), section “3. GAR KPI Stock,” disclosing EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) metrics as of 31 December 2024.
- Two GAR Stock views are presented:
  - Turnover-based data (pages 54–55).
  - Capex-based data (page 56).
- Scope and methodology:
  - Results shown for “covered assets in both numerator and denominator.”
  - Breakdown by asset class and counterparty: loans and advances, debt securities (incl. use-of-proceeds), equity instruments (not held for trading), financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations incl. investment firms and management companies, insurance undertakings), non-financial undertakings, households (mortgages, building renovation loans, motor vehicle loans), local governments (housing/other), and repossessed collateral.
  - Disaggregation by EU Taxonomy environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and marine resources (WTR), Circular economy (CE), Pollution (PPC), Biodiversity (BIO).
  - Distinguishes taxonomy-eligible vs. taxonomy-aligned exposures, and within aligned: use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities.
- Coverage:
  - Proportion of total assets covered by GAR denominator: 68.25%.
  - Category coverage examples: loans/debt/equity not HfT 34.81%; credit institutions 18.92%; other financial corporations 4.41%; insurance undertakings 2.43%; households 9.80%.
- Turnover-based key results:
  - Total GAR assets (all objectives combined): ~0.5% taxonomy-eligible; ~0.2% taxonomy-aligned; ~0.1% enabling; negligible use-of-proceeds and transitional overall.
  - Activity concentration in climate objectives; near-zero contributions for WTR, CE, PPC, BIO.
  - Non-financial undertakings show the main contribution (around 10.6–10.9% eligible; 6.6% aligned; split includes ~1.8% transitional and ~3.7% enabling).
  - Households: ~0.9% eligible overall; mortgages flagged as 33.5% eligible within the subcategory; building renovation loans shown as 100% eligible but on a very small base; motor vehicle loans 0%.
  - Financial undertakings, debt securities, and equity instruments: largely 0% eligible/aligned.
- Capex-based key results:
  - Total GAR assets: ~0.9% taxonomy-eligible; ~0.5% taxonomy-aligned; ~0.1% enabling; negligible use-of-proceeds and transitional overall.
  - Higher eligibility/alignment signals for non-financial undertakings vs. turnover view (about 25.0% eligible; 20.5% aligned; ~12.7% transitional; ~3.1% enabling), concentrated in loans and advances.
  - Households figures mirror turnover view (mortgages 33.5% eligible; building renovation loans 100% eligible on minimal exposure).
  - Securities and equity positions remain near 0% across objectives.
- Overall message: GAR coverage is substantial, but taxonomy-eligible and especially aligned exposures remain very low at portfolio level, with contributions concentrated in loans to non-financial corporates and, to a lesser extent, household mortgages/renovation, while securities portfolios, financial counterparties, and non-climate environmental objectives show negligible impact.

nodes.summary:
- Off-balance sheet green KPIs (Capex-based, flow) at 31 December 2024: Financial Guarantees and Assets under Management show 0.00% across all EU Taxonomy environmental objectives (climate change mitigation and adaptation, water, circular economy, pollution, biodiversity), and across all categories (taxonomy-eligible, taxonomy-aligned, use-of-proceeds, transitional, enabling).
- Climate change mitigation:
  - Emissions profile: Scope 1–2 from operations are small; Scope 3 from the loan portfolio dominates.
  - Business strategy: Expanding green lending is a key opportunity; targets linked to EU Taxonomy mitigation/adaptation objectives.
  - Targets and progress: Group KPI to build a HUF 1,500 billion green loan portfolio by 2025; green balance sheet exposure reached HUF 1,027 billion by end-2024. A climate target for the loan portfolio was set in 2024; aspiration to be a leading financier of a green and just transition.
  - Priority sectors: Energy (renewable generation, distribution, storage), real estate (green buildings and energy-efficiency renovations), transportation (electromobility).
  - Enablers: Leverage regulatory incentives; reduce Scope 1–2 via efficiency measures and green electricity.
  - Risk management: Transition risks to borrowers translate into bank credit risk; corporate portfolio stress-tested. ESG risks integrated across the risk ecosystem; ESG risk framework applied in corporate lending since 2021. Operational climate-related risks managed via group RCSA and scenario analysis with mitigation actions.
- Climate change adaptation:
  - Lending can facilitate, hinder, or be neutral to client adaptation; strong adaptation needs in housing, agriculture, real estate, and construction.
  - Business opportunity in financing adaptation; associated with physical risks and some transition risks tied to required investments.
  - Managed within the bank’s ESG risk management framework.

nodes.title: Climate change and environment
nodes.heading: 2.2. Climate change and environment
nodes.start_phrase: The impact of OTP Bank arises from direct and indirect greenhouse gas emissions, exacerbating climate change.
nodes.summary:
- The section centers on Climate Change and Environment, covering mitigation, adaptation, and energy, along with related risks, opportunities, policies, targets, actions, and metrics under ESRS.
- Emissions profile: OTP Bank’s direct (Scope 1–2) emissions are small relative to its financed (Scope 3) emissions, which dominate the footprint. The Bank recognizes both risk exposure (transition and physical) and business opportunities via green finance.
- Green lending strategy and targets:
  - Group ambition to lead financing of a green and just transition; KPI to build a HUF 1,500 billion green loan portfolio by 2025; green exposure reached HUF 1,027 billion by end-2024.
  - Alignment with EU Taxonomy (mitigation/adaptation). Priority sectors: energy (renewables, grids, storage), real estate (green buildings and deep renovations), and transport (e-mobility). 30.23% of the green portfolio finances renewables.
  - Use of regulatory incentives where possible.
- ESG risk integration: ESG risks embedded in group-level risk policies and processes; corporate lending applies an ESG risk framework since 2021; operational risks addressed via annual Group RCSA and scenario analysis.
- Adaptation: Lending can facilitate clients’ adaptation in sectors like housing, agriculture, real estate, and construction; associated physical and transition risks are managed within the ESG risk framework; Bank aims to capture adaptation-related business opportunities.
- Energy: Financing can reduce clients’ environmental impacts by supporting renewable and green-certified energy; financing fossil- and energy-intensive firms carries credit and reputational risks managed as above.
- Water and biodiversity:
  - Exposure to sectors with high water withdrawal and to activities potentially impacting biodiversity; current minimum expectation is client compliance with environmental and social laws and permits.
  - Deeper analysis underway to refine expectations and potentially set policies; opportunities exist to finance responsible water/biodiversity practices via green lending.
  - No standalone OTP Bank policies or targets yet for water and biodiversity; effectiveness currently not monitored.
- ESRS policy references: Group Credit Risk Policy and Corporate Lending Policy apply; Code of Ethics affirms environmental commitments; detailed policies and methods referenced in the Group Sustainability Report.
- Climate targets and actions:
  - Group plan (2024) to reduce financed GHG emissions by 2030, based on IEA NZE 2050 and national paths; OTP Bank follows Group targets. Monitoring and actions to mitigate financed emissions are in place; Executive Steering Committee approval planned for 05.02.2025.
  - Operational target: carbon-neutral Scope 1–2 by 2030 (absolute, not science-based); 2024 market-based Scope 1–2 emissions were 6,644 tCO2e; electricity largely green; real estate and fleet intensity reduction planning to be prepared in 2025.
  - Action packages: portfolio-level (climate targeting and scaling green lending) and operational (energy efficiency and renewables). Operational measures include green electricity procurement, lighting and boiler upgrades, HVAC optimization, insulation, and solar installations.
- GHG emissions and financed emissions:
  - Methodology aligned with group reporting; OTP Bank 2024 Scope 1 = 5,565 tCO2e; Scope 2 market-based = 1,079 tCO2e (total 6,644 tCO2e).
  - Significant Scope 3 (Category 15 – Investments) financed emissions were 24.836 MtCO2e in 2024 (-1% vs. 2023); 2030 target 16.855 MtCO2e (~-5.5% p.a.). PCAF-based breakdown by asset class provided; financed Scope 1–2 excluding sovereigns is the key indicator for climate targeting.
- Carbon credits and removals:
  - Purchased 7,000 tCO2e VCS-verified credits in 2024 covering Scope 1–2; project is the Saint Nikola Wind Farm in Bulgaria. Plans to complement offsets with a “habitat restoration certificate.”
  - Biodiversity and engagement initiative with Pilisi Parkerdő Zrt. to develop the 400 ha Budakeszi Wildlife Garden for ecosystem services, adaptation research, and employee engagement; no internal carbon pricing applied.
- ESG risk management and reporting: Group-wide ESG risk management foundations and environmental reporting policy apply at the individual bank level; further details referenced to the Group Sustainability Report.
- Social information (Own workforce):
  - Material topics: gender equality and equal pay; diversity; employment and inclusion of people with disabilities; training and skills development; health and safety; work-life balance; measures against workplace violence and harassment.
  - Own workforce includes employees and certain non-employee workers; practices primarily focus on employees; headcount of 10,820 employees.

nodes.title: ESG risk management
nodes.heading: 2.3. ESG risk management
nodes.start_phrase: OTP Bank pays particular attention to managing ESG risks and implementing climate change considerations into business practices.
nodes.summary:
- OTP Bank’s carbon neutrality pathway includes using carbon credits alongside energy efficiency and renewable energy to reach Scope 1–2 zero emissions by 2030; credits will be redeemed via “habitat restoration certificates.”
- Partnership with Pilisi Parkerdő Zrt. to develop the 400 ha Budakeszi Wildlife Garden as an urban forest focused on biodiversity, climate adaptation, carbon sequestration, ecosystem services, and ecotourism; serves as a platform for scientific work, employee engagement through non-financial recognition, and brand building.
- The Bank does not apply internal carbon pricing.
- ESRS E4-1 (transition plan and biodiversity) disclosures are addressed through the Materiality Assessment (ESRS 2 SBM-3).
- ESG risk management: integration of ESG and climate considerations into business and green lending; a group-wide ESG risk assessment framework covers credit, operational, market, and liquidity risks, with detailed processes and actions in the OTP Group Sustainability Report (chapter 2.4).
- Environmental reporting policy: group-level methodologies, definitions, and data requirements from the OTP Group Sustainability Report (subsection 2.3) are applied to OTP Bank; references include IRO-2.
- Social information—own workforce (ESRS S1 SBM-3): material topics are gender equality and equal pay, diversity, disability inclusion, training and skills, health and safety, work-life balance, and measures against violence and harassment. The own workforce includes employees and phased-in non-employee workers; 10,820 employees (full- or part-time), with practices primarily focused on employees.

structure.title: Social information
structure.heading: 3. Social information
structure.start_phrase: Among the topics identified by the ESRS, the following are material for OTP Bank: (1) gender equality and equal pay for work of equal value , (2) diversity, (3) employment and inclusion of people with disabilities, (4) training and skills development, (5) health and safety, (6) work -life balance and (7) measures against violence and harassment in the workplace.
structure.summary:
- OTP Bank’s carbon neutrality strategy includes the use of carbon credits alongside emission reductions from energy efficiency and renewable energy, targeting Scope 1–2 zero emissions by 2030. The Bank plans to redeem credits as “habitat restoration certificates.”
- Partnership with Pilisi Parkerdő Zrt. to develop a 400 ha Budakeszi Wildlife Garden as an urban forest prioritizing ecological and conservation values over economic ones; aims to support biodiversity, climate adaptation, carbon sequestration, and ecosystem services, engage employees via a non-financial recognition scheme, and enhance the Bank’s image.
- The company does not apply internal carbon pricing.
- ESRS E4-1 (transition plan and biodiversity) disclosures are addressed via the Materiality Assessment (ESRS 2 SBM-3).
- ESG risk management: integration of ESG and climate risks into business, with emphasis on green lending. A group-wide ESG risk assessment framework covers credit, operational, market, and liquidity risks; detailed processes and actions are in the OTP Group Sustainability Report (chapter 2.4).
- Environmental reporting (Chapter E): OTP Bank follows group-level definitions, methodologies, and data requirements per the Group Sustainability Report (subsection 2.3), including for individual-level disclosures (IRO-2).
- Social information – Own workforce: scope includes employees, agency workers, and self-employed contractors (non-employee workers phased in and reported at group external employees level). Material S1 topics: gender equality and equal pay, diversity, disability inclusion, training and skills, health and safety, work-life balance, and measures against workplace violence and harassment. Workforce totals 10,820, mostly employees; practices focus primarily on employees.

nodes.title: Own workforce
nodes.heading: 3.1. Own workforce
nodes.start_phrase: Among the topics identified by the ESRS, the following are material for OTP Bank: (1) gender equality and equal pay for work of equal value , (2) diversity, (3) employment and inclusion of people with disabilities, (4) training and skills development, (5) health and safety, (6) work -life balance and (7) measures against violence and harassment in the workplace.
nodes.summary:
- Climate strategy and carbon neutrality: OTP Bank’s 2030 Scope 1–2 zero-emissions target is pursued primarily through energy efficiency and renewables, complemented by carbon credits. Credits will be redeemed via a “habitat restoration certificate.” No internal carbon pricing is applied.
- Biodiversity and habitat project: In partnership with Pilisi Parkerdő Zrt., the Bank supports developing the 400 ha Budakeszi Wildlife Garden as an urban forest to enhance biodiversity, climate adaptation, carbon sequestration, and ecosystem services, while engaging employees through non-financial recognition and strengthening brand image.
- ESRS alignment and reporting: ESRS E4-1 transition plan and biodiversity disclosures are linked to the materiality assessment (ESRS 2 SBM-3). Group-wide ESG risk management (credit, operational, market, liquidity) frameworks and environmental reporting policies are referenced to the OTP Group Sustainability Report; OTP Bank follows group definitions, methodologies, and data requirements.
- ESG risk management: Climate and ESG risks are integrated into business and risk practices; the detailed group process underpins the Bank’s approach.
- Social information (ESRS S1): Material topics include gender equality and equal pay, diversity, disability inclusion, training and skills, health and safety, work-life balance, and measures against violence/harassment.
- Workforce scope and impacts: Own workforce includes employees and non-employee workers (with phased reporting for the latter). Most impacts mirror group-level findings; significant negative human rights risks (e.g., child or forced labor) are not present. Potential negatives include health and safety, workplace violence/harassment (mainly individual cases), and stress; the Bank aims to generate positive impacts across work-life balance, equality, training, and disability inclusion.
- Policies and safeguards: The OTP Group Code of Ethics governs human rights, equal treatment, job security, anti-harassment, and fair employment. Health and safety is managed per local regulations with regular risk assessments.
- Workforce engagement and dialogue: Engagement mechanisms include an annual employee survey (>80% response at OTP Bank) and regular consultations between HR leadership and the employees’ trade union. No global framework agreement is in place.
- Grievance channels (ESRS S1-3, S1-17): Multiple, including anonymous Ethics Reporting, union representation, and legal recourse. About 16% of ethics complaints came from employees; no discrimination cases, no OSH or union complaints, and no labor court cases in 2024.
- Targets and actions (ESRS S1-5, S1-4): Primary target is increasing employee engagement. Actions informed by survey focus on career opportunities, process improvements for well-being, and stronger senior management dialogue. HR, Legal, and Compliance oversee implementation; external audits may be used (e.g., H&S).
- Outcomes and metrics (ESRS S1-6): Engagement rose to 80% in 2024 (+4 pp), above the financial sector benchmark. Headcount at year-end 2024: 10,820 (4,180 men; 6,640 women); full-time 10,009; part-time 811; permanent 10,542; temporary 278. Turnover rate 13.34% (1,443 exits; gender and age breakdown provided).
- Diversity focus: A diversity strategy covers boards and management; programs and training promote inclusion. 84% of employees report that professional success is independent of gender, age, cultural background, ethnicity, and religion.

nodes.title: Gender equality and diversity
nodes.heading: 3.1.1. Gender equality and diversity
nodes.start_phrase: Due to its significant number of employees, the Bank has both the opportunity and the role to implement diversity.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and governance: OTP Bank’s HR, legal, and compliance functions manage employee impacts, ethics complaints, legal compliance, and actions against workplace violence/harassment, with adequate internal expertise and external support as needed.
- Engagement: Workplace engagement rose from 76% to 80% in 2024, exceeding the financial sector benchmark; positive shifts occurred across all engagement drivers. 84% of employees perceive professional success as independent of gender, age, culture, ethnicity, or religion.
- Workforce profile (ESRS S1-6): Headcount at end-2024 was 10,820 (4,180 men; 6,640 women), up ~1% YoY. Full-time: 10,009; part-time: 811. Permanent: 10,542; temporary: 278. Age distribution: under 30: 1,645; 30–49: 6,438; 50+: 2,737. Turnover in 2024: 13.34% (1,443 leavers; 489 men, 954 women; 364 under 30, 770 aged 30–50, 309 over 50).
- Diversity, disability inclusion, and gender equality:
  - Diversity strategy commits to inclusive leadership and programs to support diversity; current disability employment is low and actions to support it are not widely implemented, though discrimination is prohibited.
  - Gender equality: Equal pay for equal work is enforced via a gender-neutral remuneration policy; women are underrepresented in higher leadership roles. Strategy aims to increase women in leadership and includes training and awareness campaigns.
- Policies and standards (ESRS S1-1): Code of Ethics covers equal treatment, equal opportunities, non-discrimination, and fair employment practices. A publicly available Gender Equality Strategy (since 2021) assigns accountability to the Chief Compliance Officer and aligns with Hungarian law, MNB recommendations, and EBA GL 2017-12.
- Actions (ESRS S1-4): 2024 initiatives include women’s leadership development programs, an international Women Network, webinars and mentoring for women leaders, the OTP Digital GirlPower trainee program to boost women in digital/IT, and diversity awareness training (including unconscious bias) with a digital “Openness and Inclusion” curriculum. Effectiveness is monitored but not always against predefined criteria.
- Goals and indicators (ESRS S1-5, S1-16):
  - Targets: At least one female member on the Board of Directors and Supervisory Board; since 2021 the BoD includes one woman. Succession planning recommends at least 30% female candidates group-wide.
  - Indicators: Senior management at OTP Bank as of 31 Dec 2024 comprises 6 men (100% men). Employees with disabilities: 40. Group-level average gender pay gap: 39.15%, attributed mainly to job segregation. The ratio of the highest-paid individual’s total annual remuneration to the median employee’s is about 60% of the group-level indicator, reflecting the parent company’s context.
- Training and skills development: Broad access to professional, personal, and mandatory training, guided by annual plans informed by performance evaluations and employee input; detailed indicators are reported at OTP Group level.
- Occupational health and safety: Primary risk is stress rather than hazardous conditions. The Bank provides enhanced health services (insurance and screenings) and stress management support. OHS policy aligns with local legislation, defines roles and responsibilities, is accessible internally, and was updated in 2023 to reflect legal changes effective in 2024.

nodes.title: Training and skills development
nodes.heading: 3.1.2. Training and skills development
nodes.start_phrase: Due to its significant role as an employer, OTP Bank's training and skills development practices influence the sector and other employers.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and context: Extract from OTP Bank’s Integrated Annual Report 2024 (Management Report, stand-alone), covering own workforce topics 3.1.2 Training and Skills Development and 3.1.3 Occupational Health and Safety.

- Training and skills development:
  - OTP Bank, as a major employer, influences sector practices; financial sector employees are generally highly educated with assured access to training.
  - Broad training portfolio includes professional, personal development, and mandatory courses.
  - Annual training plans are created with employee involvement and informed by performance evaluations.
  - Policies, targets, and actions are set at group level and disclosed in the OTP Group Sustainability Report; certain indicators are being introduced gradually.

- Occupational health and safety (OHS):
  - Key risk identified is employee stress, as most roles are not in hazardous environments.
  - The Bank supports stress management and offers health services that exceed legal requirements (e.g., insurance, screenings); engagement survey feedback indicates adequate OHS management.
  - ESRS S1-1 policy: OHS Regulation aligned with local legislation, forming a comprehensive prevention strategy that defines responsibilities and processes across workplaces; subsidiaries maintain aligned policies.
  - Governance and accountability: Policy approved by the CEO; the Head of the President-CEO’s Cabinet is responsible for OHS activities. At group members, CEOs approve and are supported by operational leaders and local OHS officers.
  - Accessibility and standards: OHS regulations are available internally; framework is based on local legal requirements.
  - 2023 update: OHS Regulation revised to reflect amendments to the Act on Occupational Safety and Health, especially on OHS training and medical fitness tests, ahead of 2024 entry into force.
  - The Bank maintains an internal OHS regulatory system grounded in current legislation and guidelines.

nodes.title: Occupational health and safety
nodes.heading: 3.1.3. Occupational health and safety
nodes.start_phrase: For a significant portion of employees, stress emerges as a relevant risk, considering that the majority of employees do not work in hazardous working environment.
nodes.summary:
- Focus areas: OTP Bank’s management of its own workforce across training and skills development, occupational health and safety (OHS), work-life balance, and workplace violence/harassment, aligned with ESRS S1 disclosures.
- Training and skills development:
  - Broad training portfolio covering professional, personal, and mandatory topics.
  - Annual training plans developed with employee involvement and performance evaluation results.
  - Policies, targets, and actions are set at group level (OTP Group Sustainability Report), with gradual indicator introduction where applicable.
- Occupational health and safety:
  - Key risk identified as stress, given predominantly low-hazard office work.
  - OHS policy formalized in the Bank’s Occupational Health and Safety Regulation, aligned with local law; revised in 2023 for 2024 legislative changes.
  - Clear governance and accountability: CEO-approved policy; Head of the President-CEO’s Cabinet responsible at Bank level; local CEOs and OHS officers at subsidiaries.
  - Actions include compliance-based OHS management, investigation of near-miss incidents, regular OHS/fire/electrical safety training, change-specific trainings, and continuous availability and monitoring of training materials.
  - Health promotion and preventive care: occupational health checks for all jobs; 9,540 inspections by end-September; high-quality health insurance with 5,908 employees using services (4,087 screenings; 20,278 complaint handlings).
  - Wellbeing and stress management: lectures, webinars, workshops, health days; 2024 psychosocial risk survey (12% participation) informing programs; free confidential supportive conversations (ICF-aligned) with >1,398 sessions by end-2024; biannual skills trainings (mindfulness, stress management, communication) with ~350 participants per session.
  - Monitoring via internal audits and employee feedback.
  - Targets and indicators: no specific OHS targets set; 100% workforce coverage by OHS management system; working hours tracked via timesheets.
  - 2024 incident data (employees): 8 accidents; accident rate 0.44 per 1 million working hours; 0 occupational illnesses; 80 calendar days lost; 0 fatalities.
- Work-life balance:
  - Impacts shaped by overtime, flexible work, and childcare; significance heightened by two-thirds female workforce.
  - Engagement survey tracks perceptions; overtime generally not threatening balance.
  - Flexible arrangements and part-time options in place; ~8% of employees work part-time.
  - Group-level reporting with gradual indicator introduction.
- Workplace violence and harassment:
  - Material due to large workforce and high proportion of women; risk noted from lower female representation at senior levels.
  - No confirmed abuse cases; practices aim to ensure compliance; policies/actions covered at group level.
- ESRS S1-17 and reporting:
  - No justified discrimination cases in 2024.
  - Group-level, standardized reporting methodology for own workforce (definitions, calculations, data) aligned with IRO-2.

nodes.title: Work-life balance
nodes.heading: 3.1.4. Work -life balance
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank influences work -life balance through overtime, flexible employment opportunities, and access to childcare options.
nodes.summary:
- Focuses on ESRS S1 social topics for OTP Bank in the 2024 Integrated Annual Report.
- Health and safety: no specific H&S targets; 100% of own workforce covered by a health and safety management system; working hours tracked via timesheets.
- Work-life balance: influenced by overtime, flexible employment, and childcare options; approximately two-thirds of employees are women, making family-related impacts significant; annual engagement survey monitors work-life balance; overtime generally does not endanger balance; about 8% of employees work part-time; actions reported at OTP Group level with gradual introduction of specific indicators.
- Workplace violence and harassment: important due to large workforce and high share of women, with increased risk from lower female representation at higher levels; no confirmed abuse; compliance-focused policies and actions applied at group level.
- ESRS S1-17 incidents: no justified discrimination cases against own employees in 2024.
- Reporting policy: group-level practice for individual-level disclosures, with standardized definitions, calculation methodologies, and data requirements for own workforce.
- 2024 accidents and illnesses (employees): 8 accidents; accident rate 0.44 per 1 million working hours; 0 occupational illnesses; 80 calendar days lost; 0 fatal accidents or illnesses.

nodes.title: Workplace violence and harassment
nodes.heading: 3.1.5. Workplace violence and harassment
nodes.start_phrase: The large number of employees and the high proportion of female employees make this topic important, which is further intensified by the lower proportion of female employees at higher levels (increasing the risk of abuse).
nodes.summary:
- Health and safety (ESRS S1-5, S1-14): No specific H&S targets set. 100% of the own workforce is covered by the health and safety management system. Working hours are tracked via timesheets. In 2024 there were 8 employee accidents, an accident rate of 0.44 per 1 million working hours, 0 occupational illnesses, 80 calendar days lost, and 0 fatalities.
- Work-life balance (3.1.4): Impacts stem from overtime, flexible work options, and childcare access; particularly relevant given about two-thirds of employees are women. Monitored via the annual engagement survey. Overtime generally does not threaten balance. Around 8% of employees work part-time. Indicators are being gradually introduced, with group-level details in the OTP Group Sustainability Report.
- Workplace violence and harassment (3.1.5): Topic is important due to workforce size and gender composition and fewer women at senior levels. No confirmed abuse cases. Compliance-focused policies/actions are in place at group level.
- Incidents and human rights (ESRS S1-17): No justified discrimination cases against own employees in 2024. Reporting definitions and methodologies align with group-level policies.
- Customers (3.2; ESRS S4 SBM-3): Material topics are information security and privacy, quality information, and access to financial products/services, detailed at group level.
- Customer engagement (ESRS S4-2): Regular collection of feedback and customer satisfaction measurement using TRI*M (with NPS and SQM used by some members). Annual nationally representative survey of 1,000 people. Complaint handling is a key engagement tool. The Bank does not regularly cooperate with consumer organizations. A group-wide framework for customer-focused product, process, and service design was established in 2024.
- Channels for raising concerns (ESRS S4-3): Multiple complaint channels (ethics reporting system, website, call center, branches, postal mail; social media inquiries forwarded). Customers can also complain to the Hungarian National Bank. Procedures are regulated, rights-respecting, and non-discriminatory; the Bank seeks prompt resolution and may compensate where justified. Customers are informed about channels through various media, and all data are handled confidentially per law and the Code of Ethics.

nodes.title: Customers
nodes.heading: 3.2. Customers
nodes.start_phrase: The section details the treatment of the material topics: (1) information security and privacy, (2) quality information and (3) access to financial products and services, for which the impacts and the most affected customer groups are detailed in subchapter 3.3. Clients – Material Impacts, Risks in the OTP Group Sustainability Report.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and standards: Section 3.2 (Customers) aligned with ESRS S4, referencing OTP Group Sustainability Report subchapters, especially S4 SBM-3 (material impacts/risks), S4-2 (customer engagement), and S4-3 (channels for concerns).
- Material customer topics: Focus on (1) information security and privacy, (2) quality information, and (3) access to financial products and services; most affected customer groups detailed in the Group report.
- Customer engagement: Regular collection of feedback to improve experience using TRI*M (core), with NPS and SQM for some entities; analysis by customer segment; annual nationally representative survey (~1,000 respondents); complaints used as an engagement input; no regular cooperation with consumer organizations.
- Customer-centric design: A group-wide framework for customer-focused product, process, and service development established in 2024 (details in Group report).
- Complaints and concern-raising channels: Multiple non-discriminatory, rights-aligned, legally compliant avenues—ethics reporting system, website, call center, branches, postal mail; social media inputs routed to complaints; option to submit to the Hungarian National Bank; clear customer communication via website, publications, letters, in-branch policies, and social media; confidentiality per law and Code of Ethics.
- Complaint handling effectiveness: Dedicated system with unique case IDs and assigned owners; customer updates on process and actions; monthly/quarterly/annual reporting on volumes, status, and resolution times; analysis to detect recurring/systemic issues; monitoring of channel use and response times; coordination on multi-customer or high-loss errors.
- Continuous improvement: New complaint-handling platform initiated in 2024 to automate workflows, strengthen process control, shorten processing times, and improve reporting.
- 2024 outcomes: ~178,000 complaints closed; ~101,000 legitimate; 200 ethics reports; no confirmed serious human rights incidents involving customers.
- Business relationship decisions: Bank does not currently require partners to provide complaint channels; decisions to terminate relationships consider all available facts, including impacts on other customers.
- Information security and data protection: Treated as a unified material topic including cyber defense; recognizes high sensitivity of customer data and risks of breaches (financial penalties, customer loss, reputational harm); management anchored in a Security Policy and a Compliance Policy, with continuous enhancement of security systems and workflows.

nodes.title: Information security and data protection
nodes.heading: 3.2.1. Information security and data protection
nodes.start_phrase: This topic includes not only the protection of personal data but also the areas of information security and cyber defense, as these are interconnected topics within the Bank Group.
nodes.summary:
- Complaint handling framework: OTP Bank tracks all complaints in a dedicated system with unique IDs, clear ownership, customer updates, and regular monthly/quarterly/annual reporting on volumes, status, and resolution times. Data analysis identifies recurring/systemic issues, channel usage patterns, and response-time weaknesses. Cross-departmental follow-up occurs for multi-customer errors or major losses.
- Continuous improvement: In 2024, OTP Bank began developing a new complaint-handling platform to automate workflows, enhance process control, speed up processing, and improve reporting.
- 2024 outcomes: Approximately 178,000 complaints were closed, around 101,000 were deemed legitimate; 200 ethics reports were received; no serious customer-related human rights incidents were confirmed.
- Business partner stance: The Bank does not currently require business partners to operate complaint channels. Relationship termination proposals consider all relevant facts, including potential impacts on other customers.
- Information security and data protection: Treated as a material topic encompassing personal data protection, information security, and cyber defense due to high sensitivity and potential for significant customer and bank losses, reputational harm, and regulatory penalties.
- Governance and policies: Security principles are defined by the Security Policy; personal data handling follows the Compliance/Data Protection Policy. Regular training, advanced data security solutions, and integrated data- and consumer-protection oversight are in place. Risks are managed within operational risk via annual Group-level RCSA and scenario analysis. Policies include anti-fraud, security, and data protection (aligned across the Group) and adherence to EU/Hungarian consumer-protection regulations; no significant policy changes in 2024.
- Actions and organization: Fraud topics are overseen by the Executive Steering Committee. In 2024, the Security Directorate reallocated and expanded resources, creating specialized units (Investigation Unit, Fraud Management Support, Anti-Fraud Competence Centre) to reduce customer fraud, accelerate loss reporting, and recover funds. Broader actions include operation of a Cyber Security Centre, investigation of customer damage, customer education/campaigns, and engagement with regulators/professional bodies.
- Results and compliance: No incidents of misuse of personal data at OTP Bank in 2024 (GRI 418-1). Data processing is purpose-driven, necessary, and transparent to customers, with compliance controls in place.
- Targets: Information security and data protection targets are set out in the Group’s Anti-Fraud Strategy.
- Quality information for clients: Providing clear, comprehensible, and compliant product/service information is emphasized to support sound decisions, especially for retail/SME customers and vulnerable groups. Responsible communication is guided by a Group Tone of Voice manual; the Bank supports financial awareness through educational videos and calculators.
- Marketing and awareness policies: A responsible marketing policy and financial awareness strategy ensure accurate, fair, and comprehensive information, aligned with consumer-protection rules and the Group’s communication standards.

nodes.title: Quality information
nodes.heading: 3.2.2. Quality information
nodes.start_phrase: Quality information provision ensures target information and understanding of financial products for all customers.
nodes.summary:
- Information security, fraud management (ESRS S4-4; ESRS S4-5; GRI 418-1)
  - Executive Steering Committee oversees fraud-related issues at the highest management level.
  - Security Directorate reorganized in 2024 with added resources; creation of dedicated anti-fraud units (Investigation Unit, Fraud Management Support Unit, Anti-Fraud Competence Centre).
  - Operation of the Bank’s Cyber Security Centre, customer damage investigation, customer education/campaigns, and regulatory engagement referenced to OTP Group Sustainability Report (section 3.3.1).
  - Data protection processes are purpose-driven, necessity-based, and compliance-checked; customers are informed about personal data processing.
  - No incidents of misuse of personal data in 2024 (GRI 418-1).
  - Targets for information security and data protection are set within the Anti-Fraud Strategy (details in Group report, section 3.3.1).

- Quality information (3.2.2)
  - Impact: Ensures customers understand financial products; critical for retail, SME, and vulnerable groups.
  - Management approach: Highly regulated communications; emphasis on clear, understandable language via Group Tone of Voice manual; education through videos and calculators.
  - Policies (ESRS S4-1): Responsible marketing policy and a financial awareness strategy aligned with Group policies and UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking.
  - Actions (ESRS S4-4): Customer education on products, digital channels, and financial awareness campaigns (aligned with Group approach; details in Group report section 3.3.2).
  - Targets (ESRS S4-5): Comprehensive measurable targets to be set in 2025 to increase financial literacy/confidence, align product portfolios with individual goals, and improve brand/image; quantification to follow; 2024 effectiveness not assessed.

- Access to financial products and services (3.2.3)
  - Impact: Access influences well-being and inclusion; focus on people with disabilities and those in disadvantaged areas/situations; prudent design to protect depositors and avoid over-indebtedness; mortgages support adequate housing.
  - Management approach: Expand digital availability for convenience and broader access; improve online channel literacy; continuous accessibility improvements; offer significant state-supported mortgage options.
  - Policies (ESRS S4-1): Compliance Policy embeds ethical and consumer protection standards; accessibility strategy aligned with Group (details in Group report section 3.3.3).
  - Actions (ESRS S4-4): Accessibility initiatives for visually impaired, deaf/hard of hearing, and disabled customers; public accessibility information provided online; mobile branches; Social Lab; customer-focused product development; subsidized housing loans.

nodes.title: Access to financial products and services
nodes.heading: 3.2.3. Access to financial products and services
nodes.start_phrase: Access to financial products and services can support or hinder customers' well -being and prosperity.
nodes.summary:
- Financial awareness and quality information (ESRS S4): OTP Bank advances a Financial Awareness Strategy aligned with UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking to increase customers’ financial literacy, confidence, and goal-aligned product use. Actions include education on financial products, digital channels, and awareness campaigns. Comprehensive, measurable targets and operationalization will be set in 2025; effectiveness was not assessed in 2024.

- Access to financial products and services (ESRS S4): The Bank treats access as a material topic, expanding digitally available products to improve convenience and reach, including for residents in disadvantaged areas, while offering significant state-supported mortgage options. Policies are anchored in the Compliance Policy and an Accessibility Strategy aligned with Group strategy.

- Actions to enhance access: Physical and digital accessibility initiatives; mobile branches; Social Lab; customer-centric product development; subsidized housing loans; prevention of over-indebtedness. Ongoing engagement with advocacy bodies (SINOSZ, MVGYOSZ). Targets for accessibility and Social Lab to be refined in 2025.

- Disadvantaged areas access points (GRI G4: FS13): OTP’s extensive network supports in-person access; however, branch/ATM density is lower in disadvantaged areas. 2024 data: 57 branches (18%) and 197 ATMs (10%) located in such areas; net change vs. prior year shows branch access points -10%, ATMs +2%.

- Accessibility compliance and targets (EU Directive 2019/882): Goal by June 2025 to equip all branches with disability-support tools (tactile indicators, ticketing systems with physical buttons, induction loops, sign language tablets, mobile ramps, bells) and to expand ATM accessibility (text-to-speech, Braille, large font; aim for full function coverage). Digital channels target WCAG 2.1 Level A; comprehensive accessibility testing planned H1 2025; full accessibility of Internetbank and Mobilbank expected H1 2025. Monitoring via a unified branch database and employee accessibility training.

- 2024 accessibility progress:
  - Branches (317 total): 99.7% wheelchair-accessible; 95.6% with tactile indicators; 83.0% with automatic ticketing and physical buttons; 100% with induction loops, sign-language tablets, and hearing-impaired access.
  - ATMs (1,993 total): 76.3% wheelchair-accessible; 73.0% with Braille and voice module.

- Reporting policy: Group-level S4 reporting definitions, methodologies, and data requirements are applied at the standalone bank level.

- Governance Information – Business Conduct, Compliance, AML/CTF, Anti-corruption:
  - Emphasis on transparency, defined responsibilities, and broad compliance with environmental, social, and regulatory requirements. Employee awareness is promoted through intranet, knowledge management, trainings, events, and a compliance officer network.
  - Impacts, risks, opportunities: Ethical conduct influences stakeholder trust; non-compliance risks fines and reputational harm; AML/CTF lapses risk liquidity and correspondent relationships. Risks are managed via operational risk frameworks, annual Group Risk and Control Self-Assessment, scenario analysis, and an annual AML Risk Assessment with mitigation actions.
  - Policies (aligned with Group and publicly available): Code of Ethics (with Gift Policy), Compliance Policy (including Sanctions, Anti-Corruption, AML/CTF). These constitute the core of corporate culture and business conduct disclosures (ESRS G1-1).

structure.title: Governance Information
structure.heading: 4. Governance Information
structure.start_phrase: During the Group's operations, we put primary focus on transparency, regulation, the definition of internal responsibilities and, thus, the broadest effective compliance with environmental, social and regulatory requirements.
structure.summary:
- Section focus: Governance Information—Business Conduct within OTP Bank’s Integrated Annual Report 2024.
- Core themes: corporate culture and compliance; anti-money laundering (AML); anti-corruption and bribery.
- Purpose and impact: Emphasis on transparency, clear internal responsibilities, and broad compliance with environmental, social, and regulatory requirements; influences stakeholder trust, employee/customer ethics, and investor confidence.
- Risks and consequences: Non-compliance can lead to fines, reputational harm, liquidity issues, and loss of correspondent banking; ethical breaches can trigger dissatisfaction and complaints.
- Employee engagement: Ongoing awareness and training via intranet content, knowledge management, international conferences, e-learning, a compliance officer network, and corporate events.
- Management approach: Adherence to laws, international standards, sanctions; ethical expectations set out in the Code of Ethics; strong AML/CFT focus with prudent practices, robust customer due diligence, and collaboration with authorities and industry bodies.
- Risk management: Operational risk framework with annual Group-level Risk and Control Self-Assessment, scenario analysis, and a dedicated annual AML Risk Assessment leading to mitigation actions.
- Policy framework (ESRS G1-1): Key documents include the Code of Ethics (with Gift Policy), Compliance Policy, Sanctions Policy, Anti-Corruption Policy, and AML/CFT Policy; policies are aligned with Group standards and publicly accessible on the bank’s website under Due Diligence; related Group-level details are referenced in the Sustainability Report.

nodes.title: Business Conduct
nodes.heading: 4.1 Business Conduct
nodes.start_phrase: During the Group's operations, we put primary focus on transparency, regulation, the definition of internal responsibilities and, thus, the broadest effective compliance with environmental, social and regulatory requirements.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: Governance information on business conduct at OTP Bank within the 2024 Integrated Annual Report, structured around three material topics: corporate culture and compliance, anti-money laundering (AML/CFT), and corruption and bribery.
- Approach and culture: Emphasis on transparency, clear internal responsibilities, and broad compliance with environmental, social, and regulatory requirements; ongoing employee communication and education via intranet, knowledge management, conferences, e-learning, compliance officer network, and company events.
- Impacts, risks, opportunities: Ethical business conduct influences stakeholder trust and investor perceptions; AML is critical to prevent misuse of banking services; non-compliance risks include fines, reputational damage, liquidity issues, and potential loss of correspondent banking relationships; ethics violations can drive dissatisfaction and complaints.
- Management and risk control: Compliance with laws, international standards, sanctions, and ethical norms anchored by the Code of Ethics; continuous compliance awareness; AML/CFT due diligence and cooperation with authorities; risks managed under operational risk with annual Group-level Risk and Control Self-Assessment, scenario analysis, and a dedicated annual AML Risk Assessment informing mitigation actions.
- Policies (ESRS G1-1): Key policies include the Code of Ethics, Compliance Policy (incorporating Sanctions, Anti-Corruption, and AML/CFT policies), and a Gift Policy; all aligned with OTP Group policies and publicly accessible under Due Diligence information; detailed descriptions referenced to the OTP Group Sustainability Report.
- Actions and targets: Operation of ethics reporting and whistleblowing systems, ethics and anti-corruption training and awareness, AML whistleblowing processes—aligned with OTP Group programs.
- Corruption and bribery: Zero tolerance policy supported by a comprehensive program; risk-based assessments, reporting channels via the Code of Ethics and Partner Code, and investigations under the whistleblowing system; training integrated into ethics training; governance reporting mechanisms described.
- Outcomes (ESRS G1-4): No confirmed cases of corruption or bribery in the reporting period; no related fines.
- Regulatory proceedings (GRI 2-27): In 2024, 83 closed cases, 41 with fines totaling HUF 128.44 million; primary fines from supervisory procedures (HUF 112m) and consumer protection (HUF 15.5m); no fines for competition, anti-corruption, or data protection; one health and safety fine (HUF 0.34m); most fines pertain to 2024 practices.
- Reporting policy: Governance data definitions, methodologies, and calculations follow group-level practices as outlined in the OTP Group Sustainability Report.
