- ESRS Index: Mapping of disclosure requirements (sESRS 2, GOV, SBM, IRO, E1–E4) to report sections (“General information,” “Environmental information”); some items noted as “not yet reported due to phased introduction” (e.g., E1-9, E3-5); cross-references to the OTP Group Sustainability Report for further detail.

structure.title: ESRS Index
structure.heading: 5. ESRS Index
structure.start_phrase: sESRS 2 General disclosures BP-1 General basis for preparing sustainability statements General information
structure.summary:
- The section compiles an ESRS Index mapping each disclosure requirement to where it appears in the report (General, Environmental, Social, or Governance information), whether it is not relevant, or deferred due to phased introduction, and notes cross-references to the OTP Group Sustainability Report.
- ESRS 2 General disclosures are covered, including governance roles (GOV-1 to GOV-5), incentive linkage to sustainability (GOV-3), due diligence (GOV-4), controls over sustainability reporting (GOV-5), strategy and business model (SBM-1 to SBM-3), and materiality processes (IRO-1, IRO-2), largely under General information.
- Climate (ESRS E1) disclosures include a transition plan, policies, actions/resources, targets, Scope 1–3 emissions, GHG intensity, carbon credits/removals, and internal carbon pricing under Environmental information; expected financial impacts of climate risks/opportunities (E1-9) are not yet reported due to phase-in; certain sector-specific datapoints (e.g., fossil energy use breakdown in high-impact sectors, real estate energy class breakdown) are marked not relevant.
- Pollution (ESRS E2) and Resource use & circular economy (ESRS E5) focus on materiality processes; PRTR pollutant emissions (E2-4) are deemed not relevant.
- Water and marine resources (ESRS E3) cover policies, actions/resources, and targets; financial impact disclosures (E3-5) are deferred due to phase-in.
- Biodiversity and ecosystems (ESRS E4) include transition planning/strategy integration, policies, actions/resources, and targets under Environmental information.
- Own workforce (ESRS S1) covers policies, engagement, grievance mechanisms, actions/effectiveness, targets, workforce characteristics, diversity, health & safety, income, and incidents; several indicators are deferred (non-employee data, disability, training, work-life balance).
- Consumers and end-users (ESRS S4) include policies, engagement, grievance channels, actions/effectiveness, and targets under Social information; an entity-specific GRI G4 FS13 disclosure on access points in disadvantaged areas is included.
- Business conduct (ESRS G1) addresses culture and conduct policies, anti-corruption and bribery prevention, and confirmed cases, presented under Governance information, linked to governance roles and materiality processes.
- A separate “List of data points from EU legislation” maps specific mandated datapoints to their status and location: governance composition metrics and due diligence are referenced to the OTP Group Sustainability Report; participation in certain controversial sectors is marked not relevant; climate neutrality transition plan and benchmark-related exclusions are cross-referenced; GHG reduction targets, energy consumption, Scope 1–3 emissions, intensity, and carbon credits are reported; several climate-related financial risk/opportunity exposures are deferred due to phase-in.

structure.title: List of data points from EU legislation
structure.heading: 6. List of data points from EU legislation
structure.start_phrase: ESRS 2 GOV -1 Gender breakdown in the Board of Directors para 21. point d) OTP Group sustainability report
structure.summary:
- The excerpt is a Management Report section of the Integrated Annual Report 2024 that maps European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) disclosure requirements to OTP Bank’s available data, where they appear in the report, external references (notably the OTP Group Sustainability Report), and notes on relevance or phase-in status.

- Governance (ESRS 2, G1):
  - Board composition: gender breakdown and share of independent directors referenced to the OTP Group Sustainability Report.
  - Due diligence statement referenced to the OTP Group Sustainability Report.
  - Anti-corruption: commitments under the UN Convention Against Corruption; reporting of fines and standards disclosed under Governance information; whistleblower protection marked not relevant in the table.
  
- Strategy and business model (ESRS 2 SBM):
  - Participation in controversial sectors (fossil fuels, chemicals, disputed weapons, tobacco) listed; several marked not relevant.
  - Risks of forced and child labour in own operations disclosed under Social information; significant risks in the value chain marked not relevant.

- Climate (ESRS E1):
  - 2050 climate neutrality transition plan and Paris-aligned benchmark exclusions referenced.
  - GHG targets, Scope 1–3 emissions, gross GHG intensity, and carbon credits disclosed under Environmental information.
  - Energy consumption/structure and intensity disclosures noted; some items not relevant.
  - Portfolio exposure to physical climate risks, asset locations, and climate-related opportunities not yet reported due to phase-in; real estate energy efficiency class breakdown not relevant.

- Pollution (ESRS E2):
  - PRTR-listed pollutant emissions marked not relevant.

- Water and marine resources (ESRS E3):
  - Policies and sustainable oceans/seas disclosures included under Environmental information.
  - Total water consumption intensity reported; water recycling/reuse not relevant.

- Biodiversity and ecosystems (ESRS 2–IRO1–E4, ESRS E4):
  - Some impact, risk, and opportunity disclosures listed as environmental information or not relevant.
  - Policies on sustainable land/agriculture, oceans/seas, and deforestation referenced.

- Resource use and circular economy (ESRS E5):
  - Non-recycled waste not relevant; hazardous/radioactive waste listed.

- Social topics (ESRS S1–S4):
  - Own workforce: human rights and ILO commitment policies, accident prevention, grievance mechanisms, H&S metrics (fatalities, accident rates, days lost), gender pay gap, CEO pay ratio, and discrimination incidents disclosed under Social information; anti-trafficking and certain UNGP/OECD non-respect items marked not relevant.
  - Value chain workers and affected communities: many policy and incident disclosures marked not relevant.
  - Consumers/end-users: policies and incident reporting included under Social information.

- Detailed anti-corruption and bribery program:
  - Zero-tolerance stance codified in the Code of Ethics, Partner Code of Ethics, and Group Anti-Corruption Policy; all publicly available.
  - Whistleblowing system in place (anonymous reporting possible). In 2024: 200 reports received, 44 led to proceedings, 12 ethical breaches confirmed.
  - Mandatory training and acceptance of the Code for all employees; anti-corruption expectations communicated to partners.
  - Since 2023, anti-corruption clauses embedded in business rules and standard contracts, allowing contract termination upon breach.
  - Human-rights-related third-party requests prioritized.
  - Corruption/bribery risks managed within operational risk processes; quarterly compliance reporting to the Executive Steering Committee and Board of Directors; annual reporting to the Supervisory Board.

structure.title: Fight against corruption and against the practice of bribery
structure.heading: Fight against corruption and against the practice of bribery
structure.start_phrase: The Code of Ethics ( https://www.otpbank.hu/static/portal/sw/file/OTP_EtikaiKodex_EN.pdf ) , the Partner Code of Ethics ( https://www.otpbank.hu/static/portal/sw/file/OTP_Partneri_EtikaiKodex_EN.pdf ) published in 2023 and the Anti -Corruption Policy of OTP Bank Group, approved in 2019, contains provisions on the fight against corruption and against the practice of bribery, as well as the enforcement of legal, fair and ethical conduct (https://www.otpgroup.info/ethical -declaration ).
structure.summary:
- Focus area: OTP Bank Plc.’s anti-corruption and anti-bribery framework and non-financial performance indicators for 2024 within the Management Report (Stand-Alone) of the Integrated Annual Report.
- Governance and policies:
  - Zero tolerance for corruption and bribery affirmed in the Code of Ethics, Partner Code of Ethics (published 2023), and Group Anti-Corruption Policy (2019), all publicly available.
  - Ethical, legal, and fair conduct emphasized; employees receive training and must accept the Code as a condition of employment.
  - Business partners are informed of anti-corruption expectations; since 2023, standard contracts and business rules include explicit anti-corruption clauses with potential contract termination for breaches.
  - Partner selection based on professionalism, competence, and competitiveness; heightened prudence in tendering/preparation stages to minimize corruption risks.
  - Human-rights-related third-party requests are treated as priority.
- Whistleblowing and ethics:
  - Anonymous ethics reporting system in place; investigations conducted to detect and prevent anomalies.
  - 2024 outcomes: 200 ethics reports received; 44 cases proceeded to ethics proceedings; 12 ethics breaches established.
- Risk management and reporting:
  - Corruption and bribery risks managed within operational risk processes.
  - Quarterly compliance reports on risk changes and mitigation steps submitted to the Executive Steering Committee and Board of Directors; annual report also to the Supervisory Board.
- Non-financial performance indicators (2024):
  - Internal audit: 208 audits closed; 1,193 recommendations issued and all accepted.
  - Compliance with Budapest Stock Exchange recommendations: 72 yes, 0 no.
  - Compliance investigations: 11 data and consumer-protection cases closed.
  - Bank security: 1,049 reports, 20 report additions, 356 notifications; 889 fraud suspicions, 39 money-laundering suspicions, 122 other crimes.
  - Fraud/abuse trends and impacts:
    - Financial abuse related to housing loans noted at approximately HUF 41 million.
    - Personal loan fraud losses rose from HUF 22 million (2023) to HUF 39 million (2024).
    - No losses in 2024 related to overdrafts, baby loans, home loans, and CSOK applications.
    - Corporate credit fraud losses (MSE/MLE) fell from HUF 4.7 billion (2023) to HUF 1.2 billion (2024).
    - Online fraud against customers: damage from cash-flow misuse down 32% to HUF 7.2 billion; preventive measures averted HUF 21.7 billion (vs. HUF 6.5 billion in 2023).
    - Card fraud: declines in attempts and successful values; successful misuse totaled HUF 3.5 billion (HUF 3.2 billion on OTP-issued cards). Fraud-to-sales ratio decreased to 0.0253%, below the European average of 0.0407%.
  - Ethics statistics reiterated: 200 ethics reports with 12 confirmed offenses.

structure.title: Non-financial performance indicators
structure.heading: Non-financial performance indicators
structure.start_phrase: • Internal audit: 208 closed audits, 1,193 recommendations, 1,193 accepted recommendations.
structure.summary: The excerpt from the 2024 Integrated Annual Report’s Management Report summarizes OTP Bank’s non-financial performance and external audit-related services. It reports strong internal governance and compliance metrics: 208 internal audits with 1,193 recommendations all accepted; full adherence to Budapest Stock Exchange recommendations (72 yes, 0 no); and 11 closed data and consumer protection investigations. Bank security activity included 1,049 reports (889 suspected fraud, 39 suspected money laundering, 122 other crimes), with detailed fraud loss trends: an increase in personal loan fraud losses (HUF 22m in 2023 to HUF 39m in 2024) and about HUF 41m in housing loan-related financial abuse, but no losses in overdrafts, baby loans, home loans, or CSOK applications. Corporate credit fraud losses in the MSE/MLE segments fell sharply (HUF 4.7bn in 2023 to HUF 1.2bn in 2024). Customer losses from online fraud declined 32% to HUF 7.2bn, while preventive measures averted HUF 21.7bn (over triple the prior year). Bank card fraud decreased relative to peers; successful misuse totaled HUF 3.5bn (HUF 3.2bn on OTP-issued cards), and the fraud-to-sales ratio dropped to 0.0253%, below the European average of 0.0407%. Ethics oversight recorded 200 reports with 12 confirmed offenses. The section also lists non-audit services provided by Ernst & Young alongside the statutory audit, including ISAE 3000 assurance, forensic/fraud advisory, comfort letters, ISRS 4400 agreed-upon procedures, accounting standards consultations (including for potential future transactions), reviews of internal processes and legal/regulatory compliance, and general trainings on accounting regulation changes.

structure.title: LIST OF NON-AUDIT SERVICES BY SERVICE CATEGORIES USED BY THE BANK
structure.heading: LIST OF NON-AUDIT SERVICES BY SERVICE CATEGORIES USED BY THE BANK
structure.start_phrase: The statutory audit of OTP Bank is carried out by Ernst and Young Ltd ., in addition to which the following services were contracted:
structure.summary:
- External auditor and non‑audit services: Ernst & Young Ltd. performs the statutory audit; additional contracted services include ISAE 3000 assurance, forensic/fraud advisory, comfort letters, ISRS 4400 AUP, accounting standards consultations (including on potential transactions), internal process and compliance reviews, and general accounting regulation trainings.

- Sustainability statement basis: Prepared on a consolidated basis for 2024 under ESRS and EU Taxonomy Article 8; consolidation mirrors financial statements except ESRS E1‑6 datapoint on assets under operational control. XHTML/ESEF tagging not applied as sustainability taxonomy not yet adopted.

- Value chain coverage: Materiality assessment extends to upstream and downstream; current metrics include Scope 1–3 GHGs; plans to develop value‑chain metrics for water (E3) and biodiversity (E4) from 2025 as data availability improves.

- Reporting assumptions and uncertainties: Defined time horizons (short 1 year, medium +2 years, long >3 years); disclosures on estimates and uncertainties accompany metrics; restatement applied in EU Taxonomy chapter; uses GRI Standards 2021, GRI G4 Financial Services indicators, and entity‑specific indicators where relevant.

- Governance structure: Board of Directors, Supervisory Board, Audit Committee, and 17 permanent/special committees; disclosed composition and diversity; annual collective suitability reviews ensure requisite expertise and diversity.

- ESG governance: Board‑approved Group ESG strategy; ESG Committee (decision‑making support) and ESG Sub‑Committee (coordination/implementation) established; quarterly ESG reporting to the Board and annual reporting to the Supervisory Board; ESG coordination exists at subsidiaries.

- Security and compliance: Security Directorate oversees information/security policy and reports annually; Anti‑Money Laundering Committee handles high‑risk relationships and AML/CFT oversight; Code of Ethics and Compliance Policy approved by the Board.

- Training and competence: Regular ESG and ethics training for governing bodies and executives; broad 2023 ESG e‑learning for ~360 leaders; suitability assessments include sustainability skills.

- Business conduct oversight: Ethics Committee handles ethics cases (including group‑level matters) and guidance; AML Committee monitors AML/CFT performance and risk measures; mandatory ethics and leadership training supports competence.

- Information flows to governing bodies: Regular reporting through ESG, Compliance, Security, and HR channels; 2024 topics included climate mitigation/adaptation, energy risks, diversity, workplace violence/harassment, data protection, access to finance, AML/compliance, corruption/bribery, information security, health protection/safety.

- Remuneration and incentives: Non‑executive board members receive fixed fees; executives under the Remuneration Policy have performance‑based pay with mandatory ESG‑CSR indicator (generally 4–5% weight) covering ESG goals, integration, awareness, and reporting quality; climate aspects included within ESG‑CSR, but no explicit GHG targets in pay; additional indicators include risk appetite limits and control effectiveness.

- Due diligence approach: Elements embedded via governance, committees, stakeholder engagement, policies, actions, and metrics aligned with ESRS; impact identification for this report performed separately.

- Sustainability reporting controls and assurance: Central coordination by Marketing & Communications; internal controls, Sustainability Data Collection Platform with four‑eyes checks and automated validations; interim data collection; Steering Committee oversight; Board/Supervisory Board approvals; 2024 statement subject to limited assurance; performance incentives include data quality/timeliness.

- Business model and footprint: Universal banking group serving ~17 million clients across 10 CEE countries plus Uzbekistan; 2024 consolidated revenue HUF 4,276 bn; 48.5% of assets in Hungary; active bond issuance (including MREL); diversified lending (mortgage, consumer, corporate, SME, leasing); non‑financial subsidiaries in real estate, agriculture, and private equity; 43,118 employees.

- Value chain description: Upstream dominated by services (marketing, IT, telecom); real estate and agri units have higher environmental impacts (materials, energy, raw inputs). Downstream includes 13,700 agents; most significant impacts via lending; asset management downstream relates to managed assets; real estate tenants and agri/food longer chains noted.

- ESG strategy (2021–2025): Three pillars—responsible service provider, responsible employer, responsible social actor; annual reviews with unchanged vision/mission in 2024.

- Key targets and 2024 progress:
  - Green lending: HUF 1,500 bn target by 2025; HUF 1,027 bn achieved by end‑2024 (on track).
  - Employee engagement: Group score 77% (up 5 pp), meeting financial sector benchmark target but not global benchmark.
  - Own operations emissions: Carbon neutral since 2022 via partial offsets; OTP Bank net‑zero Scope 1–2 target by 2030.
  - External recognition: Aim to join S&P Dow Jones Sustainability Index by 2025; S&P Global CSA score improved by 9% (4 points) in 2023.

structure.title: ESG Strategy
structure.heading: ESG Strategy
structure.start_phrase: Stability and sustainability are two of the cornerstones of OTP Group's corporate strategy.
structure.summary:
- Section outlines OTP Group’s ESG Strategy within the 2024 Integrated Annual Report, reaffirming the 2021–2025 strategy approved in 2021; reviewed annually and unchanged in 2024.
- Strategic ambition: play a regional leading role in financing a fair, gradual transition to a low‑carbon economy; target green loan portfolio of HUF 1,500 billion by 2025.
- Core approach: ensure long‑term sustainability through responsible, transparent governance; act as a responsible employer; engage actively in society; provide fair, needs‑based financial services; and minimize environmental impacts.
- Three strategic pillars: responsible service provider, responsible employer, and responsible social actor.
- Vision/Mission: make ethical, socially and environmentally adequate financial solutions accessible across OTP’s CEE and Central Asia footprint; take responsibility for economic, social, and environmental impacts via pioneering, ethical operations and partnerships.
- Operationalization: integrate ESG topics across relevant departments by 2025; address business opportunities, significant risk management, and social/governance objectives.
- 2024 KPI results:
  - Responsible service provider: progress toward HUF 1,500 billion green loans by 2025; achieved HUF 1,027 billion in 2024, meeting/exceeding the annual target; active ESG risk management and sustainable investment offerings.
  - Responsible employer: focus on wellbeing, development, diversity, and engagement; Group engagement reached 77% (up 5 pp), meeting the financial sector benchmark (75th percentile) but below the global benchmark target (78%).
  - Responsible social actor: continued achievement of carbon neutrality (partly via verified credits) since end‑2022; target net zero Scope 1–2 emissions for OTP Bank by 2030; aim to join the S&P Dow Jones Sustainability Index by 2025; S&P Global CSA score improved by 9% (4 points) in 2023 year‑on‑year.
- Notes clarify definitions (green loans, carbon neutrality vs. net zero) and benchmarking/methodology for engagement and sustainability assessments.

nodes.title: Vision
nodes.heading: Vision
nodes.start_phrase: Responsible financial decisions and socially and environmentally adequate, ethical financial solutions are available for all economic participants and citizens in all of the countries covered by OTP Group’s operations.
nodes.summary:
- Section outlines OTP Group’s ESG strategy (2021–2025), reaffirmed in 2024 and reviewed annually to reflect market and regulatory changes.
- Strategic aim: lead regionally in financing a fair, gradual transition to a low‑carbon economy; target green loan portfolio of HUF 1,500 billion by 2025.
- Governance and ethos: emphasize long-term sustainability, transparency, ethical operations, responsible governance, employee responsibility, stakeholder trust, and reducing environmental impacts across CEE and Central Asia.
- Three strategic pillars:
  - Responsible service provider: green transition financing, sustainable investment products, active ESG risk management.
  - Responsible employer: enhance wellbeing, development, diversity, and employee engagement.
  - Responsible social actor: cut operational emissions; contribute to social goals and the UN SDGs via products, services, and donations.
- Integration goal: embed ESG topics into relevant business units by 2025, addressing opportunities, significant risks, and social/governance targets.
- 2024 KPI results:
  - Green loans: HUF 1,027 billion, meeting/exceeding the 2024 milestone toward the HUF 1,500 billion 2025 target.
  - Employee engagement: 77% at Group level, up 5 p.p.; meets financial sector benchmark (75th percentile) but not global benchmark (78%).
  - Climate targets: carbon neutrality (partially via verified carbon credits) achieved since end-2022; OTP Bank net zero (Scope 1–2) by 2030.
  - External recognition: aim to join S&P Dow Jones Sustainability Index by 2025; S&P Global Corporate Sustainability Assessment score improved 9% (4 points) in 2023.

nodes.title: Mission
nodes.heading: Mission
nodes.start_phrase: For us, sustainability means taking responsibility for our economic, social, and environmental impacts.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines OTP Group’s ESG Strategy (2021–2025): stability and sustainability as core pillars; annually reviewed and unchanged in 2024; goal to embed ESG across relevant departments by 2025, covering opportunities, risks, and social/governance targets.
- Vision and mission emphasize accessible, ethical, environmentally and socially responsible finance across CEE and Central Asia, with value creation through pioneering, transparent, and ethical operations.
- Three strategic pillars: responsible service provider, responsible employer, responsible social actor.
- Key targets and 2024 results:
  - Green lending: HUF 1,500 billion target by 2025; HUF 1,027 billion achieved by 2024.
  - Employee engagement: target at 75th percentile of financial sector and globally (78%); achieved 77%—meets sector benchmark, not global.
  - Emissions: carbon neutrality (via verified credits) achieved by end-2022; OTP Bank net zero Scope 1–2 targeted by 2030.
  - Market recognition: aim to join S&P Dow Jones Sustainability Index by 2025; S&P Global CSA score up 9% (+4 points) in 2023.
- All subsidiary banks now have aligned ESG strategies (including Russia, Ukraine, Moldova approved in 2024) with goals/KPIs on ESG risk, green lending, organizational frameworks, social issues, and operational environmental impacts; Board receives annual updates.
- Green financing approach integrated across business lines so any sector/client with a sustainable objective can access green terms over time; priority sectors: energy (renewables, distribution, storage), real estate (green properties, energy-efficient renovations), and transportation (electromobility).
- Highlights major challenge: collecting, evaluating, and integrating client sustainability data amid expanding regulatory/business needs; client readiness is heterogeneous; calls for IT prioritization to meet reporting, risk, and business requirements across retail, corporate, and control functions.
- Stakeholder commitments (ESRS 2 SBM-2): meeting needs of clients, investors, and employees; acting as a responsible partner per the three pillars; Code of Ethics mandates ethical conduct for employees and agents; continuous engagement to inform strategy and ensure social legitimacy and business success.
- Governance: ESG strategy approved by the Management Committee; progress and plans reviewed annually with Board oversight.
- Cross-references to definitions and disclosures (e.g., green loan portfolio definition and green lending target reporting).

nodes.title: Green Financing
nodes.heading: Green Financing
nodes.start_phrase: The details of green financing are presented in the @Green lending target disclosure requirements.
nodes.summary:
- All OTP Group subsidiary banks have approved ESG strategies by 2024, aligned with OTP Bank’s objectives. These cover ESG risk management, development of green lending, organizational setup, social topics, and reducing operational environmental impacts. Subsidiaries set KPIs, and the Board of Directors is informed on progress with annual plan reviews.
- Green financing is integrated across the Group, aiming to offer green lending to any client with a sustainable goal; maturity varies by country, sector, and segment. Priority sectors include energy (renewables, distribution, storage), real estate (green construction/purchase and energy‑efficient renovations), and transportation (e‑mobility). Detailed targets are referenced in the Green lending target disclosure.
- Key challenges center on acquiring, assessing, integrating, and reporting clients’ sustainability data. Client readiness is uneven but improving; many lacked prior measurement systems and expertise. Forthcoming regulatory and business demands will impact retail and corporate lending, risk, controlling, internal/external reporting, requiring prioritized IT solutions to meet obligations and manage climate‑related risks and opportunities.
- Stakeholder approach (ESRS 2 SBM‑2): Corporate strategy focuses on meeting the expectations of clients, investors, and employees. The ESG strategy rests on three pillars—responsible service provider, responsible employer, and responsible social actor. The Code of Ethics mandates ethical conduct for employees and agents representing the Group. Engagement is tailored by entity and stakeholder group, with continuous feedback informing strategy and ensuring social legitimacy and business success.

nodes.title: Challenges
nodes.heading: Challenges
nodes.start_phrase: One of the significant challenges for OTP Group in sustainable finance is understanding, collecting, evaluating, integrating into internal processes, and reporting on the sustainability performance, plans, and strategies of its clients.
nodes.summary:
- Groupwide ESG strategy adoption: By 2024 all OTP subsidiary banks (including Russia, Ukraine, Moldova) have approved ESG strategies aligned with OTP Bank’s objectives, covering ESG risk management, green lending development, organizational frameworks, social topics, and operational environmental impact mitigation, with KPIs set and annual Board oversight.
- Green financing approach: OTP Group integrates climate-conscious lending across business lines, aiming to offer green loan terms to any client with a sustainable objective, with maturity varying by country, sector, and segment. Key green lending sectors: energy (renewables, distribution, storage), real estate (green construction/purchase and energy‑efficient renovations), and transportation (electro-mobility). Detailed targets appear in the Green lending target disclosure requirements.
- Data and process challenges: Major hurdle is gathering, evaluating, and integrating client sustainability data for internal use and external reporting; client readiness is uneven due to historic lack of measurement systems. Forthcoming regulatory and business needs will affect retail/corporate lending, risk management, controlling, and reporting across parent and subsidiaries, requiring prioritized IT solutions to meet obligations and manage climate-related risks/opportunities.
- Stakeholder focus (ESRS 2 SBM‑2): Corporate strategy centers on meeting client, investor, and employee expectations. The ESG strategy is built on three pillars—responsible service provider, responsible employer, responsible social actor. The Code of Ethics mandates ethical conduct toward stakeholders (including agents/contracted partners). Continuous stakeholder engagement informs strategy development to ensure social legitimacy and business success.

nodes.title: Stakeholders
nodes.heading: Stakeholders
nodes.start_phrase: The goal stated in OTP Group's corporate strategy in OTP Group’s Management Report is to meet the needs and expectations of its clients, investors, and employees at the highest possible level.
nodes.summary:
- Groupwide ESG strategies: By 2024, all OTP Group subsidiary banks have approved ESG strategies aligned with OTP Bank’s objectives. These cover ESG risk management, green lending development, organizational frameworks, social topics, and reducing operational environmental impacts, with defined KPIs and annual reporting to the Board of Directors.

- Green financing approach: OTP Group integrates climate‑conscious lending across its business, aiming to offer green terms to any client with sustainable goals. Maturity varies by country, sector, and segment. Priority sectors include energy (renewables, distribution, storage), real estate (green construction/purchases and energy‑efficiency renovations), and transportation (e‑mobility). Further details are provided in the Green lending target disclosure.

- Key challenges: A major hurdle is obtaining and integrating credible sustainability data from clients, whose readiness is uneven due to historical lack of measurement systems and expertise. Forthcoming obligations will affect retail and corporate lending, risk management, internal controls/reporting, and external disclosures across the Group. Prioritized IT enhancements are critical to meet regulation and manage climate‑related risks and opportunities.

- Stakeholder framework (ESRS 2 SBM‑2): The ESG strategy commits to being a responsible service provider, employer, and social actor, underpinned by the Code of Ethics. The Group actively engages stakeholders—especially clients, investors, employees, and regulators—using surveys, market research, educational content, multi‑channel service and complaint handling (clients); reports, meetings, and Q&A (investors/analysts/shareholders); engagement surveys, performance reviews, and social dialogue (employees); and regulatory reporting and industry consultations (authorities). While stakeholder views on the strategy/business model were not explored in materiality and due diligence, stakeholder opinions are detailed under IRO‑1.

- Governance oversight of stakeholder feedback and ESG: The Board, Supervisory Board, and committees receive regular updates, including: group‑level employee engagement results; semi‑annual customer complaint handling and supervisory investigations (Hungary and foreign subsidiaries); quarterly status on regulatory investigations and recommendation implementation; internal audit reports reviewed before submission to the supervisor; and quarterly progress reports on ESG strategy implementation to the Board.

- Materiality assessment (ESRS 2, E1–E5, G1 IRO‑1): Conducted to identify impacts, risks, and opportunities for the Sustainability Statement, focusing on determining topic materiality and tailoring the depth of analysis accordingly.

nodes.title: Materiality Assessment
nodes.heading: 1.4. Materiality Assessment
nodes.start_phrase: The purpose of the materiality assessment is to enable OTP Group to identify the impacts, risks, and opportunities to be presented in the Sustainability Statement.
nodes.summary:
- Stakeholder engagement: Identifies key stakeholder groups (customers/clients, shareholders/bondholders and analysts, employees, regulators/authorities), their engagement purposes (e.g., service quality, transparent financial/ESG disclosure, employee well-being and safety, compliance and green finance), and methods (surveys, market research, reports and presentations, general meetings, customer service and complaint handling, internal communications, consultations with authorities and associations).
- Governance oversight of stakeholder matters: Board of Directors and Supervisory Board receive regular, structured updates, including semi-annual reports on customer complaints and consumer protection cases, quarterly reports on regulatory investigations and implementation of supervisory recommendations, approval of MNB-mandated internal audit reports, and quarterly ESG strategy progress updates; governing bodies can access committee and departmental materials.
- Note on scope of stakeholder input in materiality/due diligence: While stakeholder opinions are important overall, the ESRS-aligned materiality assessment and due diligence did not explore stakeholder views specifically on the strategy and business model (with further detail referenced under IRO-1).
- ESRS-aligned materiality assessment: Purpose is to identify impacts, risks, and opportunities for the Sustainability Statement and determine material topics; methodology developed per ESRS, leveraging existing OTP Group processes (@ESG organization, strategy, and risk management).
- Methodological evolution and cadence: Builds on prior GRI-based analyses (latest in early 2022 covering impact and financial materiality); the current ESRS-based approach is significantly expanded and will be reviewed annually, next in 2025.
- Identification of impacts: Companies grouped by activity sector to map own and value-chain impacts—three relevant sectors defined: financial services (most significant), real estate (development/operation/ownership serving external parties), and agriculture/food industry.
- Topic universe and OTP-specific additions: Long list compiled from ESRS topics plus GRI 2021, GRESB Real Estate criteria, UNEP FI Consumer Banking, regulatory expectations, prior assessments, and benchmarks; OTP-specific topics added include Taxation, Financial awareness, Community engagement, Attitude shaping, Privacy/information security/cybersecurity, and Corporate culture/compliance/anti–money laundering.
- Evaluation criteria and process: Impacts ranked using severity (scale, scope, irreversibility) and likelihood for negative impacts, and scale/scope (plus likelihood for potential) for positive impacts; long list narrowed to a short list of potentially material impacts; scoring conducted via a multi-round, iterative process with internal experts, banking group managers, external experts, and stakeholders.

nodes.title: Identification and Evaluation of Impacts
nodes.heading: Identification and Evaluation of Impacts
nodes.start_phrase: During the materiality assessment, OTP Group focused on factors associated with an increased risk of adverse impacts.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Describes OTP Group’s ESRS-aligned methodology for identifying and evaluating sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities, integrated with existing ESG organization, strategy, and risk management. Detailed risk processes are reported under separate ESG risk management disclosures.

- Updated materiality approach: Replaces the 2022 GRI-based materiality with a significantly revised, ESRS-driven methodology. The assessment will be reviewed annually, next in 2025. A process diagram (not shown here) illustrates methods and decision-making.

- Identification of impacts: Companies grouped by activity sector—financial services (primary), real estate (external-facing assets), and agriculture/food industry. A long list of topics was built from ESRS, GRI 2021, GRESB Real Estate, UNEP FI Consumer Banking, regulatory expectations, prior assessments, and benchmarks, then tailored with OTP-specific topics: Taxation; Financial awareness; Community engagement; Attitude shaping; Privacy/information security/cybersecurity; Corporate culture/compliance/anti–money laundering.

- Evaluation criteria and thresholds:
  - Negative impacts: assessed on scale, scope, irreversibility; potential impacts also include likelihood.
  - Positive impacts: assessed on scale, scope; potential impacts include likelihood (reversibility not applied).
  - Scoring uses a 0–5 scale per criterion (max 15 for negative impacts). Any criterion scored at 5 renders the impact material. Topics become material if at least one linked impact scores ≥9.
  - Evaluated over the time horizon when severity is expected to peak.
  - Topics assessed at ESRS subtopic or sub-subtopic level where relevant to OTP.

- Process and data: Multi-round, iterative scoring involving internal experts, Banking Group managers, external experts, and stakeholders. Used objective internal data (including prior sustainability reports) and accepted sector views to ensure consistency and comparability via standardized scoring.

- Portfolio and sector methods: For the loan portfolio, impacts were estimated using NACE-based activity mapping; due to lack of a direct ESRS mapping, multiple sources were synthesized. Sector-level materiality applied for agriculture and real estate where topics were not material group-wide.

- Climate focus: Assessed GHG emissions across own operations and value chain—Scope 1–2 data available; partial 2023 Scope 3 data for the loan portfolio and investment fund management. References to Climate Change disclosures and OTP Group Annual Report 2023. Considered the organization’s example-setting role in evaluations.

- Other environmental topics: Pollution, resource use/circular economy, and biodiversity assessed similarly across own operations and the value chain. Notes that some agricultural subsidiaries (Agromag Plusz Kft., Nemesszalóki Mezőgazdasági Zrt.) operate in/near Natura 2000 areas and manage impacts in compliance with nature conservation and environmental regulations, including required reporting.

- Stakeholder input: Diverse stakeholder sources were used to capture expectations and inform the identification and evaluation of material impacts.

nodes.title: Consultation with Stakeholders
nodes.heading: Consultation with Stakeholders
nodes.start_phrase: We used various sources to understand the opinions and expectations of stakeholders, which were considered during the identification and evaluation of material impacts.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Describes OTP Group’s approach to assessing material sustainability impacts and related financial risks and opportunities for the Integrated Annual Report 2024, aligned to ESRS topics down to subtopic/sub-subtopic level where relevant.
- Impact materiality methodology:
  - Data sources: Prior sustainability reports, internal information, and generally accepted professional views on sectoral impacts.
  - Scoring: For negative impacts, a 0–5 scale for scale, scope, and reversibility (max 15). Any characteristic scoring 5 makes the impact material regardless of other scores. For positive impacts, reversibility not assessed, requiring a higher overall effect to meet materiality.
  - Thresholds: A sustainability topic is material if at least one assigned impact scores ≥9. Impacts are evaluated over the period of greatest expected severity.
  - Granularity: ESRS sub-subtopics used where ESRS defines them and where OTP can separate the impact accordingly.
- Portfolio and sector assessment:
  - Loan portfolio impacts estimated via financed companies’ NACE codes; due to lack of a clear ESRS-to-sector mapping, sectors were identified by synthesizing multiple sources and industry impact knowledge.
  - Sector-level materiality considered for agriculture and real estate where group-level materiality does not apply.
- Thematic assessments:
  - Climate: GHG emissions used; Scope 1–2 data available; partial 2023 Scope 3 data for the loan portfolio and fund management; reference to Climate Change disclosures and the 2023 Annual Report; consideration of “setting an example” in impact evaluation.
  - Pollution, resource use, and circular economy: Assessed across own operations and value chain; no further investigation beyond this approach.
  - Biodiversity: Same approach across operations and value chain; notes agricultural subsidiaries operating in/near Natura 2000 areas (Agromag Plusz Kft., Nemesszalóki Mezőgazdasági Zrt.) and their compliance with nature protection and reporting obligations.
- Stakeholder engagement:
  - Inputs included ESG assessments/questionnaires (Sustainalytics, MSCI, Moody’s), cross-country residential TRI*M brand/satisfaction research, and a 2023 employee engagement survey (28,990 responses).
  - Targeted online stakeholder questionnaire (civil organizations, academia, authorities/supervisors/public administration, financial analysts/stock exchanges, media, employee representatives) for impact materiality; financial analysts/stock exchanges also consulted on financial materiality.
  - Outcomes: Employees’ work-life balance added as a material topic based on feedback (over one-third rated it material). Same questionnaire content used for all stakeholders for impact materiality; option to propose additional topics and provide open-ended feedback.
  - Note: Stakeholders specifically affected by pollution, resource use, and circular economy were not consulted.
- Financial risks and opportunities:
  - Identification followed an iterative process starting from ESRS topics, SASB standards for the financial sector, and ESG rating topics; no additional topics were required from SASB/ESG ratings.
  - Relevant topics shortlisted via expert workshops and consultations, with time horizons assessed (short/medium/long term).
  - No single financial materiality threshold used; thresholds taken from source documents or set during assessment due to differing impact profiles.
  - ESG risks integrated holistically into existing risk types (loan, country, counterparty, market, liquidity, operational, compliance) rather than treated as a standalone risk type.
  - Sources of financial risks/opportunities considered; for opportunities, the ESG strategy and annual plans are decisive.

nodes.title: Identification and Evaluation of Financial Risks and Opportunities
nodes.heading: Identification and Evaluation of Financial Risks and Opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: The identification of financial risks and opportunities related to sustainability topics was the result of an iterative process.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Part of OTP Group’s 2024 Integrated Annual Report outlining stakeholder engagement, materiality, and the identification/evaluation of sustainability-related financial risks and opportunities.
- Stakeholder inputs used: ESG ratings/questionnaires (Sustainalytics, MSCI, Moody’s); Residential TRI*M brand/satisfaction research; 2023 employee engagement survey (28,990 responses); an online stakeholder questionnaire targeting civil society, academia, authorities/supervisors/public administration, financial analysts/stock exchanges, media, and employee representatives.
- Materiality outcome: “Employees: work-life balance” added as a material topic based on stakeholder feedback; the impact-materiality questionnaire was standardized across stakeholder groups with options for open-ended input; stakeholders directly affected by pollution, resource use, and circular economy were not consulted.
- Financial risks/opportunities identification process: Iterative approach starting from ESRS topics, inputs used for impact materiality, SASB financial sector standards, and ESG rating topics; no additional topics emerged from SASB/ESG ratings.
- Shortlisting and time horizons: Workshops with OTP Bank experts determined relevant topics and assessed their short-, medium-, and long-term relevance.
- Materiality thresholds: No universal financial materiality threshold; thresholds derived from source documents or set case-by-case due to varied financial impacts.
- Risk governance approach: ESG risks integrated holistically into existing risk types (loan, country, counterparty, market, liquidity, operational, compliance) rather than treated as a standalone risk.
- Sources of financial risks/opportunities:
  - Opportunities aligned with ESG strategy and annual plans.
  - Lending-related sustainability risks: Group-wide Climate & Environmental (C&E) Risk Materiality Assessment initiated in 2024 per EBA; pending results substituted with a 2023 climate change stress test and NACE-based income analysis; supplemented by subsidiary Environmental Risk Materiality Assessments.
  - Operational risks: Identified via annual group-level RCSA; sustainability-attributable operational risks mapped to sustainability topics.
- Evaluation method: Risks and opportunities assessed on a three-level scale for magnitude and likelihood; items rated medium/large or large/large deemed material.
- Climate-related specifics:
  - Lending transition/physical risks assessed via the 2023 group climate stress test (using NGFS scenarios) and select subsidiary C&E assessments (Bulgarian and Croatian examples).
  - Own-operations risks evaluated via the 2023 RCSA: climate-related hazards (mainly physical and supply chain) did not meet materiality thresholds; results inform operational risk capital requirements and are reviewed by the Group Operational Risk Management Committee.
  - Subsidiary insights: Croatian assessment classed operational physical risks as low–medium (short/medium term) and medium (long term), not material; Bulgarian analysis indicated moderate exposure.
- Footnotes/coverage notes: Residential survey urban-only in Moldova, Ukraine, Uzbekistan; Uzbek employee opinion process being phased in; Russian subsidiary used a different engagement platform; NGFS referenced for climate scenarios.

nodes.title: Additional information to the assessment of climate change related topics
nodes.heading: Additional information to the assessment of climate change related topics:
nodes.start_phrase: In line with the general procedure applied during the identification and evaluation of impacts, the identification of risks and opportunities was also based on activities.
nodes.summary:
- OTP Group began a Climate & Environmental (C&E) Risk Materiality Assessment in 2024 to meet EBA requirements; because results were not yet available, the Group used a climate change stress test and analysis of income by NACE codes, plus selected subsidiary environmental risk assessments, to evaluate sustainability risks linked to lending.
- Operational risks relevant to sustainability were identified through the annual group-level Risk and Control Self-Assessment (RCSA), which maps process risks, likelihoods, and controls; sustainability-attributable risks were assigned to related sustainability topics.
- Risks and opportunities were rated on a three-level scale for magnitude and likelihood, with materiality defined for medium/large and large/large combinations.
- Transition and physical risks for lending were assessed using the 2023 group climate stress test based on NGFS scenarios; Bulgarian and Croatian subsidiaries’ C&E Risk Materiality Assessments were used as additional inputs.
- For own operations, the 2023 RCSA formed the basis for analyzing operational risks; climate-related hazards mainly fell under physical risks (including supply chain), were identified without a predefined hazard/asset list, and did not meet the materiality threshold. RCSA results inform operational risk capital requirements and indicate short-term risks, with trends highlighting medium/long-term outlooks.
- Subsidiary assessments: Croatia classified operational risks from extreme weather as low–medium in the short/medium term and medium in the long term (not material by its criteria); Bulgaria indicated moderate exposure.
- The reviewed documents did not identify assets or activities incompatible with a climate-neutral transition; climate-related risks were deemed manageable for the Group.
- Financial opportunities were guided by the ESG strategy and annual plans, notably expanding the green loan portfolio through 2025.
- Material climate-related impacts, risks, and opportunities are disclosed under ESRS SBM-3.
- Validation and governance: a multi-round internal review incorporated stakeholder feedback; the ESG Sub-Committee approved the material list (after one modification) by majority, the ESG Committee approved it unanimously, and outcomes were reported to the Board of Directors via ESG Committee briefings.

nodes.title: Validation of the evaluation and approval
nodes.heading: Validation of the evaluation and approval
nodes.start_phrase: The evaluation of impacts, risks, and opportunities was followed by a multi -round internal review.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Extract from OTP Group’s 2024 Integrated Annual Report (Management Report) presenting ESRS SBM-3 disclosure on material sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities, focused on climate change mitigation and adaptation.

- Materiality process and governance:
  - Evaluation underwent multi-round internal review, with stakeholder feedback from Hungarian and foreign subsidiaries.
  - ESG Sub-Committee approved the final list by majority after one modification; ESG Committee approved unanimously; the Committee Chair sits on the Board.
  - Results were reported to the Board of Directors via ESG Committee quarterly agendas.

- Identification and risk posture:
  - Earlier documents did not identify assets/activities incompatible with a climate-neutral transition or those needing significant transition effort.
  - Climate-related risks were deemed manageable for OTP Group.

- Strategy and opportunities:
  - ESG strategy and annual plans guide financial opportunities; expansion of green lending is a key opportunity.
  - Strategy time horizon extends to 2025; OTP’s balance sheet green exposure is increasing.

- Climate change mitigation (E1):
  - Impacts: OTP’s Scope 3 emissions (especially from the loan portfolio and asset managers) vastly exceed Scope 1–2; Scope 1–2 are relatively small per entity but significant in aggregate. Some smaller group members in agriculture, food, and real estate have relatively higher direct emissions.
  - Management: A loan portfolio decarbonization/transition plan was prepared by end-2024; KPI for green lending set through 2025; Scope 1–2 reductions via efficiency and green electricity.
  - Positive impact: Financial products and OTP’s broad customer reach foster mitigation and awareness.
  - Opportunity: Grow green lending in corporate and retail mortgages (no active green lending per OTP standards in Ukraine).
  - Risk: Client transition risks indirectly affect OTP; assessed via corporate portfolio stress testing and managed within ESG risk management.

- Climate change adaptation (E1):
  - Impacts: Lending can facilitate, hinder, or be neutral to clients’ adaptation; high adaptation needs in mortgages, agriculture, real estate, and construction.
  - Management: Promote adaptation through green lending; risks handled within ESG risk management.
  - Opportunity: Expand lending that supports adaptation.
  - Risks: Physical risks tied to lending exposure and certain transition risks from necessary adaptation investments.

- Coverage and horizons: Impacts, risks, and opportunities are considered across the value chain (upstream, OTP Group, downstream) and over short, medium, and long terms.

nodes.title: OTP Group’s Material Sustainability Impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: ESRS SBM -3 OTP Group’s Material Sustainability Impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: OTP Group's impact stems from direct and indirect greenhouse gas emissions, exacerbating climate change.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and framework: The excerpt outlines OTP Group’s material sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities across its value chain and time horizons, structured under ESRS SBM-3 and linked to ESRS 2 IRO-2. It identifies where impacts occur (upstream, own operations, downstream) and their relevance in the short, medium, and long term.

- E1 Climate change mitigation and adaptation:
  - Mitigation: The Group’s most material environmental impact is GHG emissions from financed activities (Scope 3) far exceeding operational emissions (Scopes 1–2). A loan-portfolio decarbonization plan was prepared by end-2024; a green lending KPI runs to 2025; green balance sheet exposure is growing; green electricity and efficiency reduce Scopes 1–2. Material risks stem from client transition risks assessed via stress testing and managed within ESG risk management. Opportunities center on expanding green lending (excluding Ukraine).
  - Adaptation: Lending can facilitate client adaptation in mortgages, agriculture, real estate, and construction; managed within ESG risk frameworks. Opportunities in adaptation finance; risks include physical and related transition needs.

- Energy: Negative impact via financing energy-intensive sectors; positive impact and opportunity via financing renewables and energy efficiency; credit and reputational risks when financing fossil and energy-intensive clients.

- E3 Water and marine resources (water withdrawal): Significant exposure to high-withdrawal sectors in the corporate portfolio; minimum client expectations include legal compliance and permits, with deeper practice assessments evolving alongside regulation. Positive impact through green lending; risks if clients fail to meet tightening standards or secure water availability.

- E4 Biodiversity and ecosystems: Exposure to sectors with potential negative biodiversity impacts; current expectations focus on compliance due to fewer biodiversity-specific rules, with ongoing work to understand client practices and articulate responsible expectations. No significant impacts identified for land degradation/desertification/soil sealing. Potential to encourage positive outcomes via financing conditions.

- S1 Own workforce (43,118 employees):
  - Work-life balance: Benefits, flexibility, leave, and well-being programs generate positive impacts; potential negatives if needs not addressed.
  - Health and safety: Stress is a key risk; OHS programs, preventive health checks, and stress management in place.
  - Gender equality and equal pay: Strategy and diversity policies; generally minimal pay gaps in same roles, but women underrepresented at senior levels and some subsidiaries show larger gaps.
  - Training and skills: Broad training portfolio aligned with evaluations; risk of unequal access if not well managed.
  - Inclusion of persons with disabilities: Non-discrimination in place, but supportive measures limited and employment share low.
  - Measures against violence/harassment: Ethics framework active; potential risk persists.
  - Diversity: Anti-discrimination stance, with room to improve practical implementation.

- S4 Consumers and end-users (financial services entities):
  - Information security and data protection (incl. cybersecurity): Robust systems, training, and anti-fraud support produce positive impacts, though incidents can still cause customer losses; significant legal, financial, and reputational risk if breaches occur.
  - Access to quality information: Regulated communications, education tools, and simplification efforts support informed decisions, with residual gaps due to product complexity.
  - Access to financial products and services: Digitalization to improve accessibility, including for disadvantaged areas; support for state-backed mortgage schemes; access improving but not comprehensive.

- G1 Business conduct:
  - Corporate culture, compliance, AML/CFT: Code of Ethics, ethics reporting, annual training, AML/CFT training and whistleblowing; positive impacts yet non-compliances can occur; legal, reputational, liquidity, and correspondent banking risks highlighted.
  - Corruption and bribery: Anti-corruption training, contractual clauses (expanding groupwide), and risk assessments; potential abuses cannot be fully eliminated.

- ESG risk, resilience, and financial impacts:
  - No dedicated provisions or capital buffers for ESG risks; impairments recognized in Slovenia and Bulgaria under ECB Novel Risk Recommendation, reflected in IFRS 9 ECL; additional climate risk capital needs not material.
  - ESG factors to enter rating models in 2025; operational risk losses flagged for ESG where relevant; no significant ESG-related losses in 2024; analysis and estimation of expected financial impacts planned for 2025.
  - Climate stress testing performed; no biodiversity resilience assessment due to non-financial materiality; ongoing monitoring of market and regulatory changes.

- Sanctions supplement: Operations subject to UN, EU, UK, US sanctions and Russian countersanctions; elevated exposure to Russia-related measures. Risks include inability to unwind sanctioned relationships in time, fines, license restrictions, reputational damage, and financial consequences; litigation/investigation risks acknowledged.

- Reporting policy and entity-specific disclosures:
  - Material topics and data points selected using EFRAG ID 177 guidance; voluntary data reported where feasible; phased ESRS adoption applied.
  - For own operations, only E1 climate mitigation is impact-material among environmental topics; other E1/E3/E4 not considered relevant for own operations.
  - S4 impacts are material specifically for clients; related data points reported for these client segments.
  - Entity-specific disclosures in scope: to be developed for water withdrawal and biodiversity impact drivers in the value chain; current disclosures cover information security and data protection, access to quality information, access to financial products and services, and corporate culture/compliance/AML.

nodes.title: Sanctions Supplement
nodes.heading: Sanctions Supplement: OTP Group’s operations are affected by various anti -corruption laws, sanctions enacted and applied by the UN, the UK and the EU, as well as the United States.
nodes.start_phrase: In addition, OTP Group’s operations in Russia are subject to various Russia n countersanctions.
nodes.summary:
- The report outlines OTP Group’s exposure to and compliance with international anti-corruption laws and sanctions regimes from the UN, UK, EU, and US, as well as Russian countersanctions affecting its Russian operations.
- It highlights restrictions on dealings with sanctioned countries, entities, and individuals, emphasizing heightened risk related to sanctions on Russia, Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine, and targeted Russian/Ukrainian parties, including owned/controlled entities.
- The Group notes potential exposure if customers become sanctioned and services are not ceased within permitted wind-down periods, acknowledging that evolving sanctions could have a material impact on operations.
- It details risks of investigations and litigation for alleged sanctions or anti-corruption breaches, including fines, activity restrictions, license revocation, reputational damage, and broader financial consequences.
- OTP Group identifies entity-specific disclosures for material topics: water withdrawal (value chain; disclosure under development), direct drivers of biodiversity loss (value chain; disclosure under development), information security and data protection, access to quality information, access to financial products and services, and corporate culture/compliance/anti-money laundering.
- Under ESRS 2 IRO-2, the Group reports on disclosure requirements tied to material sub-topics, using EFRAG ID 177 to link topics and define data points; it voluntarily reports feasible data points and applies phased ESRS options where relevant.
- For environmental topics, only climate change mitigation is considered materially impactful for the Group’s own operations; other E1, E3 (water and marine), and E4 (biodiversity and ecosystems) data points are deemed not relevant to own operations.
- S4 (Consumers and End-users) impacts and risks are material for specific client segments within Group banks, and the report includes the corresponding data points for these clients.

nodes.title: Disclosure Requirements in ESRS covered by the undertaking’s sustainability statement and general reporting policy
nodes.heading: 1.5. Disclosure Requirements in ESRS covered by the undertaking’s sustainability statement and general reporting policy
nodes.start_phrase: Among the disclosure requirements and data points in the thematic standards of ESRS, we report those that are related to the material sub -topics for OTP Group.
nodes.summary:
- Sanctions and anti-corruption exposure: OTP Group’s operations are affected by UN, UK, EU, and US sanctions and Russian countersanctions. The Group faces risks if customers become sanctioned, if wind-downs cannot be executed in time, and from potential investigations, fines, license impacts, reputational damage, and financial losses.
- Material topics and entity-specific disclosures: Current focus includes information security/data protection, access to information, access to financial products/services, and corporate culture/compliance/AML. Water withdrawal and biodiversity-loss drivers are material in the value chain; entity-specific disclosures for these will be developed later.
- ESRS reporting approach (ESRS 2 IRO-2): Reporting is limited to material sub-topics, mapped using EFRAG ID 177. Voluntary data points are provided when feasible; phased-in options are used where allowed. For own operations, only climate change mitigation is material; other E1 topics, E3 (water), and E4 (biodiversity) are not considered material for own operations. S4 (consumers/end-users) is material for certain client segments, with related data reported.
- Policies, actions, and targets: Disclosures cover the parent and specified subsidiaries across multiple countries; OTP Bank Romania (sold mid-year) is excluded. Asset managers are included where SFDR-linked climate information is relevant. For S1 (own workforce), entities with over 250 employees are covered. Where no policy/action/target exists, this is stated. Metrics aim for full coverage, with a threshold applied to ESRS S1-16 (compensation metrics); metrics are assured by the service provider, with no other external validation.
- Entity-specific disclosure methodology and definitions: Plans to develop entity-specific metrics for topics not covered by ESRS (notably S4 and, pending data, E3/E4). Definitions provided for operational control and business relationships. Associates/joint ventures are included beyond equity share when assessing value-chain impacts. Governance disclosures include board composition (gender, independence) and criteria. Country breakdown and total income are defined.
- Environmental strategy and progress: OTP seeks regional leadership in financing a fair, gradual low-carbon transition, expanding green loans and corporate bonds in 2024, enhancing risk management, and aiming to reduce operational footprint. A climate target-setting document establishes 2030 Scope 3 (Category 15) GHG targets in absolute and relative terms (not an ESRS E1-1 transition plan).
- Material impacts, risks, and opportunities:
  - E1 Climate change: Own operations’ GHG emissions (negative impact); green financial products and internal practices (positive impacts/opportunities); transition and physical risks in the loan/investment portfolios.
  - E2 Water and marine resources: Portfolio exposure to high water-abstraction sectors (negative), opportunities via green lending, and water-dependency/compliance risks.
  - E4 Biodiversity and ecosystems: Portfolio exposure to sectors harming biodiversity (negative) and potential to influence client behavior through expectations (positive).
- EU Taxonomy Regulation disclosures: Prepared per Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178, reporting on exposures within prudential consolidation (CRR 575/2013). Confirms applicability under Articles 19a/29a and Article 8 disclosure obligations and reiterates OTP’s commitment to sustainable finance and social responsibility.

structure.title: Environmental Information
structure.heading: 2. Environmental Information
structure.start_phrase: OTP Group aims to take a regional leadership role in financing a fair and gradual transition to a low carbon economy, and building a sustainable future.
structure.summary:
- Outlines OTP Group’s environmental strategy and goals: aiming for regional leadership in financing a fair, gradual transition to a low‑carbon economy; substantial growth in green loans and corporate bonds in 2024; completion of a climate target‑setting document for 2030 covering Scope 3 category 15 emissions (absolute and intensity targets) and instruments to meet them; enhancements to risk management; and efforts to reduce the Group’s operational environmental footprint.
- Summarizes material impacts, risks, and opportunities:
  - E1 Climate change: negative impact from direct and indirect GHG emissions across own operations and portfolios; positive impacts and financial opportunities via green financial products and internal practice‑driven mindset change; financial risks from transition and physical risks in the loan portfolio.
  - E2 Water and marine resources: potential negative impact from financing high water‑abstraction sectors; positive impact via green lending; financial risks from water dependency and environmental compliance in the portfolio.
  - E4 Biodiversity and ecosystems: potential negative impact from funding sectors harmful to biodiversity; potential positive influence by setting expectations to encourage responsible customer behavior.
- Points to further detail under ESRS SBM‑3 and subsequent sections.
- Presents EU Taxonomy Regulation disclosures framework: methodology per Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178; reporting scope for credit institutions aligned with prudential consolidation under Regulation (EU) No 575/2013; coverage of entities subject to non‑financial reporting under Directive 2013/34/EU (Articles 19a/29a); and Article 8 requirements on including how and to what extent activities are Taxonomy‑aligned.
- Reaffirms OTP Bank’s commitment to sustainable financing and social responsibility.

- Presentation of a climate target-setting document as a milestone: 2030 GHG targets defined in absolute and intensity terms for Scope 3 category 15; noted as not a transition plan under ESRS E1‑1.
- Summary of material impacts, risks, and opportunities:
  - E1 Climate change: negative impacts from direct and indirect GHG emissions across own operations; positive impacts and financial opportunities via green financial products and internal practices; financial risks from transition and physical risks in loan and investment portfolios.

nodes.title: EU Taxonomy Regulation Disclosures
nodes.heading: 2.1.1. EU Taxonomy Regulation Disclosures
nodes.start_phrase: OTP Bank is committed to sustainable financing and social responsibility.
nodes.summary:
- OTP Group’s environmental strategy: aims to lead regionally in financing a fair, gradual transition to a low‑carbon economy; expanded green loan and corporate bond portfolios in 2024; issued a climate target‑setting document for 2030 (Scope 3 category 15, absolute and intensity targets; not an ESRS E1‑1 transition plan); strengthened risk management; seeks to cut operational environmental footprint.

- Material environmental topics and impacts:
  - Climate (E1): own operations and portfolios contribute to direct/indirect GHG emissions (negative); opportunities through green financial products and internal practices that shape mindsets; portfolio financial risks from transition and physical climate risks; financial opportunities in green lending.
  - Water (E2): potential negative impact via financing high water withdrawal sectors; opportunities via green lending; portfolio risks from water dependency and environmental compliance.
  - Biodiversity (E4): potential negative impacts via funding biodiversity‑affecting sectors; potential positive leverage by setting client expectations for responsible behavior.

- EU Taxonomy Regulation disclosures:
  - Reporting aligned to Regulation (EU) 2020/852 and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178; scope based on prudential consolidation under CRR 575/2013.
  - Discloses stock and flow metrics, transitional and enabling activities, and specialized vs general‑purpose lending.
  - Consolidated KPIs include exposures of subsidiaries, fund managers, and credit institutions.
  - Certain exposures excluded from mandatory KPIs: corporates not subject to Articles 19a/29a disclosures and non‑EU subsidiary banks; these are discussed in the green lending section.
  - Qualitative methodology and data details provided per Annex XI.
  - The Commission Notice (C/2024/6691) Appendix 2 table not published due to late issuance; to be included next year. Separate chapter covers asset manager KPIs (OTP Fund Management).

- Key performance indicators (GAR) and trends:
  - 2024 GAR stock improved:
    - Turnover‑based: 0.10% (vs 0.05% in 2023), HUF 30,365 million environmentally sustainable assets.
    - Capex‑based: 0.29% (vs 0.09% in 2023), HUF 82,911 million environmentally sustainable assets.
  - 2024 GAR flow increased to 0.13% (turnover) and 0.45% (capex).
  - KPI coverage remains ~65% of total assets; both GAR assets and total balance sheet grew by >13%.
  - Financial institutions: taxonomy‑eligible exposures reached ~2.5%; aligned ~0.10%, aided by broader taxonomy reporting availability.
  - Non‑financial corporates: taxonomy‑eligible exposures exceed 8.5% (turnover basis); aligned ratio above 3%.
  - Households: taxonomy‑eligible ratios ~28% overall; 57% for real‑estate‑secured exposures; ~37% for retail motor vehicle finance. Bank does not count these as aligned when only substantial contribution is met due to DNSH evidence gaps; household category interpreted as total gross exposure (EU and non‑EU) per 2024 Commission Notice.

- 2023 restatement for managed assets in GAR templates:
  - Turnover basis (Template 1, Row 55): total AUM +1,526,575 million HUF; taxonomy‑eligible +124,025 million HUF; aligned +9,337 million HUF.
  - Capex basis (Template 1, Row 55): total AUM +1,526,575 million HUF; taxonomy‑eligible +314,352 million HUF; aligned +14,882 million HUF.
  - As a result, 2023 consolidated sustainability data in this report are not comparable to last year’s publication; comparative GAR KPIs are still provided as required by Article 8.

- KPI coverage and exclusions snapshot (2024):
  - GAR stock coverage over total assets: 64.76%; assets excluded from numerator: 27.43%; assets excluded from denominator: 35.24%.
  - Additional KPIs: GAR flow coverage 58.52%; assets under management taxonomy‑aligned activities equal to 0.37% (turnover) and 0.68% (capex).
  - Fees and commissions and trading book KPIs will apply starting in 2026.

nodes.summary:
