- Defines the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) perimeter for on-balance sheet exposures, covering loans and advances, debt securities, equities, investments (subsidiaries, JVs, associates), fair value categories, and repossessed real estate collaterals.
- States OTP Group’s ESG strategy to expand the green loan portfolio and ensure EU Taxonomy alignment through Group green frameworks (referenced in Voluntary GAR reporting).
- Specifies exclusions:
  - From both numerator and denominator: exposures to central governments, central banks, and supranational issuers.
  - From the GAR numerator: trading assets, on-demand interbank loans, exposures to undertakings not subject to NFRD (Directive 2013/34/EU Articles 19a/29a), derivatives, cash/cash-equivalents, and other assets (e.g., goodwill).
- Describes consolidation and reporting approach:
  - Gross exposures aggregated per Annex III into Template 1, incorporating OTP Fund Management’s separate report.
  - Assets under management included on a consolidated basis in the asset GAR (summary Template 0) using Fund Manager total assets.
- Details data sources: analytical credit and risk databases, FINREP balance sheet data; taxonomy alignment determined via issuer data requests and public sources.
- Explains KPI construction using both turnover- and Capex-based alignment, requiring duplication of KPI cells; numerator covers Taxonomy-aligned financing across loans, debt, equities, and repossessed collaterals, while the denominator covers the total of these and all other covered on-balance sheet assets.
- Notes timing: KPIs for trading book items and fees/commissions become applicable from 1 January 2026 (Annex V, point 1.2.3).

nodes.title: Findings concerning Annex VI of Regulation No. 2021/2178, worksheet ‘0’
nodes.heading: Findings concerning Annex VI of Regulation No. 2021/2178, worksheet ‘0’
nodes.start_phrase: The use of CAPEX and turnover -based reporting has necessitated the duplication of KPI cells.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose: Explains the methodology and scope for reporting EU Taxonomy-aligned KPIs—especially the Green Asset Ratio (GAR)—under Regulation (EU) 2021/2178 in OTP Group’s consolidated reporting.
- Asset scope for GAR: Includes on-balance sheet loans and advances, debt securities, equity holdings, investments in subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates, financial assets at fair value (designated and non-trading), and repossessed real estate collaterals.
- Strategic focus: OTP Group’s ESG strategy prioritizes growing the green loan portfolio; alignment with EU Taxonomy is managed through Group green frameworks (referenced in Voluntary GAR reporting).
- Regulatory exclusions: Excludes exposures to central governments, central banks, and supranational issuers from both numerator and denominator; excludes from numerator trading book assets, on-demand interbank loans, exposures to non-NFRD undertakings, derivatives, cash/cash-like assets, and other non-relevant categories (e.g., goodwill).
- Data aggregation and sources: GAR compiled per Annex III guidance; Template 1 populated using OTP Fund Management’s separate reporting; assets under management reflected on a consolidated basis in summary template 0; financial data sourced from analytical credit/risk databases and FINREP; taxonomy alignment based on issuer data requests and public disclosures.
- KPI construction (Annex VI, worksheet ‘0’): KPI cells duplicated to accommodate both turnover- and CapEx-based reporting; numerator includes assets financing Taxonomy-aligned activities based on counterparties’ turnover and CapEx KPIs; denominator includes all covered on-balance sheet assets in scope. Trading book and fees/commissions KPIs apply from 1 January 2026.
- Template 1 (Annex VI): Duplicated by counterparty turnover vs. CapEx inputs; numerators differ for general-purpose loans with unknown use, bond exposures, and equity holdings in non-financial undertakings.
- Customer segmentation: Analysis by financial undertakings, non-financial undertakings, retail (residential property, home renovation, car loans), local governments (housing finance—rental or known green purpose), and repossessed collateral (residential and commercial real estate). Data as of 31 December 2023 (Tables T-1).
- Financial undertakings methodology: Uses latest available taxonomy reports; applies a 0.01% portfolio materiality threshold; reasonable efforts made to maximize portfolio coverage.
- Non-financial undertakings methodology: Identifies NFRD-obliged entities per subsidiary and local rules; Hungary filters per Accounting Act C./2000 thresholds (employees >250; total assets > HUF 10bn; revenue > HUF 20bn over two consecutive years) using external and internal data.
- Treatment of exposures: Known-purpose loans assessed via bank eligibility/alignment checks; unknown-purpose loans and equity exposures assessed using counterparties’ disclosed turnover/CapEx eligibility and alignment. If no public data, exposures not counted for eligibility/alignment.
- Data completeness: Acknowledges potential gaps in identifying all NFRD-obliged customers; plans to fully identify relevant non-financial partners and integrate required data into IT systems.
- Specialized/project finance: Special lending segment loans examined; project finance debt securities reviewed within bond exposures.

nodes.title: Findings concerning Annex VI of Regulation No. 2021/2178, Template 1
nodes.heading: Findings concerning Annex VI of Regulation No. 2021/2178, Template 1
nodes.start_phrase: The template has been duplicated on the basis of counterparty turnover and CapEx data.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Presents the Bank’s EU Taxonomy (Reg. 2021/2178, Annex VI) disclosures and methodology for Green Asset Ratio (GAR), with templates duplicated for turnover- and CapEx-based views. Numerators differ across the two GARs for general loans with unknown purpose, bond exposures and equity to non-financial undertakings.
- Portfolio segmentation: Financial undertakings; non-financial undertakings; retail customers (residential property, home renovation, car loans); local governments (housing financing only—rental or known green loan purpose); and collateral obtained via possession (residential and commercial real estate).
- Data basis and thresholds: Tables use latest data as at 31.12.2023. For financial undertakings, taxonomy data collected on a best-efforts basis; exposures below 0.01% of portfolio size not assessed for taxonomy purposes.
- Non-financial undertakings/NFRD coverage:
  - NFRD scope defined per subsidiary under local rules; example filtering in Hungary (any two over two consecutive years: >250 employees; >HUF 10bn total assets; >HUF 20bn net sales).
  - Methodology distinguishes known vs unknown loan purposes: known purposes assessed via the Bank’s eligibility/alignment checks at transaction level; unknown purposes and equity exposures assessed using counterparties’ disclosed turnover and CapEx eligibility/alignment.
  - If no public taxonomy data exists for a counterparty, its exposure is excluded from eligibility/alignment reporting.
  - Best-efforts identification of NFRD-obliged customers; acknowledges possible gaps; short-term plan to achieve full, up-to-date identification and integrate data into IT systems.
  - Specialized lending identified in controlling systems assessed as “special lending”; project-finance bond exposures reviewed.
- Households methodology:
  - GAR for residential real estate and renovation based on technical screening criteria for buildings (Delegated Regulations 2021/2139 and 2023/2486; activities 7.1–7.7; 3.1–3.2).
  - “Gross exposure to households” interpreted as all household exposures; taxonomy assessment applies only to exposures secured by residential real estate; non-residential real estate is excluded.
  - To avoid double counting, building modernization (Annex I, Section 7.2) is reported only in the specified template row and excluded from residential collateralized loans.
  - Car loan GAR calculated per Section 6.5 (transition activities included); disclosures cover loans granted after Regulation 2021/2178 application start and include loan flows.
  - DNSH for residential exposures cannot currently be verified; therefore, no taxonomy-aligned residential real estate data is shown for 2024.
  - In the residential category, special lending value equals taxonomy-aligned value.
  - No unequivocal rental housing financing identified; fields left blank. Non-rental housing or other known green loan purposes are excluded from the GAR numerator.
  - Repossessed real estate: numerator includes gross carrying amount compliant with buildings criteria (Section 7.7); denominator is total gross book value of seized real estate collateral.
- Template/worksheet interpretations:
  - Worksheet 2: Column (a) lists 4-digit NACE core activities for all NFRD-scope counterparties; table shows EU Taxonomy-eligible and -aligned exposures by NACE.
  - Worksheet 3: Discloses loan portfolio GAR KPI calculated from Template 1 using Commission formulae; duplicated for turnover- and CapEx-based metrics.
  - Worksheet 4: Duplicated for turnover and CapEx; reports current-year portfolio inflows/changes.

- Rental housing: No identifiable exposures; related fields left blank. Non‑rental housing and other known green loan purposes excluded from GAR numerator per legal interpretation.
- Repossessed collateral: Numerator includes gross carrying amount of seized commercial/residential real estate meeting building criteria (Annex I Sec. 7.7); denominator is total gross book value of seized real estate collateral.

nodes.start_phrase: The following is the mandatory report for the OTP Fund Manager.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Mandatory consolidated management report for OTP Fund Manager within the Integrated Annual Report 2024, reference date 31 December 2024, covering OTP Fund Manager and its subsidiaries (DSK Asset Management EAD, LLC AMC OTP Capital, OTP Alapkezelő Zrt., OTP Invest d.o.o., OTP INVEST Društvo za upravljanje UCITS i AIF AD Beograd). 2024 results are consolidated; 2023 figures reflect OTP Fund Manager as a standalone legal entity, limiting comparability.
- KPI framework: EU Taxonomy-aligned investment indicators for assets under management (equities and bonds; sovereigns excluded), using turnover- and CapEx-based weights. Look-through for collective investments applied only where MSCI ESG Research provides underlying breakdowns.
- 2024 headline results:
  - Taxonomy-aligned weighted averages: 0.80% (turnover-based; HUF 22,290m) and 1.66% (CapEx-based; HUF 45,959m).
  - KPI coverage: 63.87% of total AuM (HUF 2,776,316m); 63.87% of roughly EUR 11bn in assets considered.
  - Denominator composition: large shares in non-EU undertakings not subject to Articles 19a/29a (non-financial 39.90%, financial 24.89%); EU undertakings not subject (non-financial 1.39%, financial 4.95%); undertakings subject to 19a/29a (non-financial 7.24%, financial 11.19%); other counterparties/assets 10.43%; no derivatives.
  - Eligibility split: non-eligible activities 87.53% (HUF 2,430,102m); eligible but not aligned 7.62% (HUF 211,491m).
  - Numerator composition: taxonomy-aligned exposures mainly in non-financial undertakings (turnover 0.68%, CapEx 1.47%); negligible alignment in financial undertakings; small aligned share in “other counterparties and assets” (turnover 0.13%, CapEx 0.18%).
  - Environmental objectives: alignment concentrated in climate change mitigation and adaptation (primarily enabling activities); minimal amounts across water/marine, circular economy, pollution prevention, and biodiversity objectives.
- 2023 headline results (standalone entity basis):
  - Taxonomy-aligned weighted averages: 0.54% (turnover; HUF 14,222m) and 1.05% (CapEx; HUF 27,842m).
  - KPI coverage: 83.22% (HUF 2,644,791m).
  - Denominator composition: high exposure to non-EU undertakings not subject to 19a/29a (non-financial 35.43%, financial 44.25%); EU undertakings not subject (non-financial 0.72%, financial 3.06%); undertakings subject to 19a/29a (non-financial 6.29%, financial 7.40%); other counterparties/assets 2.84%.
  - Eligibility split: non-eligible 79.69% (HUF 2,107,555m); eligible but not aligned 14.73% (HUF 389,520m).
  - Numerator: alignment driven by non-financial undertakings; financial undertakings near zero; environmental alignment largely in climate mitigation and adaptation.
- Trend and comparability:
  - Increase in taxonomy-aligned ratios from 2023 to 2024: turnover-based from 0.54% to 0.80%; CapEx-based from 1.05% to 1.66%.
  - Coverage declined in 2024 due to consolidation scope and data availability.
  - 2023 sustainability data restated; figures in this report are not comparable to those published in last year’s report.
- Methodology and data limitations:
  - Sole external data source: MSCI ESG Research; no other ESG providers or internal data collection used.
  - Reporting limited by Articles 19a/29a applicability; significant portion of investments lack usable taxonomy data.
  - Only mitigation and adaptation fully considered in the period; other objectives primarily populated by non-financial companies.
  - Due to MSCI’s flags, detailed breakdown is available only into transitional and enabling activities (Annex VI); Annex IV totals also include aligned activities without such flags, so figures may differ.

- GAR evolution: Green Asset Ratio increased year over year from 0.54% to 0.80% on a turnover basis and from 1.05% to 1.66% on a CAPEX basis.
- Strategic stance: No overarching target for Taxonomy-aligned activities; investment evaluation emphasizes greenhouse gas emissions, waste and pollutant emissions, and water stress.
- Restatement: 2023 EU Taxonomy eligibility and alignment KPIs have been restated; 2023 consolidated sustainability data in this report are not comparable to those published last year.

nodes.title: Explanation of the nature and objectives of the economic activities aligned with the taxonomy, and the explanation of the evolution of these activities over time starting from the second year of implementation, distinguishing between business -related, meth odological, and data -related elements.
nodes.heading: Explanation of the nature and objectives of the economic activities aligned with the taxonomy, and the explanation of the evolution of these activities over time starting from the second year of implementation, distinguishing between business -related, meth odological, and data -related elements.
nodes.start_phrase: OTP Fund Management does not have a general, overarching goal for economic activities aligned with the taxonomy but considers the environmental objectives of sustainability when evaluating a given investment, focusing primarily on greenhouse gas emissions, waste and pollutant emissions, and water str ess.
nodes.summary:

- Methodology and data limits: reliance solely on MSCI ESG Research; limited target-company reporting under Directive 2013/34/EU reduces usable data. Only climate change mitigation and adaptation were fully assessed; other environmental objectives were reflected only for non-financial companies. Taxonomy breakdown available only into transitional/enabling categories; Annex IV vs Annex VI figures differ due to missing flags.
- GAR trend: taxonomy-aligned GAR increased year over year from 0.54% to 0.8% (turnover) and from 1.05% to 1.66% (CAPEX).
- Investment approach: no single overarching taxonomy-aligned target; investments evaluated against environmental objectives focusing on GHG emissions, waste/pollutants, and water stress. 2023 taxonomy KPI data have been restated, making them non-comparable with last year’s publication.
- OTP Climate Change Fund: ESG-integrated strategy benchmarked to 70% MSCI ACWI IMI SDG 7 Affordable and Clean Energy Select, 25% MSCI EMU Climate Change ESG Select, 5% RMAX. Exclusions: >5% revenue from arms/tobacco; >50% from coal, gas, or oil extraction. Portfolio ≥70% in companies with strong MSCI ESG ratings (AAA–BBB developed; AAA–BB EM). Aims at climate mitigation/adaptation; commits to ≥51% sustainable investments, including 10% taxonomy-aligned.

nodes.title: The OTP Climate Change Fund
nodes.heading: The OTP Climate Change Fund
nodes.start_phrase: The OTP Climate Change Fund integrates sustainability considerations into investment decision -making as follows:
nodes.summary:
- Overview of three OTP funds’ approaches to integrating ESG and sustainability: OTP Climate Change Fund, OTP Omega Fund of Funds, and OTP Ecotrend Fund.

- OTP Climate Change Fund:
  - Integrates sustainability into investment decisions using an ESG-focused reference index: 70% MSCI ACWI IMI SDG 7 Affordable and Clean Energy Select, 25% MSCI EMU Climate Change ESG Select NETR EUR, 5% RMAX.
  - Benchmarks favor companies with higher ESG scores; SDG 7 alignment and emissions-aware weighting.
  - Investment process filters benchmark constituents and can include select off-benchmark securities that contribute to sustainability or have strong ESG profiles; limited inclusion of unrated but sustainability-leading companies.
  - Exclusions: >5% revenue from arms manufacturing or tobacco; no investments in companies with >50% revenue from coal, natural gas, or oil extraction.
  - Portfolio must hold at least 70% in shares with “good, sustainable” MSCI ratings (AAA–BBB for developed markets; AAA–BB for emerging markets).
  - Primary aim: mitigate and support adaptation to climate change; invests in companies whose products enable others’ climate contributions (EU Taxonomy Article 16).
  - Not a fund with a dedicated sustainability objective, but commits to at least 51% sustainable investments, including a minimum 10% taxonomy-aligned environmentally sustainable investments.

- OTP Omega Fund of Funds:
  - Invests in a mix of actively and passively managed funds.
  - ESG ratings for underlying funds may or may not be published by MSCI, depending on consultant and manager decisions.
  - No sustainability objective; commits to investing at least 51% in sustainable programs, with no allocation to taxonomy-aligned environmentally sustainable investments.

- OTP Ecotrend Fund:
  - Promotes environmental features primarily via its bond portfolio, including green government bonds.
  - Targets financing of six green sectors: renewable energy, energy efficiency, waste and water management, land use and living natural resources, clean transport, and climate adaptation.
  - No formal sustainability objective and no commitment to a minimum ratio of sustainable investments.

nodes.title: OTP Omega Fund of Funds
nodes.heading: OTP Omega Fund of Funds
nodes.start_phrase: The Fund invests in other actively and passively managed funds in accordance with the fund of funds structure.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of how three OTP funds integrate ESG and sustainability considerations in their strategies and allocations.

- OTP Climate Change Fund:
  - Uses an ESG-focused reference index: 70% MSCI ACWI IMI SDG 7 Affordable and Clean Energy Select, 25% MSCI EMU Climate Change ESG Select NETR EUR, 5% RMAX.
  - Indices support SDG 7 and climate objectives by overweighting higher-ESG companies and adjusting for emissions and positive climate contributions.
  - Investment universe filtered from reference indices; exclusions include companies with >5% revenue from arms or tobacco and >50% from coal, natural gas, or oil extraction.
  - Can include off-benchmark names that contribute to sustainability or have strong ESG profiles; limited inclusion for firms without ESG ratings if they lead on sustainability.
  - Portfolio must hold at least 70% in shares with “good, sustainable” MSCI ratings (AAA–BBB for developed markets; AAA–BB for emerging markets).
  - Primary aim: mitigate and support adaptation to climate change, consistent with Article 16 of the EU Taxonomy.
  - No formal sustainability objective, but commits to at least 51% sustainable investments, including a minimum 10% taxonomy-aligned environmentally sustainable investments.

- OTP Omega Fund of Funds:
  - Invests in a mix of actively and passively managed funds.
  - MSCI provides ESG ratings for some, but not all, underlying funds due to business considerations.
  - No explicit sustainability objective; commits to at least 51% in sustainable programs but will not invest in taxonomy-aligned environmentally sustainable investments.

- OTP Ecotrend Fund:
  - Promotes environmental features primarily via its bond portfolio, with planned allocations to green government bonds.
  - Targets financing in six green sectors: renewable energy, energy efficiency, waste and water management, land use and living natural resources, clean transport, and climate adaptation.
  - No sustainability objective and no minimum commitment to sustainable investments.

nodes.title: OTP Ecotrend Fund
nodes.heading: OTP Ecotrend Fund
nodes.start_phrase: The Fund seeks to make a commitment to promoting environmental features, primarily through its bond portfolio.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines how OTP Fund Management integrates ESG and EU Taxonomy considerations into investment decisions across specific funds and in group-level reporting.
- OTP Climate Change Fund:
  - Benchmark: 70% MSCI ACWI IMI SDG 7 Affordable and Clean Energy Select, 25% MSCI EMU Climate Change ESG Select NETR EUR, 5% RMAX; ESG-focused indices overweight higher-ESG companies.
  - Investment process: screens reference-index constituents; excludes companies with >5% revenue from arms or tobacco and >50% from coal, gas, or oil extraction; may include off-benchmark names contributing to sustainability or leading on ESG, with limits for unrated names.
  - Portfolio construction: at least 70% in shares with “good” MSCI ESG ratings (AAA–BBB for developed markets; AAA–BB for emerging markets).
  - Objective: support climate change mitigation and adaptation; commits to at least 51% sustainable investments, including ≥10% EU Taxonomy-aligned (actual ~30% at end-2024), though it does not claim a formal sustainability objective.
- OTP Omega Fund of Funds:
  - Invests in active and passive funds; ESG ratings by MSCI are available for some underlying funds.
  - Commits to ≥51% sustainable investments but no investment in EU Taxonomy-aligned assets; no formal sustainability objective.
- OTP Ecotrend Fund:
  - Promotes environmental features mainly via bonds, notably green government bonds across six green sectors (renewables, energy efficiency, waste/water, land/natural resources, clean transport, adaptation).
  - No formal sustainability objective and no minimum sustainable investment ratio.
- KPI reporting: 2024 KPI figures changed versus 2023 due to portfolio mix, coverage, and data expansion; individual drivers were not isolated; two data points are insufficient to infer trends.
- EU Taxonomy/SFDR compliance:
  - OTP Fund Management integrates sustainability risks and is increasing the share of SFDR-rated products with significant sustainable investments.
  - For products with Taxonomy commitments, applies DNSH indicators alongside ESG-provider metrics to assess Taxonomy alignment.
  - As of 2024, one fund (OTP Climate Change Fund) has a ≥10% Taxonomy-alignment commitment.
- Voluntary green portfolio reporting:
  - Beyond the mandatory Green Asset Ratio, OTP Group discloses its total green portfolio, methodology, and definitions.
  - Green portfolio reached HUF 1,027 billion by end-2024 (+56% YoY); target HUF 1,500 billion by 2025, with retail and corporate sub-targets.
  - Corporate green portfolio: +64% YoY; >80% of total sustainable portfolio; sustainable exposures at 2.3% of gross book value (+>50% YoY); corporate green bond portfolio +35% YoY, 40% consolidated GBV ratio, >5% of sustainable portfolio.
  - Retail green portfolio: predominantly Hungary; green share +>13% YoY; retail represents ~19% of sustainable portfolio.
  - Green lending present in nine countries (HU, BG, SI, HR, RS, UZ, ME, AL, MD); ambition to offer green lending across all sectors and segments, with maturity varying by market.
  - Notes linkage to ESRS climate change subtopics for action planning; the Group does not specifically address ESRS subtopics in detail in this section.

nodes.title: Description of the compliance with Regulation (EU) No. 2020/852 in the financial undertaking’s business strategy, product design processes and engagement with clients and counterparties.
nodes.heading: Description of the compliance with Regulation (EU) No. 2020/852 in the financial undertaking’s business strategy, product design processes and engagement with clients and counterparties.
nodes.start_phrase: OTP Fund Management is committed to taking sustainability risks into account in its investment decisions and to continuously increasing the number of SFDR -rated products that invest in a significant share of sustainable investments.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Extract from OTP Group’s 2024 Integrated Annual Management Report focused on sustainability/ESG KPIs, EU Taxonomy/SFDR alignment, and green portfolio reporting and targets.
- KPI comparability: 2024 KPIs differ from 2023 due to portfolio composition, coverage, and expanded data; individual change drivers were not isolated and two years are insufficient to establish trends.
- Regulatory alignment: OTP Fund Management integrates sustainability risks into investment decisions and expands SFDR-rated products. For products committed under the EU Taxonomy, DNSH indicators are applied alongside external ESG provider metrics to assess Taxonomy compliance.
- Taxonomy-aligned investing: OTP Climate Change Fund has a minimum 10% EU Taxonomy alignment commitment; actual alignment was about 30% at end-2024.
- Voluntary reporting: The Group provides a voluntary green portfolio report detailing portfolio composition, methodologies, and definitions, supplementing mandatory Taxonomy green asset ratio disclosure with additional market/regulatory metrics.
- Green portfolio growth: Green portfolio reached HUF 1,027 billion by end-2024, up 56% year-over-year. A Group-wide KPI at subsidiary level tracks progress.
- Targets: Management approved 2025 goals targeting HUF 1,500 billion green loan portfolio across retail and corporate segments.
- Corporate segment: Corporate green portfolio grew 64% year-over-year; sustainable corporate assets account for over 80% of total sustainable portfolio; sustainable exposures reached 2.3% of gross book value (>50% improvement). Corporate green bond portfolio grew 35% year-over-year, maintaining a 40% consolidated gross book value ratio, and exceeded 5% of the sustainable portfolio.
- Retail segment: Majority concentrated in Hungary; green share rose by over 13% year-over-year; retail represents about 19% of the total sustainable portfolio, with expected further growth as data quality improves.
- Geographic scope: Green loan portfolios active in nine countries (Hungary, Bulgaria, Slovenia, Croatia, Serbia, Uzbekistan, Montenegro, Albania, Moldova); expansion ongoing.
- Business integration: The Group embeds green/climate-conscious lending across sectors, aiming to offer green terms for any client with a qualifying sustainable objective; rollout pace varies by country, industry, and segment.
- ESRS notes: Increasing the green portfolio aligns with climate-related action areas, though specific ESRS sub-topics are not separately addressed.

nodes.title: 2.1.1. Voluntary Reporting
nodes.heading: 2.1.1. Voluntary Reporting
nodes.start_phrase: OTP Group wishes to present its sustainability efforts in the most transparent way possible.
nodes.summary:
- KPI data for 2024 vs. 2023 changed due to portfolio composition, coverage, and expanded data; no trend can be inferred from two years, and individual change drivers were not analyzed.
- Compliance approach to EU Taxonomy (Regulation (EU) 2020/852): integrating sustainability risks into investment decisions, expanding SFDR-rated products, and applying DNSH indicators alongside ESG provider metrics for funds with Taxonomy commitments.

- Voluntary reporting: OTP Group discloses a broader “green portfolio” beyond mandatory GAR, including methodology and definitions aligned with internal frameworks and market/regulatory standards.
- Green portfolio growth and targets: reached HUF 1,027 billion by end-2024 (+56% YoY); 2025 target of HUF 1,500 billion, with segment-specific goals (retail and corporate).
- Corporate segment: green portfolio +64% YoY; corporate sustainable assets >80% of total sustainable portfolio; sustainable exposures equal 2.3% of gross book value; corporate green bonds +35% YoY, 40% consolidated gross book value ratio, >5% share of sustainable portfolio.
- Retail segment: majority in Hungary; green share +13% YoY; retail ≈19% of total sustainable portfolio.
- Geographic footprint: green loan portfolios active in nine countries (Hungary, Bulgaria, Slovenia, Croatia, Serbia, Uzbekistan, Montenegro, Albania, Moldova); aim to offer green financing across all sectors and segments over time.
- GHG impact: expected impacts of green lending to be disclosed under E1-4; not yet measured.
- Definition and scope of OTP Group’s green portfolio: based on the Green Lending Framework, Sustainable Finance Framework, MNB green programs, and EU Taxonomy; includes EU and non-EU exposures and clients outside NFRD/CSRD scope (thus broader than GAR).
- Key 2024 portfolio metrics (illustrative from table):
  - Total assets: HUF 44,852,131 million; Total GAR assets: HUF 29,047,630 million.
  - Non-financial corporations: HUF 833,809 million green (7.87% of segment; 1.86% of total assets; 2.87% of total GAR assets).
  - Households: HUF 193,634 million green (1.41% of segment; 0.43% of total assets; 0.67% of total GAR assets).
  - Overall green portfolio equals about 2.29% of total assets and 3.54% of total GAR assets.

nodes.title: OTP Group’s Green Portfolio
nodes.heading: OTP Group’s Green Portfolio
nodes.start_phrase: OTP Group's sustainable frameworks are defined by the Green Lending Framework, the Sustainable Finance Framework, the MNB's green housing, as well as green corporate and municipal capital requirement discount programs, and the EU Taxonomy.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: OTP Group’s green lending and sustainable finance activities within the 2024 Integrated Annual Report (Management Report, Consolidated), including definitions, scope, metrics, frameworks, and data governance.
- Impact measurement: The expected GHG emission reduction from green lending is referenced under disclosure E1-4 but has not yet been measured.
- Definition and scope of the green portfolio: Comprised of exposures meeting criteria in the Group’s Green Lending Framework, Sustainable Finance Framework, the Hungarian National Bank’s (MNB) green programs (housing, corporate and municipal capital relief), and the EU Taxonomy. Includes green loans and bonds outside the EU and clients not subject to NFRD/CSRD, thus extending beyond the mandatory GAR perimeter.
- GAR linkage and key figures: The green portfolio is presented relative to total assets and total GAR assets to reconcile with mandatory Taxonomy reporting. Headline numbers (HUF million): total assets 44,852,131; total GAR assets 29,047,630. Non-financial corporates: 833,809 green (7.87% of that segment; 1.86% of total assets; 2.87% of total GAR assets). Households: 193,634 green (1.41% of that segment; 0.43% of total assets; 0.67% of total GAR assets). Overall green portfolio approximates 2.29% of total assets and 3.54% of total GAR assets, with breakdowns for loans/advances and debt securities.
- Portfolio composition: Diversified across renewable energy, corporate real estate, electromobility, and green residential mortgages; smaller but growing shares in agriculture and corporate green bonds.
- Frameworks and governance:
  - Green Loan Framework: Updated in July 2023 with external second-party opinion and approved by the MNB; loans meeting framework conditions qualify for the MNB Green Corporate and Municipal Capital Relief Program (Category B). Extended beyond Hungary to Bulgaria, Slovenia, Croatia, Serbia, Albania, and Montenegro.
  - Sectoral coverage: Aligned with EU Taxonomy (energy, manufacturing, transportation, construction & real estate, forestry, waste management) and Climate Bonds Initiative Taxonomy (energy, industry, transportation, buildings, land use and marine sources, waste and pollution control); also allows water management-related financing.
  - Client scope: Non-retail customers (multinationals, SMEs, municipalities, residential housing associations). Eligibility assessed via the Green Alignment Assessment Tool (GAAT) with country-specific requirements.
- Classification approach and criteria:
  - Corporate exposures identified by loan purpose and transaction-level assessment aligned with EU Taxonomy and, where relevant, MNB capital relief rules; Taxonomy-aligned exposures assessed against technical screening criteria.
  - Retail exposures assessed by loan purpose and alignment with green criteria in the frameworks. DNSH and Minimum Social Safeguards were not assessed for retail; verification of minimum safeguards is performed where applicable for EU Taxonomy compliance.
- Data and systems: 2024 saw IT and controlling enhancements; further significant data infrastructure improvements are needed for group-wide tracking of sustainable exposures and use of non-financial data for classification.
- Sustainable Finance Framework: Supports both environmental and social financing; updated in 2024 with external validation (SPO) and publicly available on the Group’s website.
- Risk context note: Highlights drought as a key physical climate risk for agricultural clients; related investments may involve water supplementation with implications for surface and groundwater resources.

nodes.title: OTP Group’s Green Loan and Sustainable Finance Frameworks
nodes.heading: OTP Group’s Green Loan and Sustainable Finance Frameworks
nodes.start_phrase: The Group has developed its green loan and sustainable finance frameworks by taking into account internation best practices.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on OTP Group’s Green Loan and Sustainable Finance Frameworks, developed in line with international best practices and supported by external second-party opinions.
- Green Loan Framework updated and approved by the Hungarian National Bank in July 2023, making eligible loans qualify for MNB’s Green Corporate and Municipal Capital Relief Program (Category B).
- 2024 saw IT and controlling enhancements, but significant further improvements are needed in data infrastructure to track sustainable exposures group-wide and to use non-financial data for classification.
- Portfolio classification:
  - Corporate exposures identified as green based on loan purpose and transaction-level assessments aligned with the EU Taxonomy and MNB rules; taxonomy-aligned exposures follow EU Taxonomy technical screening criteria.
  - Retail green exposures assessed by loan purpose against framework-aligned green criteria; the Group did not assess DNSH (Do No Significant Harm) and MSS (Minimum Social Safeguards) criteria.
- Green Loan Framework expansion beyond Hungary to Bulgaria, Slovenia, Croatia, Serbia, Albania, and Montenegro, tailored to each country’s climate mitigation/adaptation priorities.
- Sector coverage:
  - EU Taxonomy: energy, manufacturing, transportation, construction & real estate, forestry, waste management.
  - CBI Taxonomy: energy, industry, transportation, buildings, land use and marine sources, waste and pollution control.
  - Also permits water management-related financing.
- Scope: non-retail customers (multinationals, SMEs, municipalities, residential housing associations). Eligibility evaluated with the Green Alignment Assessment Tool (GAAT), using country-specific conditions and documentation; verification of minimum safeguards where applicable.
- Sustainable Finance Framework supports environmental and social funding; updated in 2024 with external validation and published on OTP Group’s website.
- Context note: drought is a key physical climate risk in agriculture, with mitigation investments often involving water supplementation that can affect surface and groundwater quantity and quality.

nodes.title: Green Loan Framework

nodes.title: Sustainable Finance Framework
nodes.heading: Sustainable Finance Framework
nodes.start_phrase: OTP Group’s funding activities continued to be supported in 2024 by the @Sustainable Finance Framework , covering both environmental and social sustainability areas.
nodes.summary:
- OTP Group’s Green Loan and Sustainable Finance Frameworks are aligned with international best practices and the EU Taxonomy, endorsed by external experts (Second Party Opinions). The Green Loan Framework was updated and approved by the Hungarian National Bank (MNB) in July 2023, making eligible loans qualify for MNB’s Green Corporate and Municipal Capital Relief Program Category B.
- 2024 saw IT and controlling enhancements, but further data infrastructure improvements are needed for group-wide tracking of sustainable exposures and use of non-financial data for classification.
- Portfolio classification:
  - Corporate exposures are identified by loan purpose and transaction assessment; Taxonomy-aligned exposures follow EU Taxonomy technical screening criteria.
  - Retail exposures are assessed by loan purpose against green criteria aligned with the EU Taxonomy; DNSH and Minimum Social Safeguards were not assessed for retail.
  - The Green Alignment Assessment Tool (GAAT) supports eligibility checks with country-specific conditions; verification of minimum safeguards is included where applicable.
- Green Loan Framework:
  - Extended beyond Hungary to Bulgaria, Slovenia, Croatia, Serbia, Albania, and Montenegro.
  - Covers sectors per EU Taxonomy (energy, manufacturing, transportation, construction & real estate, forestry, waste management) and Climate Bonds Initiative Taxonomy (energy, industry, transportation, buildings, land use and marine, waste and pollution control); also includes water management-related financing.
  - Applies to non-retail clients (multinationals, SMEs, municipalities, residential housing associations).
- Sustainable Finance Framework:
  - Updated in 2024 with external validation; enables issuance of green and social instruments (including bonds) aligned with ICMA Green and Social Bond Principles and LMA Green/Social Loan Principles.
  - Excludes financing for fossil fuel production, nuclear energy, weapons/defense, mining, gambling, and tobacco.
  - Eligible green categories: green buildings, renewable energy, clean transportation.
  - Eligible social categories: job creation and unemployment mitigation, including SME financing with positive social impact.
  - Annual investor reporting on allocation and impact; 2023 Allocation and Impact Reports published; 2024 reports due summer 2025. OTP Mortgage Bank separately reports on green mortgage bond allocations.
- 2024 corporate green lending results:
  - Combined corporate green loan and bond portfolio grew from HUF 508 billion to HUF 834 billion, driven by renewable energy projects, sustainable real estate, and increased financing for biomass/biogas.
  - Green SME loans more than doubled, exceeding HUF 90 billion.
  - Launched Széchenyi Investment Loan Max+ (green variant D) in Hungary with preferential rates for green investments under KAVOSZ criteria.
  - Internal developments to embed sustainability in lending expected to further boost green volumes.
  - Subsidiaries emphasized renewable energy and electric vehicle financing; the mix of solar, wind, and hydropower varies by country due to geographic and regulatory factors.

nodes.title: Corporate Green Lending
nodes.heading: Corporate Green Lending
nodes.start_phrase: In 2024, OTP Group significantly expanded its green loan and bond portfolio, in line with its ESG strategy.
nodes.summary:
- OTP Group’s Sustainable Finance Framework enables issuance of green and social instruments aligned with ICMA Green/Social Bond Principles and LMA Green/Social Loan Principles, with strict exclusions (fossil fuels, nuclear, weapons/defense, mining, gambling, tobacco).
- Eligible use-of-proceeds categories:
  - Green: green buildings, renewable energy, clean transportation.
  - Social: job creation and unemployment mitigation, including SME financing with positive social impact.
- Transparency and reporting: annual allocation and impact reporting until full allocation; 2023 reports published, 2024 reports due summer 2025; OTP Mortgage Bank publishes annual green mortgage bond allocation reports aligned with Green Bond Principles and Hungary’s Green Mortgage Loan program.
- Corporate green financing: portfolio expanded from HUF 508bn to HUF 834bn in 2024, driven by renewable energy and sustainable real estate; increased financing of sustainable fuels (biomass/biogas); green SME loans more than doubled, surpassing HUF 90bn.
- Hungary: launch of Széchenyi Investment Loan Max+ (Option D) with KAVOSZ—state-supported green loans for SMEs at preferential rates aligned with OTP’s green criteria; internal lending process enhancements to further integrate sustainability.
- Subsidiaries: continued momentum in renewable energy and electric vehicle financing; technology mix (solar, wind, hydro) varies by country with geography/regulation.
- Real estate EU Taxonomy challenges: complex primary energy demand requirements and inconsistent national rules/documentation (energy certificates) hinder Taxonomy-based green real estate lending.
- Retail green lending: portfolio reached HUF 193bn by end-2024; HUF 25.68bn disbursed in 2024 via OTP Green Mortgage Loan and Green “Évnyerő” Mortgage Loan (differ mainly in repayment structure) for new builds, purchases, and energy-efficient renovations.
- Legacy Hungarian Green Home Program (ZOP) loans from 2021–2022 remain a major share (>HUF 150bn) focused on energy-efficient new housing.
- Croatia: strong growth in green home loans; Sunny Loan portfolio reached HUF 15bn by year-end 2024 for energy-efficient new and used homes/renovations.
- Climate risk and governance: Group Credit Risk Policy integrates ESG/climate risks into core credit risk management for non-retail and leasing; aims for safe growth within risk appetite and adaptability to market change; group-wide scope across banks and leasing companies; annual review and Board approval.
- Regulatory alignment: policy reflects MNB expectations (Recommendation 11/2022) and EBA Guidelines on loan origination and monitoring (EBA/GL/2020/06); references to ESRS E1-2, E3-1, E4-2.

nodes.title: Retail Green Lending
nodes.heading: Retail Green Lending
nodes.start_phrase: The green loan portfolio for retail customers reached HUF 193 billion by the end of 2024 .72
nodes.summary:

- Outlines the Group Credit Risk Policy under climate change policies: integrates environmental and climate risks into the broader ESG risk framework and credit risk processes, including an ESG risk assessment methodology for non-retail and leasing; aims for safe growth within risk appetite and flexibility to adapt to market changes; addresses risks related to climate mitigation, adaptation, and energy transition.

nodes.title: 2.2. Climate Change
nodes.heading: 2.2. Climate Change
nodes.start_phrase: As OTP Group continues to expand its international exposure, the complexity of lending processes and the range of credit products it offers have increased.
nodes.summary:
- Real estate financing faces difficulty meeting EU Taxonomy criteria due to primary energy demand calculations and uneven national rules/documentation (energy certificates), hindering green loan issuance.
- Retail green lending highlights:
  - Total retail green portfolio reached HUF 193 billion by end-2024.
  - HUF 25.68 billion disbursed in 2024 via two products launched in 2023 (OTP Green Mortgage Loan and Green “Évnyerő” Mortgage Loan) aimed at new home purchases/construction and energy-efficient renovations; they differ in repayment structure.
  - Hungarian Green Home Program (2021–2022) remains the largest component, exceeding HUF 150 billion, focused on energy-efficient new homes.
  - In Croatia, the green home loan portfolio grew strongly to HUF 15 billion; the Sunny Loan supports new/used home purchases and renovations that meet energy efficiency criteria.
- Climate Change Policies (ESRS E1-2, E3-1, E4-2): Group Credit Risk Policy
  - Establishes group-wide minimum credit risk management requirements amid growing international exposure and product complexity.
  - Integrates ESG, including environmental and climate risks, into the main risk management framework.
  - Embeds an ESG credit risk assessment methodology for non-retail and leasing transactions; designed to be flexible to market changes.
  - Addresses risks tied to climate change mitigation, adaptation, and the energy transition.
  - Scope: applies to domestic and international banking and financial subsidiaries, including leasing companies.
  - Governance: reviewed annually and approved by OTP Bank’s Board of Directors.
  - Alignment: consistent with MNB Recommendation 11/2022 on ESG within credit risk management and EBA Guidelines on loan origination and monitoring (EBA/GL/2020/06).
- Footnote clarification: the HUF 193 billion reflects current exposure of green product structures in Hungary and certain subsidiaries; a significant domestic share qualifies for the MNB green capital requirement discount; excludes green mortgages tied to non-green structures.

nodes.title: Group Credit Risk Policy
nodes.heading: Group Credit Risk Policy
nodes.start_phrase: As OTP Group continues to expand its international exposure, the complexity of lending processes and the range of credit products it offers have increased.
nodes.summary:
- Highlights challenges aligning real estate financing with EU Taxonomy, chiefly due to differing national rules and availability of energy certificates, complicating green loan provision based on primary energy demand.
- Reports retail green lending progress:
  - Total retail green portfolio reached HUF 193 billion by end-2024.
  - HUF 25.68 billion disbursed in 2024 via OTP Green Mortgage Loan and Green “Évnyerő” Mortgage Loan (for new energy-efficient homes, construction, and renovations; differing repayment structures).
  - Hungarian Green Home Program (2021–2022) remains the bulk (> HUF 150 billion) focused on energy-efficient new builds/purchases.
  - In Croatia, the Sunny Loan portfolio grew to HUF 15 billion, supporting energy-efficient purchases, construction, and renovations.
- Outlines climate-related policies (with ESRS references):
  - Group Credit Risk Policy: sets group-wide minimum credit risk requirements; integrates ESG/climate risks across risk types; includes an ESG credit risk framework for non-retail and leasing; reviewed annually by OTP Bank’s Board; aligned with MNB Recommendation 11/2022 and EBA loan origination/monitoring guidelines.
  - Corporate Lending Policy (OLLP): defines corporate lending principles, risk appetite, ESG risk integration, assessment methods, and ESG-related limits; group-wide standard requiring subsidiaries to embed ESG (Russia and Uzbekistan exempt from mandatory ESG implementation in 2025); approvals at Board/local levels.
  - Asset management climate policies under SFDR/PAI: OTP Fund Management, OTP Real Estate Fund Management, and DSK Asset Management commit to reducing GHG emissions/carbon footprint and energy intensity through investment selection and potential divestment; CEOs accountable; policies publicly available.
- Notes absence of specific policies on water, biodiversity, and ecosystems pending deeper risk analysis; affirms environmental commitment in the Group’s Code of Ethics.
- Sets targets (ESRS E1-4, E3-3, E4-4, E1-9):
  - Portfolio-specific GHG emission reduction target (climate target setting).
  - Green lending growth target.

nodes.title: Corporate Lending Policy / Operational Lending Limits and Guidelines (OLLP)
nodes.heading: Corporate Lending Policy / Operational Lending Limits and Guidelines (OLLP)
nodes.start_phrase: The Corporate Lending Policy (OLLP) defines the general principles of corporate lending, including segment - and product -specific guidelines, related financing conditions and operational lending limits.
nodes.summary:
- The section outlines OTP Group’s Corporate Lending Policy (OLLP), which sets group-wide principles for corporate lending, including segment- and product-specific guidelines, financing conditions, and operational lending limits. It embeds ESG risk integration, adds lending guidelines for environmental and climate risks, defines how to assess related financial risks, and sets ESG-related limits tied to significant loan portfolio risks in climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, and energy.
- Scope and governance: The policy applies across the Group; subsidiaries must integrate ESG elements into local lending policies. Russian and Uzbek subsidiaries are exempt from mandatory ESG implementation in 2025 but have received voluntary guidance. The Hungarian policy is approved by OTP Bank’s Board; subsidiaries’ policies are approved locally.
- Asset management climate policies: Certain OTP Group asset managers have adopted climate mitigation policies under SFDR, disclosed via Principal Adverse Impact (PAI) Statements. OTP Fund Management targets reductions in GHG emissions/carbon footprint and energy intensity through careful investment selection and possible divestment. OTP Real Estate Fund Management aims for a declining trend in GHG and energy indicators. DSK Asset Management has a general mitigation goal. Scope covers OTP Asset Management, DSK Asset Management, and OTP Real Estate Investment Fund Management; CEOs are accountable; policies are publicly available on company websites via PAI statements.
- The Group currently has no policies on water, biodiversity, and ecosystems; development is pending deeper risk analysis. The Code of Ethics affirms commitment to environmental sustainability.
- Targets (ESRS E1-4, E3-3, E4-4, E1-9): Two main climate goals—(1) a portfolio-specific GHG emission reduction target as part of climate target setting and (2) a green lending target—applicable to climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, and energy.

nodes.title: Climate Change Mitigation policies in Asset Management
nodes.heading: Climate Change Mitigation policies in Asset Management
nodes.start_phrase: Certain OTP Group asset management companies have adopted climate change mitigation policies as part of their Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation ( SFDR ).73
nodes.summary:
- Corporate Lending Policy (OLLP): Sets Group-wide principles, segment/product lending guidelines, financing conditions, and operational lending limits. Integrates ESG risks consistently, including specific guidance on environmental and climate risks and related financial risk assessment tools and limits. Links lending limits to material portfolio risks in climate mitigation, climate adaptation, and energy. Subsidiaries must embed ESG elements in local policies; Russian and Uzbek subsidiaries are exempt from mandatory ESG implementation in 2025 (voluntary guidance provided). OTP Bank’s Board approves the Hungarian policy; local bodies approve subsidiary policies.

- Asset management climate policies: Selected OTP Group asset managers apply climate change mitigation policies under SFDR via PAI Statements. OTP Fund Management targets reductions in GHG emissions/carbon footprint and energy intensity by selective investment and, if needed, phasing out holdings. OTP Real Estate Fund Management aims for a sustained decline in GHG and energy-use indicators. DSK Asset Management targets general impact mitigation. Scope covers OTP AM, DSK AM, and OTP Real Estate Investment Fund Management; CEOs are accountable. Policies are publicly available on company websites.

- Other environmental policies: No Group policies yet on water, biodiversity, and ecosystems; development requires deeper risk analysis. The Code of Ethics affirms commitment to environmental sustainability.

- Targets and climate target setting (ESRS E1-4, E3-3, E4-4, E1-9): Two main goals—reduce financed portfolio GHG emissions and increase green lending. In 2024, OTP set 2030 targets for financed emissions aligned with IEA NZE 2050 scenarios and national decarbonization plans, tailored to the Group’s portfolio mix. Targets are interpreted as a baseline contingent on a successful global transition; OTP cannot ensure outcomes unilaterally but will take measures within its influence. Primary metric: intensity of financed Scope 1–2 emissions (gCO2e per euro of exposure) for the loan portfolio excluding sovereigns; relative reduction is prioritized over absolute levels. Absolute targets are derived from relative ones using a static balance sheet assumption and are considered secondary. No interim targets to 2030 due to data and methodological uncertainty. 2030 goal: -29.8% vs 2023, reducing intensity from 219 to 154 gCO2e/euro (HUF reported with 2023 FX held constant).

nodes.title: Climate target setting
nodes.heading: Climate target setting
nodes.start_phrase: In line with regulatory expectations, in 2024 OTP Group defined targets75 to reduce its financed GHG emissions by 2030.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: OTP Group’s climate target setting and green lending objectives within the 2024 Integrated Annual Report (Management Report, consolidated).
- Target-setting framework:
  - 2030 financed emissions targets derived from IEA Net Zero 2050 scenarios and national decarbonization plans, adjusted for OTP’s country/asset/sector portfolio mix.
  - Targets represent a “baseline scenario”: if the wider economy follows NZE 2050 and OTP’s client mix does not become more carbon‑intensive, the Group should meet its targets; OTP cannot ensure achievement if the external trajectory diverges.
  - Targets apply to financing provided by OTP Group (not to assets managed by OTP’s asset/fund managers).
- Primary 2030 target (financed Scope 1–2, excluding sovereign):
  - Relative intensity reduction of -29.8% vs 2023.
  - Intensity from 0.57 g CO2e/HUF (≈219 g/€) to 0.40 g CO2e/HUF (≈154 g/€); CAGR of -4.9%.
  - Static balance sheet illustration: total financed Scope 1–2 emissions decline from 9,183,905 tCO2e (2023) to 6,447,102 tCO2e (2030).
  - Calculated using PCAF Scope 3 Category 15 financed emissions; reported in HUF per CSRD, assuming constant 2023 HUF/EUR; no interim targets due to data/method limits and scenario granularity.
- Supplementary absolute targets:
  - Required by regulation; derived from relative targets under a static balance sheet assumption.
  - Deemed subordinate: meeting relative targets is considered success even if absolute targets are missed (e.g., due to acquisitions or market share changes).
- Broader portfolio target (all financed GHGs, incl. Scopes 1–3 and sovereign):
  - Intensity reduction of -32.6% from 1.13 to 0.76 g CO2e/HUF by 2030; CAGR -5.5%.
  - Static balance sheet illustration: total financed GHGs from 25,007,832 to 16,855,279 tCO2e.
  - Acknowledges high methodological uncertainty, especially for Scope 3 and sovereign; OTP will judge success primarily against the Scope 1–2 (ex‑sovereign) relative target.
- Uncertainty and revision policy:
  - Financed emissions quantification has high uncertainty; OTP may retroactively adjust base year data, indicators, or targets as data/methods improve or due to inflation, portfolio shifts, policy changes, or other events, with explanations provided.
- Potential steering measures (directional, discretionary, not commitments):
  - Options include: more green loans; lower financing ratios (attribution factor); reduce/exit financing of coal‑fueled power plants and mining; reduce exposure to heavy industries and vehicle loans; finance more electric cars.
  - Estimated impacts expressed as reductions in g CO2e per HUF (or €) of exposure reallocated; estimates based on 2023 intensities, static balance sheet, and not fully scalable; implementation may be constrained by maturities, demand, feasibility, and broader considerations (financial, social, stakeholder impacts, energy security).
  - Approval of the climate target‑setting document by the Executive Steering Committee planned for 05.02.2025; OTP Group currently has no transition plan (decision on development expected soon).
- Green lending target:
  - Goal to build a HUF 1,500 billion green loan portfolio by 2025, supporting a fair and gradual transition; applies in all countries except Russia (consumer‑lending focus) and Ukraine (war conditions).
  - Green exposures include corporate green loans/bonds and retail green loans per OTP’s definition.
  - Target is not science‑based; aligned with transition financing and expected to support revenue growth.
  - Portfolio growth trajectory shown: ~HUF 267bn (2022), 656bn (2023), 1,027bn (2024), plan 1,500bn (2025).
- Operational emissions and additional targets:
  - No group‑level operational climate mitigation goal yet; some subsidiaries have partial Scope 1–2 targets; a Paris‑aligned group target planned for 2026.
  - OTP Bank aims for carbon‑neutral operations by 2030 (Scope 1–2 net‑zero to 0 tCO2e), not science‑based and no base year specified; uses green electricity; 2024 market‑based Scope 1–2 emissions were 6,644 tCO2e, mainly from natural gas and vehicle fuels; plan to reduce property and fleet intensity to be finalized in 2025.
  - Year‑to‑year comparability limited due to ESRS methodology changes.

nodes.title: Green lending target
nodes.heading: Green lending target
nodes.start_phrase: As in its ESG strategy declared in 2021, OTP Group's unchanged goal is to play a regional leading role in financing a fair and gradual transition to a low -carbon economy and to build a sustainable future with responsible solutions.81
nodes.summary:
- Focus: OTP Group’s green lending ambitions and climate-related operational targets within the 2024 Integrated Annual Report.
- Green lending target: Build a HUF 1,500 billion green loan portfolio by 2025, aiming to lead regionally in financing a fair, gradual transition to a low‑carbon economy.
- Scope of green exposures: Includes corporate green loans and bonds, plus retail green loans per OTP Group’s internal definition.
- Country coverage: Green lending pursued in all countries except Russia (consumer lending dominates) and Ukraine (war prevents standards‑compliant green lending).
- Nature of target: Not science‑based; aligned with business objective to finance transition and drive revenue growth; developed with input from relevant OTP departments.
- Progress: Group green exposure has been measured since 2022 and shows steady growth through 2024, with a plan to reach HUF 1,500 billion in 2025 (2024 around HUF 1,027 billion).
- Operational climate targets: No group‑level mitigation target yet; some subsidiaries have partial Scope 1–2 targets. A Paris‑aligned, group‑level target is planned for 2026. Emissions are monitored, but reduction effectiveness is not yet measured.
- OTP Bank (parent) target: Carbon‑neutral operations by 2030 for Scope 1–2 (absolute net‑zero, no base year specified), not science‑based; departments involved in setting the goal.
- 2024 emissions: OTP Bank market‑based Scope 1–2 emissions were 6,644 tCO2e; electricity largely from green energy; ~75% of emissions from natural gas and vehicle fuel. A property and fleet emissions‑intensity reduction plan is in preparation, to be finalized in 2025.
- Reporting notes: Green financing spans all ESRS climate subtopics; comparability with prior years is limited due to ESRS methodology changes.

nodes.title: Additional targets
nodes.heading: Additional targets
nodes.start_phrase: We do not publish a group -level goal for operational activities related to climate change mitigation.
nodes.summary:
- OTP Group’s 2021 ESG strategy targets a regional leadership role in financing a fair, gradual transition to a low‑carbon economy.
- Green lending target: build a HUF 1,500 billion green loan portfolio by 2025 at group level. Green lending applies in all countries except Russia (consumer lending predominant) and Ukraine (war; no standard‑compliant green lending until conflict ends).
- Definition and governance: “Green exposures” include corporate green loans/bonds and retail green loans per OTP’s own taxonomy. The goal is not science‑based but aligned with transition financing and expected to drive revenue growth; relevant internal departments set the target. Green exposures have been measured since 2022.
- Progress toward target (end‑year group portfolio): 2022 HUF 267 bn; 2023 HUF 656 bn; 2024 HUF 1,027 bn; 2025 plan HUF 1,500 bn.
- Operational climate targets: no group‑level mitigation target yet; some subsidiaries have partial Scope 1–2 goals. A Paris‑aligned group target is planned for 2026. Emissions are monitored, but effectiveness of reduction measures is not comprehensively measured.
- OTP Bank (Hungary) operational goal: carbon‑neutral Scope 1–2 operations by 2030 (absolute net‑zero, no base year; not science‑based). 2024 market‑based Scope 1–2 emissions: 6,644 tCO2e. Electricity largely from green sources; ~75% of emissions from natural gas and vehicle fuels. A plan to cut property and fleet emissions intensity is being prepared for completion in 2025.
- Subsidiary actions: several foreign subsidiaries commit to reducing operational emissions, chiefly via green electricity procurement; monitoring occurs locally, with no group aggregation of effectiveness.
- Water, biodiversity, ecosystems: no group targets yet; only limited water‑related measures exist; effectiveness not monitored. Further impact assessment is needed before defining measures.
- Actions and resources (ESRS references): two main measure packages—(1) portfolio‑specific measures tied to climate target setting (ESRS E1‑4) and (2) green lending measures; OTP Fund Management contributes via funds with environmental objectives. Operational GHG reduction measures are less material and reported in aggregate.
- Scope 1–2 reduction measures underway/planned: green electricity purchasing (Hungary, Slovenia, Croatia, Serbia in 2024; continuation in 2025), lighting/boiler replacements, HVAC optimization, insulation, solar panels. Serbia and Albania moved to more energy‑efficient HQs; Albania HQ is LEED Gold. Effectiveness tracked at subsidiary level; not consolidated.
- GHG emissions reporting: ESRS E1‑6 table (gross Scope 1, 2, 3) referenced; comparability with earlier years limited due to ESRS methodology changes.

nodes.title: Actions and resources
nodes.heading: Actions and resources
nodes.start_phrase: OTP Group has defined two main packages of measures regarding climate change: firstly, the portfolio -specific measures defined within the climate target setting detailed in the @E1 -4 disclosure requirement, and secondly, the green lending measures83 presented in chapter @2.1. 2 and @Credit Rating .
nodes.summary:
- Focus on OTP Group’s ESG approach to climate and environmental topics within the 2024 Integrated Annual Report, aligned to ESRS (E1-3, E3-2, E4-3, and E1-6).
- Subsidiaries have committed to reducing operational emissions, primarily via green electricity procurement; emissions are monitored, but the effectiveness of reduction measures is not comprehensively measured or aggregated.
- The Group currently has no defined goals for water, biodiversity, or ecosystems and does not monitor the effectiveness of related policies; further impact assessment is needed before setting measures (only limited water-related measures exist).
- Two main climate action packages: portfolio-specific measures tied to climate target setting (referenced in E1-4) and green lending initiatives; OTP Fund Management contributes through funds with environmental objectives.
- Operational Scope 1–2 reduction measures are considered less significant overall and summarized at aggregate level; key actions include:
  - Extensive green electricity procurement (notably in 2024 by OTP Bank, OTP Bank Slovenia, OTP Bank Croatia, and OTP Bank Serbia, with continuation planned for 2025).
  - Energy-efficiency upgrades (lighting and boiler replacements, HVAC optimization, insulation, and solar installations).
  - Moves to more efficient headquarters in Serbia and Albania (Albania HQ LEED Gold).
  - Effectiveness tracked at subsidiary level with diverse methods; results not consolidated.
- Biodiversity and ecosystem measures have not yet been defined pending deeper impact analysis.
- OTP Group’s gross Scope 1, Scope 2, and Scope 3 GHG emissions and intensity are presented (per ESRS E1-6) in a table referenced but not included in this excerpt.
- Note that the cited measures also relate to climate mitigation/adaptation, energy, and water withdrawal.

nodes.title: Emissions, GHG Intensity
nodes.heading: Emissions, GHG Intensity
nodes.start_phrase: OTP Group 's gross Scope 1, Scope 2, and Scope 3 GHG emissions are presented in the table below.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on OTP Group’s climate and environmental management within its 2024 Integrated Annual Report, aligned with ESRS requirements (E1-3, E3-2, E4-3, E1-6).
- Subsidiaries commit to reducing operational emissions, mainly via green electricity procurement; emissions are monitored, but effectiveness of reduction measures is not aggregated group-wide.
- No group-level goals yet for water, biodiversity, or ecosystems; effectiveness of related policies is not monitored, pending deeper impact assessments (water has some measures).
- Two principal climate action packages: portfolio-specific measures tied to climate target-setting and an expanded green lending program; OTP Fund Management contributes via funds with environmental objectives.
- Operational Scope 1–2 reduction measures are secondary and implemented mainly by larger banks: green electricity purchasing (notably in Hungary, Slovenia, Croatia, Serbia, with continuation planned for 2025), LED/lighting and boiler replacements, HVAC optimization, insulation, solar panels, and relocation to energy-efficient buildings (Albania HQ LEED Gold).
- 2024 GHG emissions reported:
  - Scope 1: 118,470 tCO2e.
  - Scope 2: 58,076 tCO2e (location-based) and 48,834 tCO2e (market-based); 0% from emissions trading schemes.
  - Scope 3 (significant Category 15 – investments): 24,835,989 tCO2e, down 1% vs 2023; 2030 milestone at 16,855,279 tCO2e, implying a planned annual reduction rate of about 5.5% from the base year.
  - Biogenic emissions: 734 t in 2024.
- Total 2024 GHG intensity: 5.85 tCO2e per million HUF net revenue (both location- and market-based).
- Use of certified green energy: 36.49% of total electricity consumption covered by guarantees of origin/RECs; no certified district heating; 31.23% of Scope 2-related energy consumption is certified.
- Scope 3 reporting exclusions: financed emissions of assets managed by OTP’s fund management subsidiaries (not consolidated assets) and, for 2023 data, the OTP Bank Romania group.
- Financed emissions perspective (2023): OTP considers the sum of financed Scope 1–2 emissions across PCAF asset classes (excluding sovereigns) as the most reliable indicator—about 9.2 million tCO2e; 73% from business loans, 20% from vehicle financing, with real estate portfolios contributing a small share; client Scope 3 and sovereign estimates deemed highly uncertain.
- Allocation of 2024 operational emissions between the consolidated financial reporting group and operational management shows minor differences (e.g., Scope 1: 114,940 vs 3,530 tCO2e; Scope 2 market-based: 41,561 vs 7,273 tCO2e), reflecting internal management boundaries.
- Emphasis that biodiversity/ecosystem measures are not yet defined; further impact analysis is required before setting targets or tracking effectiveness.
- Overall, the section consolidates OTP Group’s climate actions, operational efficiency steps, green energy uptake, financed emissions stance, and key 2024 GHG metrics, while noting gaps in non-climate environmental target-setting and measurement.

nodes.title: Scope 3 / Category 15 emissions
nodes.heading: Scope 3 / Category 15 emissions
nodes.start_phrase: Scope 3 / 15 emissions are also referred to as "OTP Group financed emissions" or "our financed emissions".
nodes.summary:
- Focuses on OTP Group’s greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions for 2024 with comparisons to 2023 and longer-term milestones.
- Scope 1 emissions in 2024: 118,470 tCO2e; 0% under regulated emissions trading schemes. Biogenic emissions: 734 t.

Notes high uncertainty in Scope 3 and sovereign estimates.

nodes.title: Financed GHG emissions (Scope 3 / Category 15) of OTP Group in 2024
nodes.heading: Financed GHG emissions (Scope 3 / Category 15) of OTP Group in 2024
nodes.start_phrase: OTP Group prepared a preliminary estimation for its financed emissions for 2024.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: OTP Group’s financed greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions (Scope 3, Category 15) reported under the PCAF standard, with detailed breakdowns by asset class for 2023 (excluding OBR Group) and preliminary estimates for 2024, plus financed-emission intensities and data quality notes.
- Asset classes covered: listed equity and corporate bonds; business loans, unlisted equity and project loans; commercial real estate financing; mortgages; vehicle loans; and sovereign debt (tracked separately and excluded from the main climate target).
- 2023 highlights:
  - Total exposure: ~HUF 22.1 trillion; average PCAF data quality score: 3.5.
  - Key metric for targets: financed Scope 1–2 intensity excluding sovereigns = 0.57 g CO2e/HUF.
  - Most GHG-intensive segments: corporate/business lending and vehicle financing.
  - Emission intensities by asset class show highest values in vehicle loans and business lending; mortgages and commercial real estate are much lower. Some scope items are marked n.a. where not applicable.
- 2024 preliminary estimates:
  - Total exposure: ~HUF 26.7 trillion; average PCAF data quality score: 3.3.
  - Total financed emissions across scopes reported by asset class; financed Scope 1–2 intensity excluding sovereigns = 0.47 g CO2e/HUF, a 19% decrease vs 2023.
  - Drivers of the decline: HUF depreciation vs EUR; repayment by major polluters; reduced attribution factors as some borrowers’ balance sheets grew while OTP loans stayed flat; lower share of heavy machinery in vehicle financing; and changes in data quality. Most drivers are outside OTP’s control.
  - Caution: the decline should not be seen as a trend; OTP flags limitations and low robustness in PCAF methodology, noting potential for reversal next year.
  - Asset-class intensities remain highest in vehicle loans, then business loans and listed equity/corporate bonds; mortgages and commercial real estate stay low; sovereign intensity drops from 0.76 to 0.67 g CO2e/HUF.
- Data limitations: 2024 estimates are based on less complete borrower data due to reporting lags (e.g., 2024 financials available only by May 2025), affecting estimation certainty.
- Managed assets: Group asset/fund managers’ financed emissions estimated at ~5.8 Mt CO2e in 2024 (coverage-adjusted), calculated by MSCI (real estate funds internally). These are not included in OTP Group’s consolidated financed emissions because the assets are not owned or consolidated.

nodes.title: Financed Emissions of Managed Assets
nodes.heading: Financed Emissions of Managed Assets
nodes.start_phrase: Besides the above, OTP Group has group members which are asset and fund managers.
nodes.summary:
- Presents OTP Group’s 2024 financed emissions (Scope 3/Category 15) by PCAF asset classes, including exposures, financed Scope 1/2/3, totals, and average data quality scores; sovereign debt is reported separately.

- Explains drivers of the intensity decrease: HUF/EUR FX effect, repayment by major emitters, changes in borrower balance sheets reducing attribution factors, lower share of heavy machinery in vehicle financing, and data quality changes; warns results are not predictive and highlights PCAF methodology limitations and potential volatility.
- Reports financed emissions of assets managed by OTP’s asset/fund managers at an estimated 5.8 MtCO2e (coverage-adjusted) for 2024; estimates by MSCI except real estate funds; these are not counted in OTP Group’s financed emissions because the assets are not owned/consolidated.
- Describes carbon credits and removals: OTP Bank retired 7,000 tCO2e VCS (Verra) credits from the St. Nikola Wind Farm (Bulgaria) to cover Scope 1–2; not a corresponding adjustment under Paris Agreement Article 6; net-zero Scope 1–2 by 2030 remains the goal. Plans to transition from offsets to ecosystem restoration certificates.

nodes.title: ESG risk management
nodes.heading: 2.4. ESG risk management
nodes.start_phrase: The Group pays particular attention to managing ESG risks and implementing climate protection aspects into business practices.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Excerpt from OTP Bank Group’s Consolidated Management Report in the 2024 Integrated Annual Report, covering GHG intensity methodology and ESG risk management (including credit risk integration).

- GHG intensity:
  - Metric defined as Total GHG emissions (tCO2e) divided by Net revenue (in million HUF).
  - Calculated using both location-based and market-based methods.
  - Net revenue per IFRS equals Interest income and similar + Fee and commission income + Other operating income, referencing the 2024 consolidated income statement.

- ESG risk management governance and oversight:
  - Alignment with Hungarian National Bank Green Recommendation 10/2022 on climate and environmental risks; regular reporting to the Board, Management Committee, ESG Committee, and Risk Management Committee.
  - Monitoring EBA and ECB supervisory expectations; ECB JST supervision applies to DSK Bank (Bulgaria) and OTP Bank Slovenia; DSK, Slovenia, and Croatia integrate ESG risk per local supervisory rules.
  - ESG risk managed through extensive internal, non-public frameworks and policies (governance, three lines of defense, remuneration and performance rules, credit/market/operational risk policies, risk strategy and appetite, corporate lending/OLLP, greenwashing risk directive, collateral valuation, etc.).
  - Voluntary standards referenced: NGFS, GHG Protocol, PCAF.

- Integration of ESG risks into group risk management:
  - ESG incorporated into Group Risk Strategy, Risk Appetite Statement (RAS), risk-type frameworks, and OLLP; gradual introduction of ESG-related risk limits already in RAS and OLLP.
  - A group-level ESG risk strategy (2023–2025) to deepen ESG factor implementation, including:
    - Climate and Environmental Materiality Assessment of significant sectors across short (<1 year), medium (1–5 years), and long (>5 years) horizons (aligned with EBA timeframes, differing from standard OTP horizons).
    - Development of the Group Climate and Environmental Risk Heatmap.
    - Further refinement of ESG-related risk appetite and limits to support a sustainable portfolio.

- Credit risk (corporate lending):
  - Since 2021, a corporate ESG risk framework applies, comprising:
    - ESG exclusion list for prohibited/controversial activities.
    - Sectoral ESG risk heatmap mapping NACE activities by environmental/social impact.
    - Client- and transaction-level ESG risk assessment and due diligence; for motor-vehicle leasing, ESG category based on engine environmental impact (EU emission standards).
  - Continuous enhancement of methods as data/methodologies evolve.
  - Regulatory compliance in Hungary: from 2025, phased adoption of MNB-mandated special examination framework and minimum ESG questionnaire for client due diligence.
  - OLLP (except for Uzbek and Russian subsidiaries) includes environmental/climate risk lending guidance, financial risk assessment based on environmental risks, and dedicated renewable energy financing guidelines and examination frameworks.
  - Internal (currently non-public) policy on coal mining and coal-based power financing under review, with intent to publish upon completion.

nodes.title: ESG Risk Management Function and Integration of ESG Risks into Risk Management Procedure
nodes.heading: 2.4.1. ESG Risk Management Function and Integration of ESG Risks into Risk Management Procedure
nodes.start_phrase: OTP Bank has incorporated ESG risks into its group -level risk management guidelines and procedures, enabling the identification and management of these risks to minimize emerging credit, reputational, regulatory, and legal risks.

- Describes integration of ESG risks across OTP Group’s risk ecosystem: Group Risk Strategy, Risk Appetite Statement (RAS), risk-type frameworks, and Operational Lending Limits and Guidelines (OLLP), with a gradual approach to ESG-related risk limits.
- Introduces a 2023–2025 group-level ESG risk strategy to deepen implementation and awareness, including:
  - Climate and Environmental Materiality Assessment of physical and transition risks over short (<1 year), medium (1–5 years), and long (>5 years) horizons.
  - Enhancements to ESG elements of risk appetite, setting limits to support a sustainable portfolio.
  - Development of a Group-level Climate and Environmental Risk Heatmap and implementation of relevant environmental factors.
- Details corporate credit risk management for ESG:
  - Since 2021, application of an ESG framework in corporate lending built on an exclusion list, a sectoral ESG risk heatmap (by NACE), and client/transaction-level ESG risk assessments.
  - Special methodology for motorized leasing based on vehicle emission standards.
  - Ongoing method refinement as data and methodologies improve.
