- Outlines OLLP corporate lending guidelines (excluding Uzbek and Russian subsidiaries) that embed environmental/climate risk criteria and financial risk assessment rules; includes guidance for financing renewable energy projects.
- Mentions an internal, non-public coal mining and coal-based energy financing guideline under review, with intent to publish after completion.
- Emphasizes the aim to mitigate credit, reputational, regulatory, and legal risks through comprehensive ESG risk integration.

nodes.title: Credit Risk
nodes.heading: 2.4.2. Credit Risk
nodes.start_phrase: To manage the credit risk aspect of ESG risks, OTP Group has been applying its ESG risk management framework in corporate lending since 2021.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and standards: Outlines OTP Bank Group’s ESG risk management approach, aligned with NGFS, GHG Protocol, and PCAF.
- ESG integration in risk management: Embeds ESG across group risk strategy, Risk Appetite Statement, risk-type frameworks, and Operational Lending Limits and Guidelines (OLLP), with a gradual rollout of ESG-related limits.
- ESG risk strategy (2023–2025): Establishes group-level ESG focus programs; conducts Climate and Environmental Materiality Assessment for significant sectors across short (<1 year), medium (1–5 years), and long (>5 years) horizons aligned with EBA; informs the Group Climate & Environmental Risk Heatmap and refines ESG elements of risk appetite and limits.
- Corporate credit risk framework (since 2021): Uses an ESG exclusion list, a sectoral ESG risk heatmap (by NACE), and client/transaction-level ESG risk assessments; applies a distinct method for motorized leasing based on EU vehicle emission standards; methods evolve with data/methodology enhancements.
- Regulatory alignment (Hungary): Preparing to comply with the MNB’s 2025 phased requirements, including a special examination framework and minimum ESG questionnaire for environmental/climate risk due diligence.
- Policies and sectoral guidance: OLLP (excluding Uzbek and Russian subsidiaries) includes environmental/climate risk lending and financial risk assessment guidance; adds guidelines for renewable energy financing; maintains an internal coal-related financing guideline under review with intent to publish.
- ESG limits and monitoring: Implements group-level limits tied to the exclusion list; introduced 2023 numerical limits in Hungary and select subsidiaries to cap high-ESG-risk new transactions; limits recorded in the Risk Appetite Statement or Corporate Lending Policy (non-public); compliance monitored monthly/quarterly; plans for additional ESG-specific limits and lending guidelines. Monthly group ESG credit exposure reporting to the Credit and Limit Committee and quarterly to the Board.
- Collateral management—immovable property: OTP Mortgage Bank’s ESG methodology for commercial real estate in Hungary (since Feb 2023) with simplified E/S/G factors, to be expanded per C&E Materiality Assessment; ESG data fields in corporate loan/collateral systems, partially auto-populated from the state Lechner Knowledge Center (e.g., energy efficiency). Methodology sharing with subsidiaries ongoing.
- Retail real estate classification: Residential collateral categorized by energy rating (Low A+++–B; Medium C–D; Moderately high E–F; High G–I), updated quarterly to track transition risk; physical risk factors (drought, flood, heatwave) integrated into valuation and monitoring.
- Collateral management—movable property: IT-supported ESG framework for vehicle collateral, classifying into ESG1–ESG4 with results shown in the collateral registry; methodologies disseminated to subsidiaries. Merkantil Bank applies its own ESG methodology for leasing assets per Group Credit Risk Policy appendix.

nodes.title: Collateral management
nodes.heading: Collateral management
nodes.start_phrase: In the case of collateralized commercial real estate, the ESG assessment methodology developed by OTP Mortgage Bank has been applied in the Hungarian operations since February 2023.
nodes.summary:
- Establishment and expansion of group-level ESG credit risk limits, including a 2023 numerical cap in Hungary and select subsidiaries to limit high-ESG-risk share of new transactions; limits embedded in the Risk Appetite Statement and Corporate Lending Policy, monitored monthly/quarterly.
- Ongoing development of ESG risk methodology with plans for additional risk limits and ESG-specific lending guidelines.
- Regular internal reporting of ESG credit risk exposure: monthly to the Credit and Limit Committee and quarterly to the Board for the corporate loan portfolio.
- Collateral management enhancements focused on ESG:
  - Commercial real estate: OTP Mortgage Bank’s ESG assessment applied in Hungary since Feb 2023, using simplified E/S/G factors to be expanded per C&E Materiality Assessment; ESG data fields added to systems; partial automation via the state Lechner Knowledge Center; emphasis on energy efficiency metrics; sharing methodology with subsidiaries in progress.
  - Subsidiaries: rollout of ESG methodologies for vehicle-related collateral per agreed timelines; Merkantil Bank uses its own ESG methodology for leasing assets per Group Credit Risk Policy.
  - Immovable property: recording of location, technical, and energy characteristics; ESG-specific data fields enabled in corporate collateral registries.
  - Retail residential collateral: classification by energy rating into Low (A+++–B), Medium (C–D), Moderately high (E–F), and High (G–I) risk tiers; quarterly updates to track portfolio transition risk.
  - Integration of physical climate risk (drought, flood, heatwave) into valuation and monitoring.
  - Movable vehicle collateral: IT-supported ESG risk identification framework; classification into ESG1/2/3/4 categories shown in the corporate collateral registry; guidelines shared with subsidiaries.

nodes.title: Immovable property
nodes.heading: Immovable property
nodes.start_phrase: OTP Mortgage Bank considers and records the location, technical, and energy characteristics of commercial or residential real estate in its own records during the valuation of real estate collateral.
nodes.summary:
- The Group is expanding ESG-related credit risk limits: a group-level limit on the ESG exclusion list and, since 2023, numerical caps in Hungary and certain subsidiaries to restrict the share of new high-ESG-risk transactions. These limits are set in the Risk Appetite Statement and Corporate Lending Policy (not public) and monitored monthly and quarterly. Further ESG-specific lending guidelines and limits are planned.
- From 2023, the Group produces monthly internal reports on ESG credit risk exposure for the corporate loan portfolio to the Credit and Limit Committee and quarterly reports to the Board of Directors.
- Collateral management integrates ESG: OTP Mortgage Bank’s ESG assessment for commercial real estate has been applied in Hungary since February 2023, reflecting the bank’s significant CRE exposure. ESG data fields were added to the corporate loan registry, partially auto-populated from the state Lechner Knowledge Center, prioritizing energy efficiency metrics. Methodology sharing with subsidiaries is in progress.
- Subsidiary implementation: ESG methodologies for vehicle-related collateral are being rolled out per agreed timelines. Merkantil Bank applies its own ESG methodology for leasing assets under the Group Credit Risk Policy appendix.
- Immovable property: OTP Mortgage Bank records location, technical, and energy characteristics for real estate collateral; ESG-specific data fields are in place. In retail, residential collateral is categorized by energy rating to track transition risk quarterly: Low (A+++–B), Medium (C–D), Moderately high (E–F), High (G–I).
- Physical climate risks (drought, flood, heatwave) are embedded in real estate collateral valuation and monitoring.
- Movable property (vehicles): An IT-supported framework classifies vehicle collateral into ESG1/2/3/4 categories, with results shown in the corporate collateral registry; guidance is being disseminated to subsidiaries.

nodes.title: Movable Property
nodes.heading: Movable Property
nodes.start_phrase: For movable collateral relating to vehicles, OTP Bank has also developed an IT -supported framework for identifying ESG risks.
nodes.summary:
- The Group embeds ESG considerations into credit risk management through limits and policies:
  - A group-level ESG exclusion list is applied, with a 2023 numerical cap (Hungary and some subsidiaries) on the share of new high-ESG-risk transactions.
  - Limits are set in the Risk Appetite Statement or Corporate Lending Policy (not public), monitored monthly and quarterly.
  - Methodology is being enhanced, with plans for additional ESG risk limits and ESG-specific lending guidelines.
  - Since 2023, monthly group-level ESG credit risk exposure reports go to the Credit and Limit Committee; quarterly to the Board.

- Collateral management integrates ESG assessments:
  - Commercial real estate in Hungary uses an OTP Mortgage Bank ESG assessment (since Feb 2023), reflecting the Bank’s substantial CRE exposure.
  - ESG data fields were added to the corporate loan registry; partial automation leverages the state Lechner Knowledge Center, prioritizing collateral energy efficiency. Methodology sharing with subsidiaries is ongoing.
  - Vehicle-related collateral ESG methodologies are being rolled out across subsidiaries per agreed timelines; Merkantil Bank applies its own ESG method for leasing assets per Group Credit Risk Policy.

- Immovable property practices:
  - OTP Mortgage Bank records location, technical, and energy features for CRE/retail real estate collateral; ESG-specific data fields exist in the corporate collateral registry.
  - Retail residential collateral is classified by energy certificate/estimated efficiency into risk tiers (Low: A+++–B; Medium: C–D; Moderately high: E–F; High: G–I), updated quarterly to track transition risk.
  - Physical risk factors (drought, flood, heatwave) are embedded in valuation and monitoring.

- Movable property practices:
  - An IT-supported framework classifies vehicle collateral into ESG1–ESG4; results appear in the corporate collateral registry and are shared with subsidiaries.
  - An “ESG card” in the collateral registry stores environmental data for:
    - Vehicles (e.g., passenger cars, trucks, buses, agricultural machines, boats, aircraft, trams, trailers, etc.)
    - Other movable assets (solar power plant technology)
  - Vehicle risk categorization is automated based on asset traits, including EURO emission standards.

- Climate risk stress testing and ICAAP integration (ESRS E1 SBM-3):
  - Climate change mitigation presents primarily transition risk; adaptation introduces physical risk, with some adaptation investments treated within transition dynamics.
  - The 2023 group-level climate stress test evaluates transition and physical risks in:
    - Short/medium term (next 3 years), emphasizing transition risk.
    - Long term (to 2050), covering both transition and physical risks, using NGFS scenarios (orderly, disorderly, hot house).
  - Scope includes corporate credit risk, trading book market risk, and operational risk from short-term transition pressures.
  - ESG risks are integrated into existing risk frameworks; not treated as a standalone risk type in ICAAP. ESG-related credit risks are assessed as not significant; no additional ICAAP capital is held specifically for ESG.
  - Exposure benchmarking compares the Group to an average Eurozone bank using:
    - Transition: country carbon intensity of operating economies.
    - Physical: country-level risk ratings from external sources.

nodes.title: Stress -test ESRS E1 SBM -3
nodes.heading: Stress -test ESRS E1 SBM -3
nodes.start_phrase: Climate change mitigation is a significant risk associated with OTP Group's lending activities, primarily as a transition risk, including expectations related to decarbonization.
nodes.summary:
- Establishment of an “ESG card” within the collateral registry to capture environmentally relevant data for movables, with two categories: vehicles (e.g., cars, trucks, buses, agricultural machinery, boats, aircraft, rail vehicles, trailers) and other movables (solar power plant technology). Vehicle collateral is automatically classified into risk categories using asset characteristics and EURO emission standards, supporting exposure monitoring of the movable collateral portfolio.
- Climate risk stress testing framework (ESRS E1 SBM-3) embedded in ICAAP, assessing transition and physical risks across short/medium term (3-year) and long term (to 2050) horizons; scope covers corporate credit, trading book market risk, and operational risk tied to short-term transition dynamics.
- ESG risks are integrated holistically into existing risk frameworks rather than treated as a standalone risk; ESG within credit risk is assessed as not significant, and no additional ICAAP capital is held specifically for ESG risks.
- Long-term strategic analysis uses NGFS scenarios (orderly, disorderly, hot house) and benchmarks OTP Group’s exposure against an “average Eurozone bank,” finding higher transition risk due to greater carbon intensity in operating countries, while physical risk exposure is not above the Eurozone average.
- Quantified expected credit losses to 2050: minimal short-term increases under orderly/disorderly transitions (a few basis points), and a manageable but higher post-2040 increase under the hot house scenario (about +15 bps per year), with corporate portfolio results extrapolated to the full balance sheet using ECB 2021 stress-test outputs.
- A short–medium term corporate credit risk model focuses on transition risk using sector/country GVA paths from ECB 2022 and EBA 2023 “short-term disorderly” scenarios; results indicate manageable losses. Physical risks are excluded for the short–medium horizon. The framework is integrated into prudential stress testing and has been reviewed in the 2024 SREP.
- The Group relies on externally developed, internally consistent climate scenarios (NGFS, IEA, ECB, EBA) rather than creating its own. Analyses are conservative and do not factor potential business adaptation (e.g., reducing financing in vulnerable regions), which would likely further lower projected losses.
- Advancement of climate risk modeling and data infrastructure: creation of a geospatial database linking clients’ financials with climate risk metrics; identification of acute and chronic physical risks material to Hungary; acquisition and processing of ESG physical risk data, with plans to expand group-level mapping of additional ESG risk factors.

nodes.title: Credit Rating93
nodes.heading: Credit Rating93
nodes.start_phrase: In line with regulatory expectations, the Bank has started developing risk modeling procedures related to climate change and environmental risks and integrating them into its current lending processes.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on OTP Group’s climate risk assessment and integration into risk management, lending, and credit rating.
- Transition vs. physical risk exposure: operating countries show higher transition risk than the Eurozone average due to greater carbon intensity; physical risk exposure is not higher than the Eurozone average.
- Long-term scenario analysis to 2050 using NGFS pathways (orderly, disorderly, hot house) with expected credit loss ratios estimated; corporate portfolio results extrapolated to the full balance sheet.
- Results indicate minimal short-term lending loss increases under orderly/disorderly transitions; more material but manageable loss increases post-2040 under the hot house scenario (~+15 bps/year).
- Short–medium term (3-year) corporate credit risk model emphasizes transition risk, leveraging ECB 2022 and EBA 2023 “short-term disorderly” scenarios; outcomes show manageable corporate credit losses.
- Models incorporated into the prudential stress-testing framework and reviewed by supervisors, including the 2024 SREP.
- OTP Group does not craft bespoke climate scenarios; it relies on consistent, externally issued scenarios (NGFS, IEA, ECB, EBA) covering climate, commodity prices, and macro variables.
- Analyses are conservative and do not factor in potential adaptive actions (e.g., reducing exposure in vulnerable regions), which would likely lower projected losses.
- Development of climate and environmental risk modeling within lending processes: creation of a geospatial database linking client financials with climate risk metrics; identification and sourcing of acute and chronic physical risk data for Hungary, with group-wide expansion underway.
- ESG integration into credit risk: primary application in PD models; environmental risks considered relevant by default (collateral exposure to physical hazards and potential transition-related investment costs).
- Implementation progress: ESG module integrated into customer rating (including joint ventures) and initiation of ESG factors in mortgage assessments via a physical risk module and residential energy efficiency.
- Physical risk assessment approach: simplified climate risk heat mapping across sectors, subsectors, and geographies using Risk = f(Vulnerability, Hazard, Insurance); vulnerability aligned to NACE codes and hazard scored by location.
- Example indicator: modified Pálfai Drought Index applied to assess drought risk in Hungary, with initial focus on the highly exposed agricultural sector.

nodes.title: Credit Rating System
nodes.heading: Credit Rating System
nodes.start_phrase: Assessing physical risks involves significant technical challenges, including the need for detailed geographical data to determine the severity of potential weather events at different locations.
nodes.summary:
This section of the consolidated Management Report explains how the Bank integrates environmental, social, and governance (ESG) considerations—especially climate-related physical and transition risks—into credit and operational risk management.

Key points:
- Credit risk integration:
  - ESG aspects are embedded primarily in the Probability of Default (PD) model, focusing on collateral exposure to acute and chronic physical hazards (e.g., storms, floods, droughts) and potential transition-driven investment needs.
  - In 2023, the Bank began developing and rolling out climate and environmental risk modeling procedures within lending processes. The ESG module has been implemented in OTP Bank’s customer rating system and is being extended across the Group.
  - ESG factors are now reflected in ratings of joint ventures and are being integrated into mortgage loan assessments based on a physical risk module and residential collateral energy efficiency.
- Portfolio physical risk assessment:
  - A simplified climate risk heat-mapping approach is used to quickly assess physical risks across sectors, subsectors, and geographies.
  - Risk is modeled as a function of Vulnerability (sectoral sensitivity), Hazard (location-specific exposure), and Insurance.
  - Vulnerability is scored by NACE sector for each identified physical risk (very low to very high).
  - Hazard is scored by location (low to very high) using the customer’s collateral, site, or HQ address.
- Physical risk indicators and indices:
  - Drought Index: Uses the modified Palfai Drought Index to assess drought risk, with emphasis on agriculture given recent severe droughts in Hungary.
  - Flood Index: Aligned with EU Floods Directive; covers risks from unembanked watercourses, embankment failures/insufficiencies, and precipitation/groundwater; uses national river basin plans (e.g., VGT3) and related vulnerability/risk maps.
  - Storm Index: Counts annual days with wind gusts ≥20 m/s.
  - Frost Index: Tracks days with minimum temperatures ≤−2°C (spring/autumn) and ≤−15°C (winter), highlighting impacts on agriculture and forestry.
- Operational risk management:
  - ESG risks have been embedded in the operational risk framework since 2021; approach unchanged in 2024.
  - Annual, group-wide risk and control self-assessments include ESG-relevant expected loss estimates and scenario analyses.
  - Quarterly monitoring against a group-level ESG operational risk tolerance; loss data tracked with attention to ESG impact and data quality.
- ESG data system development:
  - The Bank identifies relevant chronic and acute physical risk drivers for its physical risk database, spanning:
    - Temperature-related (e.g., heat stress, temperature variability)
    - Wind-related (e.g., changing wind patterns, storms, cyclones)
    - Water-related (e.g., changing precipitation, floods, drought, sea level rise, saline intrusion)
    - Surface cover-related (e.g., soil degradation/erosion, landslides, subsidence, wildfires, coastal erosion)
  - These drivers inform portfolio-level risk mapping and integration into credit processes.

nodes.title: Managing operational risks
nodes.heading: 2.4.3. Managing operational risks
nodes.start_phrase: In terms of operational risk, severe weather conditions can affect business continuity, and there is reputational risk from failing to adapt to the continuously increasing regulatory and supervisory ESG requirements.
nodes.summary:
- Defines physical climate risk indices:
  - Flood Index aligned with EU Floods Directive (2007/60/EC); Hungarian categories: unembanked watercourse flooding, flooding from embankment failure/insufficiency, and flooding from precipitation/groundwater rise; references Hungary’s VGT3 (2022) and related vulnerability/risk maps.
  - Storm Index: number of days with wind gusts ≥20 m/s.
  - Frost Index: spring/autumn (≤−2°C) and winter (≤−15°C) thresholds; index counts days with minimum temperature ≤−2°C; notes severe impacts of late spring frost on agriculture/forestry.

- Operational ESG risk management:
  - Recognizes severe weather impacts on business continuity and reputational risk from ESG regulatory non-compliance.
  - ESG risks embedded in the operational risk framework since 2021 (unchanged in 2024), with group-level risk and control self-assessments incorporating ESG loss expectations and scenario analyses.
  - Quarterly monitoring against a group ESG operational risk tolerance; tracking loss data and ESG data quality.
  - Establishes a comprehensive physical risk taxonomy for the ESG Data System, covering chronic (e.g., changing temperature/wind/precipitation patterns, sea level rise, water/soil stress) and acute hazards (e.g., heat/cold waves, cyclones/storms/tornadoes, drought, heavy precipitation, flooding, wildfires, landslides, avalanches, subsidence, glacial lake outburst).

- Market risk management:
  - Applies the Green Recommendation; sets ESG rating-based position limits for trading and discretionary portfolios; discretionary portfolios also use an ESG exclusion list.
  - Considers Principal Adverse Impacts via MSCI standardized PAI statements since 1Q 2023 (with gaps for fossil fuels and energy efficiency); coverage improving; observation ongoing without explicit limits/policy.
  - Performs weekly ESG stress tests on corporate bond portfolios in trading and banking books.

- Liquidity risk:
  - Developing a methodology to integrate ESG-related liquidity risk assessment.

- ESG risk management at OTP Fund Management:
  - Uses MSCI ESG Research ratings (CCC to AAA) to set and monitor sustainability risk levels for funds/portfolios.
  - Considers sustainability risk in portfolio construction/rebalancing and takes measures if risk exceeds targets.
  - SFDR-classified funds must meet minimum sustainable investment shares and ESG rating criteria.
  - Provides regular sustainability risk reports to portfolio managers/management; quarterly summaries to the Board; portfolio managers ensure aggregate portfolio sustainability risk aligns with expected levels.
  - Excludes companies involved in controversial weapons and sovereigns of authoritarian regimes; emphasizes environmental impacts such as GHG intensity, waste/harmful emissions, and water use.

nodes.title: Managing Market Risks
nodes.heading: 2.4.4. Managing Market Risks
nodes.start_phrase: In market risk management, sustainability risks are considered in accordance with the Green Recommendation.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of ESG integration into market risk management, aligning with a Green Recommendation.
- Use of ESG rating–based position limits for trading and discretionary portfolios; application of an ESG exclusion list in discretionary portfolios.
- Adoption of MSCI standardized PAI statements for discretionary portfolio management from 1Q 2023; reporting covers all identified indicators except fossil fuels and energy efficiency due to data gaps; portfolio coverage improving; PAIs monitored without set limits or explicit policy.
- Weekly ESG stress tests on corporate bond portfolios across trading and banking books.
- Development of a methodology to integrate ESG-related liquidity risks within Integrated Risk Management.
- At OTP Fund Management, ESG risk is embedded in the risk framework: portfolio sustainability risk assessed via MSCI ESG ratings (CCC to AAA); portfolios created/rebalanced to meet expected ESG risk levels, with mitigation if exceeded.
- SFDR-classified funds must meet minimum sustainable investment proportions and ESG rating thresholds.
- Regular sustainability risk reporting to portfolio managers and management; quarterly summaries to the Board; portfolio managers responsible for keeping aggregate ESG risk in line with targets.
- Exclusions include companies linked to controversial weapons and sovereign bonds of authoritarian regimes.
- Emphasis on environmental impact metrics such as greenhouse gas intensity, waste and harmful emissions, and water usage.

nodes.title: Liquidity Risks
nodes.heading: 2.4.5. Liquidity Risks
nodes.start_phrase: Given its relevance, Integrated Risk Management has begun developing an integration methodology for assessing liquidity risks related to ESG risks.
nodes.summary:
- The report outlines how ESG considerations are embedded in market risk management, following the Green Recommendation, including ESG rating–based position limits for trading and discretionary portfolios and an ESG exclusion list for discretionary portfolios.
- Principal adverse impacts (PAI) in discretionary portfolio management are monitored using MSCI standardized PAI statements (available since 1Q 2023); coverage is improving, though fossil fuels and energy efficiency are excluded due to data gaps. Observation is ongoing without formal limits or explicit policy.
- Weekly stress tests are performed on ESG risks within corporate bond portfolios across both trading and banking books.
- For liquidity risk, an integration methodology is being developed to assess liquidity risks linked to ESG factors.
- At OTP Fund Management, ESG risk management is part of the overall risk framework: funds and portfolios are rated by MSCI ESG Research (CCC–AAA), targeted sustainability risk levels are set for portfolio construction and rebalancing, and corrective actions are taken if expected levels are exceeded.
- SFDR-classified funds must meet defined thresholds for the minimum share of sustainable investments and for ESG ratings.

nodes.title: ESG Risk Management at OTP Fund Management
nodes.heading: 2.4.6. ESG Risk Management at OTP Fund Management
nodes.start_phrase: At OTP Fund Management, ESG risk management is an integral part of the comprehensive risk management framework.
nodes.summary:
- Market risk management integrates sustainability in line with the Green Recommendation, using MSCI ESG ratings to set position limits for trading and discretionary portfolios, and applying an ESG exclusion list in discretionary portfolios.
- Principal adverse impacts (PAI) in discretionary portfolio management are monitored via MSCI standardized PAI statements (from Q1 2023); coverage is improving, but indicators on fossil fuels and energy efficiency face data gaps, and there are no PAI limits or explicit policy yet.
- Weekly stress tests assess ESG risks of corporate bond portfolios in both trading and banking books.
- Liquidity risk: the Integrated Risk Management function is developing a methodology to incorporate ESG-related liquidity risks.

- OTP Fund Management embeds ESG risk into its overall risk framework, determining portfolio sustainability risk with MSCI ESG Research ratings (CCC–AAA).
- Portfolio construction/rebalancing targets an expected sustainability risk level; if exceeded, corrective measures are taken.
- SFDR-classified funds must meet criteria on minimum sustainable investment shares and ESG ratings.
- Regular sustainability risk reporting goes to portfolio managers and management, with quarterly board summaries; portfolio managers are responsible for keeping aggregate sustainability risk in line with targets.
- Exclusions include companies linked to controversial weapons and sovereign bonds of authoritarian regimes; environmental metrics emphasized include GHG intensity, waste/harmful emissions, and water use.

- Social Information – Own Workforce: OTP Group positions employees as a core asset and commits to responsible employment practices across the Group, in line with ESRS S1 SBM-3.
- Workforce scope covers employees, non-employee contracted workers, and individual entrepreneurs, though practices primarily target employees; the majority (43,118) are full- or part-time employees.
- Material impacts, risks, and opportunities identified:
  - Working conditions/work-life balance: positive impacts from supportive practices; risk if employee interests are overlooked.
  - Health and safety: stress identified as a key risk even in generally non-hazardous roles.
  - Equal treatment and opportunities: near parity in pay for equal roles; lower representation of women in senior management remains a negative impact.
  - Inclusion of persons with disabilities: strong potential positive impact due to scale, but current employment rate is low.
  - Diversity: strong stance against discrimination; practices present areas for further development.
  - Training and skills: broad access to training and regular performance reviews; risks if equal opportunity is not ensured.
  - Measures against violence/harassment: elevated risk due to the Group’s size and workforce composition.
- Impacts generally affect most employees across countries; while headcount varies by country (influencing impact magnitude), no country-specific significant impacts were identified.

structure.title: Green lending criteria and definitions used in the voluntary Green Portfolio Report
structure.heading: Green lending criteria and definitions used in the voluntary Green Portfolio Report
structure.start_phrase: Green exposure defined based on the bank's green definition: on -balance loans, advances, leasing, and bond exposures that have undergone an internal green rating process and meet the technical screening criteria of any of the following frameworks: OTP Group Green Loan Framework , OTP Group Sustainable Finance Framework , the green housing, green corporate and municipal capital requirement discount program of the Hungarian National Bank, and the NHP Green Home.
structure.summary:
- Reports financed GHG emissions for assets managed by OTP Group’s fund and asset management entities in 2024, split by asset class with PCAF data quality, managed assets, and coverage-adjusted emissions:
  - Assets not in real estate funds: PCAF score 3.7; HUF 4,209 billion managed; Scope 1–2: 1,616,427 tCO2e; Scope 3: 3,210,721 tCO2e; Total: 4,827,148 tCO2e.
  - Assets in real estate funds: PCAF score 5.0; HUF 691 billion managed; Scope 1–2: 4,055 tCO2e; Scope 3: 16,386 tCO2e; Total: 20,441 tCO2e.

- Describes GHG removals, carbon credits, and internal carbon pricing (ESRS E1-7, E1-8):
  - OTP Bank retired 7,000 tCO2e of Verra VCS credits in 2024, covering Scope 1–2, supporting the Sant Nikola Wind Farm in Bulgaria; a mitigation project without Article 6 corresponding adjustments.
  - Carbon-neutral operations strategy includes credits while pursuing energy efficiency and renewable energy to achieve Scope 1–2 net zero by 2030.
  - Plans to shift from carbon credits to ecosystem restoration certificates.
  - Partnership with Pilisi Parkerdő Zrt. to develop the 400-hectare Budakeszi Vadaskert urban forest for biodiversity, climate adaptation, carbon sequestration, ecosystem services, employee engagement, and reputation building.
  - No internal carbon pricing applied.

- Notes on transition plan and biodiversity integration (ESRS E4-1), disclosed under ESRS 2 SBM-3.

- Outlines reporting policy for Chapter E and green lending criteria:
  - Definition of green exposure for the voluntary Green Portfolio based on internal green rating and alignment with OTP Group Green Loan Framework, OTP Group Sustainable Finance Framework, Hungarian National Bank (MNB) green capital requirement discount programs, and the NHP Green Home program.
  - National MNB programs (2020–2021) provide baseline criteria; EU Taxonomy eligibility/alignment addressed in the OTP frameworks.
  - Green criteria for non-financial corporates anchored in OTP frameworks and MNB program; these underpin the voluntary green lending portfolio.
  - OTP Group Green Loan Framework updated with SPO and approved by MNB in July 2023; qualifying loans recognized as “Category B” under the MNB program; coverage spans large corporates to micro-enterprises, municipalities, and condominiums.
  - Retail green lending centered on MNB’s Green housing capital requirement discount and NHP Green Home, aligned with Hungarian/EU rules (e.g., 9/2023 Decree on building energy performance and NZEB).

- Clarifies differences between mandatory EU Taxonomy GAR KPIs and the voluntary green portfolio:
  - Voluntary GAR: centrally maintained, monthly monitoring, includes non-NFRD clients and non-EU exposures; expert-based criteria assessment.
  - Mandatory GAR: semi-annual, per EU 2021/2178; uses prescribed Taxonomy KPIs and gross carrying amounts, focusing on NFRD corporates with unknown use of proceeds and on exposures with known aligned use of proceeds.

- Details Scope 1–2 emissions boundaries and methodology:
  - 50.a: Emissions from assets within the IFRS-consolidated group (financial control), including IFRS 16 assets.
  - 50.b: Emissions from entities/arrangements under operational control outside full consolidation (associates, JVs, jointly controlled operations/assets).
  - Not subject to emission trading schemes; ETS-related Scope 1 not relevant.
  - Same calculation approach for 50.a and 50.b; estimates used where invoices are missing, with immaterial uncertainty.
  - Scope 1 includes vehicle fuel/energy, natural gas, and refrigerants from air conditioners/server coolers; CH4 and N2O from biogenic sources accounted separately; biofuel content uses defaults or actuals when available.

structure.title: Retail green lending
structure.heading: Retail green lending
structure.start_phrase: In terms of residential green lending, the Green housing capital requirement discount program of the Hungarian National Bank and the NHP's Green Home program form the core of the lending.
structure.summary:
- Overview of OTP Group’s approach to EU Taxonomy: references to eligibility and alignment through the OTP Group Green Loan and Sustainable Finance frameworks.
- Green lending foundations: OTP Group Green Lending Framework, Sustainable Finance Framework, and the Hungarian National Bank’s (HNB) green corporate and municipal capital requirement discount program as the basis for the voluntary green lending portfolio.
- 2023 update: Green Loan Framework updated with a Second Party Opinion and approved by the HNB in July 2023; loans meeting the Framework qualify as “Category B” under the HNB discount program.
- Scope of Green Loan Framework: covers nonresidential customers from large corporates to micro-enterprises, municipalities, and condominiums.
- Retail green lending: anchored in HNB’s Green housing capital requirement discount program and the NHP Green Home program, aligned with Hungarian and EU rules (e.g., Decree 9/2023 and NZEB requirements).
- Differences between voluntary green portfolio and mandatory EU Taxonomy metrics: the voluntary GAR portfolio is centrally maintained, monitored monthly, includes non-NFRD entities and non-EU exposures, with expert-based assessments; mandatory GAR KPIs are compiled semi-annually per EU 2021/2178 using Taxonomy KPIs and gross carrying amounts for NFRD corporates (unknown use of proceeds) and known aligned exposures.
- Scope 1–2 GHG emissions methodology and boundaries: 
  - 50.a financial control boundary for consolidated IFRS entities (including IFRS 16 assets).
  - 50.b operational control for non-consolidated entities (associates, JVs, unconsolidated subs, and joint arrangements).
  - Not subject to emission trading schemes; same calculation approach for 50.a and 50.b.
  - Estimates used when invoices are missing with immaterial uncertainty.
  - Scope 1 includes vehicle fuels/energy, natural gas, and HVAC/server cooling; CH4 and N2O from biogenic emissions reported separately; biofuel ratios use defaults unless specific data available.

structure.title: Main differences between the mandatory EU taxonomy indicators and the voluntary green portfolio:
structure.heading: Main differences between the mandatory EU taxonomy indicators and the voluntary green portfolio:
structure.start_phrase: The voluntary GAR portfolio is defined in a centrally maintained Group controlling database, monitored monthly, and extends to companies and households that are not subject to NFRD, as well as those outside the EU.
structure.summary:
- Overview of OTP Group’s green finance approach, referencing core frameworks for EU Taxonomy eligibility/alignment: OTP Group Green Loan Framework and Sustainable Finance Framework.
- Green criteria for non-financial corporates guided by OTP frameworks and the Hungarian National Bank’s (HNB) green corporate and municipal capital requirement discount program.
- Update to the OTP Group Green Loan Framework approved by the HNB in July 2023, supported by a Second Party Opinion, enabling “Category B” eligibility under the HNB discount program for loans meeting framework criteria.
- Scope of the Green Loan Framework covers nonresidential customers, from large corporates to micro-enterprises, municipalities, and condominiums.
- Retail green lending anchored in the HNB Green Housing capital requirement discount program and the NHP Green Home program; alignment with Hungarian and EU rules (e.g., 9/2023 Decree on building energy performance and NZEB requirements).
- Distinction between voluntary green portfolio (GAR) and mandatory EU Taxonomy indicators: the voluntary GAR is centrally maintained, monitored monthly, includes EU and non-EU clients and households beyond NFRD scope, with expert-based eligibility assessment.
- Mandatory GAR KPIs are prepared semi-annually per EU 2021/2178, using Taxonomy KPIs and gross carrying amounts: includes NFRD corporate exposures with unknown use of proceeds and exposures with known, Taxonomy-aligned use of proceeds.
- Scope 1–2 GHG emissions boundaries: 
  - 50.a: assets within the IFRS-consolidated group under financial control (including IFRS 16).
  - 50.b: operationally controlled entities and arrangements outside 50.a (associates, JVs, unconsolidated subs, joint operations/assets).
- The Group is not subject to emissions trading schemes; thus ETS-related Scope 1 emissions are not applicable.
- Emissions calculation methodology is consistent for 50.a and 50.b; estimates used where invoices are missing, with immaterial uncertainty.
- Scope 1 includes vehicle fuel/energy, natural gas, and refrigerants (AC and server coolers); biogenic CH4 and N2O reported separately; biofuel shares use default values unless specific fuel data is available.

structure.title: Scope 1 -2 emissions
structure.heading: Scope 1 -2 emissions
structure.start_phrase: 50. a Emission of the Group preparing consolidated financial statements: emissions derived from the assets listed in the balance sheet of entities belonging to the consolidated accounting group according to IFRS, in a financial control approach, including emissions derived from assets under IFRS 16.
structure.summary:
- Outlines OTP Group’s approach to EU Taxonomy compliance and references the bank’s key frameworks: OTP Group Green Loan Framework and Sustainable Finance Framework, which define green criteria for non-financial corporates alongside the Hungarian National Bank’s green capital requirement discount program.
- Notes the July 2023 update of the Green Loan Framework (with external SPO) approved by the Hungarian National Bank, enabling qualifying loans to count as “Category B” under the Hungarian green capital discount program.
- Defines the Green Loan Framework’s scope: nonresidential customers from large corporates to micro-enterprises, including municipalities and condominiums.
- Describes retail green lending foundations: the Hungarian National Bank’s Green housing capital requirement discount program and the NHP Green Home program, aligned with Hungarian and EU building-energy regulations (e.g., 9/2023 Decree and NZEB requirements).
- Explains differences between voluntary green portfolio metrics and mandatory EU Taxonomy GAR KPIs:
  - Voluntary GAR: centrally maintained, monthly monitored, includes EU- and non-EU clients and households beyond NFRD scope; expert-based eligibility assessment.
  - Mandatory GAR: semiannual, per EU 2021/2178; limited to NFRD corporates’ exposures with unknown use of proceeds and exposures with known EU Taxonomy-aligned use of proceeds.
- Details Scope 1 and 2 GHG accounting boundaries and methods:
  - Scope definitions for entities under financial control (50.a) and under operational control including investees/joint arrangements (50.b).
  - Not subject to emission trading schemes; minor data gaps estimated (e.g., invoices, refrigerants) with low uncertainty.
  - Scope 1 includes vehicle fuels, natural gas, air conditioners/server coolers; biogenic CH4 and N2O reported separately; IPCC AR6 factors used.
  - Scope 2 covers electricity and district heating; both location-based and market-based disclosed; renewable electricity via GoOs/RECs assigned zero market-based factor; share of contractual instruments reported.
  - Emission factor sources: national inventories/IPCC/EMEP-EEA/DEFRA; electricity residual mix via AIB or IFI grid factors; district heating via national sources or DEFRA; coverage of relevant GHGs clarified.
  - Agricultural non-mechanical GHGs disclosed using GHG Protocol Agricultural Guidance and AKI calculator (IPCC 2006/2019 methods) for crop and livestock categories; biogenic emissions reported separately.
- Summarizes Scope 3 approach:
  - High-level estimation conducted for Categories 1–14 (PCAF Score 5/Option 3c); detailed calculation focuses on Category 15 (financed emissions).
- Describes financed emissions (Scope 3 Category 15) methodology:
  - Uses PCAF Standard with attribution based on financing ratio (loan or exposure over financed asset/total assets).
  - Incorporates clients’ Scopes 1 and 2 (considered relatively more reliable) and acknowledges high uncertainty and speculative nature of clients’ Scope 3.
  - Highlights limited availability and assurance of client-reported emissions (data from 111 corporate clients, <4% of business loan portfolio) and intent to improve internal data management.
  - Uses external emission intensity datasets and proxies where needed:
    - PCAF/Exiobase for corporates (mostly excludes downstream Scope 3; 2019 data may cause overestimation due to price level changes).
    - PCAF/CRREM 2023 for commercial and residential real estate (combined Scopes 1+2; may differ from national data).
    - PCAF Motor Vehicle Loan Dataset for vehicle loans (by country and major vehicle classes).
    - Sovereign exposures per PCAF Standard sources.
  - Ensures consistency with Pillar 3 ESG risk disclosure methods and data.

structure.title: Category 15 emissions – emissions financed through investments
structure.heading: Category 15 emissions – emissions financed through investments
structure.start_phrase: AR 46. A., b. Scope 3 / Category 15 GHG emissions of OTP Group are those that are related to emissions of clients to which OTP Group provides funds in the form of loans or equity, or through investing into their securities.
structure.summary:
- Financed emissions (Scope 3 Category 15): OTP Group attributes a share of clients’ GHG emissions to the bank proportional to the financing ratio (attribution factor). It includes clients’ Scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions, but OTP considers Scope 1–2 estimates relatively reliable and Scope 3 highly uncertain/speculative.

- Methodology and data: Financed emissions quantified per PCAF Standard, as required by ESRS/CSRD, and aligned with the Group’s Pillar 3 ESG risk disclosures. Due to scarce client-reported data (emissions reported by only 111 corporate clients, <4% of portfolio, mostly unaudited), OTP estimates borrower emissions using financial data and external emission intensity factors:
  - Corporates: PCAF/Exiobase 2019 intensity data; may omit most downstream Scope 3 and can bias results (possible Scope 3 underestimation; potential overestimation from using 2019 intensities with higher 2023/24 price levels while national emissions largely stagnated).
  - Real estate: PCAF/CRREM 2023 building intensities (combined Scope 1+2), which can differ from national data.
  - Vehicle loans: PCAF Motor Vehicle Loan dataset by country and main vehicle types.
  - Sovereign exposures: per PCAF sovereign guidance.
  - Proxies used where country/asset data are missing. OTP plans to analyze internal data management gaps as CSRD expands data availability.

- GHG intensity ratio: Calculated as Total GHG emissions (tCO2e) / Net revenue (million HUF), reported on both location-based and market-based bases. Net revenue follows the 2024 consolidated IFRS (interest income and similar + fee and commission income + other operating income).

- ESG risk management: The Group integrates ESG/climate risks across risk types (credit, market, liquidity, operational) and aligns with the Hungarian National Bank’s Green Recommendation 10/2022. Compliance is reported to the Board, Management Committee, ESG Committee, and Risk Management Committee. The Group monitors EBA/ECB expectations; ECB has direct supervision over DSK Bank (Bulgaria) and OTP Bank Slovenia. DSK, OTP Slovenia, and OTP Croatia have integrated ESG risk factors per local supervisory expectations.

- Governance and internal frameworks: Sustainability-related risk management is guided by a suite of internal, non-public policies, including governance and organizational regulations, risk strategy and appetite, credit and market risk policies, collateral and operational risk policies, lending guidelines, remuneration and performance rules, and a CEO directive on greenwashing risk.

structure.title: GHG intensity
structure.heading: GHG intensity
structure.start_phrase: AR 53. A., b., c. GHG intensity ratio is calculated by the following formula: Total GHG emissions (tCO2eq) / Net revenue (Monetary unit in million HUF) .
structure.summary:
- Part of OTP Bank Group’s Integrated Annual Report 2024 (Management Report, consolidated) focusing on GHG intensity metrics and ESG risk management.
- Defines the GHG intensity ratio as total GHG emissions (tCO2e) divided by net revenue (in million HUF), calculated using both location-based and market-based methods.
- Specifies net revenue for the ratio per IFRS consolidation: interest income and similar, fee and commission income, and other operating income from the 2024 Consolidated Income Statement.
- Describes the Group’s integration of ESG and climate considerations into business and risk practices, including attention to risks related to green lending.
- Confirms comprehensive risk policies (credit, market, liquidity, operational) aligned with prudential banking regulations.
- Establishes ESG risk management alignment with the Hungarian National Bank’s Green Recommendation 10/2022, with regular compliance reporting to the Board, Management, ESG, and Risk Management Committees.
- Notes monitoring of EBA and ECB supervisory expectations; highlights ECB direct supervision of DSK Bank (Bulgaria) and OTP Bank Slovenia, and ESG risk integration at DSK, OTP Slovenia, and OTP Croatia per local supervisory guidance.
- Lists key internal, non-public governance documents underpinning sustainability-related risk management, including group governance and operational regulations, risk strategy and appetite, credit and market risk policies, collateral valuation, operational risk, performance and remuneration policies, and a CEO directive on managing greenwashing risk.

structure.title: Social Information
structure.heading: 3. Social Information
structure.start_phrase: The employees of OTP Group represent one of its most important values and a crucial building block of its success.
structure.summary:
- Section focus: Social Information – Own Workforce within OTP Group’s Integrated Annual Report 2024, aligned to ESRS S1 SBM-3.
- Employer stance: Employees are a key value; OTP Group positions itself as a responsible employer across all operations.
- Material impacts, risks, and opportunities:
  - Working conditions and work–life balance: Positive impact from supportive practices; risk if employee interests are not adequately considered.
  - Health protection and safety: Predominantly non-hazardous roles, but stress presents a notable negative risk for many employees.
  - Equal treatment and opportunities:
    - Gender equality and equal pay: Generally small gender pay differences in the same roles; persistent underrepresentation of women in higher management.
    - Employment and inclusion of persons with disabilities: Group scale enables positive impact potential; current employment rate is low.
    - Diversity: Strong potential to promote diversity; all discrimination prohibited; internal practices provide development opportunities.
  - Training and skills development: Broad access to training and regular performance evaluations at several subsidiaries; risk if equal opportunity is not ensured.
  - Measures against violence and harassment: Elevated potential risk due to Group size and workforce composition.
- Scope of workforce considered: Employees, non-employee contracted workers, and individual entrepreneurs engaged by Group entities. Significant impacts apply to all, but practices primarily target employees due to limited influence over external workers.
- Workforce scale and distribution: 43,118 employees (full-time and part-time). No country- or region-specific significant impacts identified; impact magnitude varies by country according to employee numbers (see ESRS S1-5).
- Cross-references: Further details on impacts, risks, opportunities, and management are indicated under ESRS SMB-3 and subsequent chapter sections.
- Thematic grouping: Gender equality and equal pay, diversity, and disability inclusion are addressed together.

nodes.title: Own Workforce
nodes.heading: 3.1. Own Workforce
nodes.start_phrase: The employees of OTP Group represent one of its most important values and a crucial building block of its success.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Integrated Annual Report 2024, Management Report (Consolidated), Social Information 3.1 Own Workforce for OTP Group.
- Strategic stance: Employees are a key asset; the Group aims to act as a responsible employer to achieve business goals with a well-prepared, committed workforce.
- Reporting framework: ESRS S1 SBM-3 used to identify material impacts, risks, and opportunities across OTP Group’s entire operations related to its own workforce.
- Workforce scope: Includes employees, non-employee contracted workers, and individual entrepreneurs under contract; practices primarily focus on employees due to limited influence over external workers.
- Workforce size: 43,118 employees (full-time and part-time).
- Material topics and key impacts/risks:
  - Working conditions and work-life balance: Positive impact from balance-supportive practices; risk if employee interests are not adequately considered.
  - Health protection and safety: Negative impact mainly from stress risks despite generally non-hazardous roles.
  - Equal treatment and opportunities:
    - Gender equality and equal pay: Positive impact with near-parity pay for similar roles; risk from lower female representation at higher management levels.
    - Employment and inclusion of persons with disabilities: Positive potential due to Group scale and reach; current low employment rate is a negative.
    - Diversity: Positive potential to drive diversity; all discrimination prohibited; practices noted as an area for further development.
  - Training and skills development: Positive access to training and regular performance evaluations at several subsidiaries; risk of unequal access in some practices.
  - Measures against violence and harassment: High potential risk due to Group size and workforce composition.
- Materiality coverage: Significant (or potentially significant) impacts affect most employees; no country/region-specific significant impacts identified, though impact magnitude varies by country due to headcount.
- Cross-references: Further details available under ESRS SMB-3 and ESRS S1-5 within the chapter; topics on gender equality/equal pay, diversity, and disability inclusion are addressed together.

nodes.title: Material impacts, Risks and Opportunities
nodes.heading: Material impacts, Risks and Opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: Regarding own workforce, the impacts always arise within the entire OTP Group’s operations.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines OTP Group’s approach to managing social topics related to its own workforce under ESRS S1. It defines the workforce to include employees, non-employee contracted workers, and individual entrepreneurs, with most influence on the 43,118 employees and more limited influence on external workers. A double materiality analysis identifies group-wide impacts—generally not country-specific, though magnitude varies with workforce size—covering work-life balance, health and safety (with stress as a broad risk and higher physical risks in agricultural roles), gender equality and equal pay (small pay gaps in similar roles but underrepresentation of women in senior leadership), inclusion of persons with disabilities (currently low employment levels), diversity and non-discrimination, training and skills development (broad access and regular performance evaluations, with risks if equal opportunity isn’t ensured), and prevention of workplace violence and harassment (heightened risk due to group size and workforce composition). OTP Group reports no significant risks of child, forced, or compulsory labor, and no workforce harms linked to environmental transition plans. The Group aims to maximize positive impacts (e.g., work-life balance, training, diversity, disability employment) while mitigating negative ones (e.g., stress, safety, harassment), with actions typically targeted to specific groups but not differentiated by contract type. A group-level Code of Ethics is the core policy, prohibiting discrimination, promoting equal opportunity, safeguarding human rights, ensuring workplace safety, and addressing harassment; it protects vulnerable groups and is aligned with UNGPs, the UN Global Compact, OECD Guidelines, and ILO core conventions. Health and safety are managed locally in line with regulations, commonly through regular risk assessments. References are made to ESRS S1 SBM-3, S1-1, and S1-5 for further detail.

nodes.title: Policies related to own workforce
nodes.heading: Policies related to own workforce
nodes.start_phrase: Key content: The comprehensive policy for OTP Group's own workforce is the Code of Ethics of OTP Bank Plc and OTP Group (presented in the @4.1. Corporate Governance disclosure requirement).
nodes.summary:
- Scope and stance on human rights: OTP Group reports no significant negative human rights risks (e.g., child, forced, or compulsory labor) in its operations. Transition plans to reduce environmental impacts have not created negative workforce impacts.
- Key workforce impacts: Potential negatives include health and safety risks, workplace violence/harassment (mainly individual cases), and broader stress risks. Targeted positive impacts focus on work-life balance, gender equality and equal pay, training/skills development, diversity, and employment of people with disabilities.
- Coverage and vulnerable groups: Measures apply across employment types, often with defined target groups (e.g., women, people with disabilities) and vary by country emphasis. A group-level Code of Ethics prohibits discrimination and addresses harassment, covering protected characteristics (gender, ethnicity, religion, age, disability, family status, etc.).
- Occupational health and safety: Group members manage H&S per local regulations; most conduct regular risk assessments. Higher-risk roles exist in agricultural entities (work with animals/machinery).
- Policy framework (ESRS S1-1): The Code of Ethics is the core workforce policy, committing to respect for human rights, equal treatment, workplace safety, harassment prevention, and fair employment. It aligns with UNGPs, UN Global Compact labor principles, OECD Guidelines on human rights, and ILO core conventions (freedom of association, collective bargaining, equal pay, anti-discrimination). Additional topic-specific policies exist outside the Code.
- Workforce engagement (ESRS S1-2): An annual, group-wide employee engagement (commitment) survey is the primary feedback tool. In 2024, 91% of invited employees (31,134 respondents) participated; all countries exceeded 80% response except Slovenia; Uzbekistan’s Ipoteka Bank joined for the first time. Results inform unit-level action plans; oversight by the MD of Human and Organizational Development. Results communicated via intranet, newsletters, and forums; effectiveness tracked through participation, key engagement indicators, year-over-year changes, action plan evaluations, and global financial sector benchmarks. Data enable demographic analysis.
- Consultation and representation: Most subsidiaries have trade unions; HR leaders regularly consult them. No global framework agreement with employee representatives on human rights is in place.
- Grievance and remediation channels (ESRS S1-3, S1-17): Multiple, including anonymous mechanisms and an ethical reporting system for all workers. Trade unions and occupational safety representatives support issue-raising and mitigation. Employees may also use external legal avenues (e.g., courts); regulatory bodies (occupational safety authorities, labor inspectors) function primarily as compliance mechanisms.

nodes.title: Processes for engaging with own workforce
nodes.heading: Processes for engaging with own workforce
nodes.start_phrase: Within OTP Group, engagement with the workforce and employee representatives occurs through multiple channels, always complying with legal requirements .
nodes.summary:
- Focus: OTP Group’s workforce engagement, consultation, grievance mechanisms, outcomes, and targets aligned with ESRS S1 (S1-2, S1-3, S1-5, S1-17).
- Employee Engagement Survey:
  - Annual, group-wide (most member companies; certain agricultural entities excluded). In 2024, 91% participation (31,134 employees); Uzbekistan’s Ipoteka Bank joined for the first time.
  - Anonymous feedback on compensation, work organization, and human capital; unit-level action plans created with employees.
  - Operational lead: Managing Director, Human and Organizational Development Directorate of OTP Bank.
  - Results communicated via intranet, newsletters, forums/meetings; reported to top management (Presidential/Divisional/Regional and Executive Steering Committee).
  - Database enables demographic impact analyses; effectiveness tracked via participation, key engagement indicators, prior-year action evaluations, year-over-year shifts, and sector/global benchmarks.
- Consultation with employee representatives:
  - Most subsidiaries have trade unions; HR heads regularly consult on employee issues.
  - No global framework agreement with employee reps on human rights.
- Grievance and remediation channels:
  - Multiple, including anonymous options and an ethical reporting system for all workers.
  - Trade unions and occupational safety representatives help surface concerns; employees can also use legal avenues (e.g., courts), with regulatory bodies noted in governance context.
  - Complaints handled per law, Code of Ethics, internal labor rules, and collective agreements accessible to all employees.
- 2024 cases and outcomes:
  - 166 total complaints received across channels.
  - About 17% of ethical reports (106) came from own employees; no monetary compensation initiated from these.
  - No discrimination reports or justified cases within own workforce; none filed to OECD NCPs.

nodes.summary:

- Group policy framework:
  - OTP Bank’s 2021 Strategy for Gender Equality aims for equal opportunities, an inclusive, discrimination-free workplace, and a diverse, high-performing, collaborative culture.
  - Scope: OTP Bank; Accountability: compliance managing director reporting to the President-CEO and the Ethics Committee.
  - Publicly available on the Bank’s website and internal platforms.
  - Aligned with Hungarian law (Act CCXXXVII of 2013, Hpt. 112(3)f), Hungarian National Bank recommendations, and EBA GL 2017-12; complaints handling referenced in S1-3.

- Subsidiary policies and governance:
  - Bulgaria (DSK Bank): 2024 “Diversity, Inclusion, and Belonging” policy; focus on gender equality and equal pay; accountable Head of HR & Transformation; dedicated team; structured methodology, KPI reviews with senior management; regular oversight by Nomination & Remuneration Committee and Supervisory Board.
  - Slovenia: DIEB policy ensures discrimination- and harassment-free lifecycle; Head of HR accountable; requires plans/measures, leadership accountability, and KPI tracking (annual/quarterly/monthly).
  - Croatia: Diversity & Inclusion Policy for all employees; action plans and training; references UDHR and ILO Fundamental Principles; CEO holds ultimate responsibility.

- Integration into internal regulations:
  - Positions filled based on qualifications, experience, and role requirements; explicit non-discrimination clauses across OTP Group.
  - Slovenia highlighted as good practice: diversity embedded in charter, Code of Ethics, executive board selection policies, and regulations against discrimination, mobbing, and psychosocial risks.

- Key programs and actions in 2024:
  - OTP Bank:
    - International Women Network across subsidiaries to prepare women for senior leadership; webinars and mentoring for high-potential female leaders.
    - OTP Digital GirlPower talent pipeline to increase women’s participation in digital/IT.
    - Unconscious bias and inclusion training; “Openness and Inclusion” e-learning for all employees, foundation for inclusive leadership development.
  - DSK Bank (Bulgaria):
    - Culture & Change team leads diversity/equal opportunity agenda; refined gender pay-gap methodology; regular KPI reporting and senior management reviews.
    - Developing internal rules/procedures for monitoring diversity and pay gaps.
    - Return-to-work procedure for maternity/paternity leave; LaDySK female leaders’ community supports reintegration and aims to increase women among B-1104 candidates; clear activity plan and coordination.
  - OTP Bank Serbia:
    - Measures under the Gender Equality Act include equal access to information, health insurance adjustments (e.g., for pregnant women/newborns), efforts to balance gender representation (including targeted preferences while ensuring non-discrimination), maintaining balanced gender ratios in top management, gender-sensitive language, and gender-disaggregated data reporting to authorities.
    - Effectiveness monitored via court case incidence and employee feedback.
  - Uzbekistan: Additional HR reporting line for equal opportunity violations (beyond ethics hotline).
  - Russia: Compliance with legal quotas for employing persons with disabilities, proportionate to workforce size.
  - Ukraine: E-learning on interacting with persons with disabilities.

- Monitoring and effectiveness:

- Most affected customer groups: financially vulnerable individuals; elderly (lower digital literacy); children and young adults; people with disabilities.
- Policy framework: compliance with EU consumer-protection legislation (transposed into Hungarian law); human rights embedded via Code of Ethics across customer policies and remediation.
- Consumer engagement (ESRS S4-2): regular satisfaction measurement via TRI*M (group-wide), plus NPS and SQM at some subsidiaries; representative annual surveys (1,000/country); analysis by customer segments; no regular cooperation with consumer organizations.
- Customer-centric development: Group-wide Service Design Framework (2024) with portal, tools, training, and expert support; Montenegrin “Customer Live Voice” workshops (youth, retirees, sailors) to gather direct feedback.
- Remediation and grievance channels (ESRS S4-3): multiple accessible complaint channels; regulated, non-discriminatory handling aligned with human rights and local laws; dialogue-focused resolution; restoration or fair compensation for justified cases.

nodes.title: Processes for engaging with consumers and end-users about impacts
nodes.heading: Processes for engaging with consumers and end -users about impacts
nodes.start_phrase: To improve the customer experience, OTP Group regularly collects customer feedback and measures customer satisfaction.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: ESRS S4-2 (engagement with consumers/end-users) and ESRS S4-3 (remediation and complaint channels), anchored in the Group’s Code of Ethics across customer policies and interactions.
- Customer feedback and satisfaction measurement: group-wide, standardized TRI*M methodology conducted annually per country with a representative 1,000-person sample; supplemented by NPS and SQM in some subsidiaries; analysis by customer segments; benchmarking against competitors.
- Complaint handling as a key engagement tool: multiple accessible channels; regulated, non-discriminatory processes aligned with human rights and local laws; emphasis on dialogue for prompt resolution; restoration or appropriate remediation and fair compensation in justified cases.
- Customer-centric product development: launch of the OTP Group Service Design Framework (2024) to enable data- and research-based product, service, and process design; includes a Service Design Portal, one-day customer-centricity training, methodology card set, digital templates, expert support (Service Design Group, Research Group, CX Design CoE), and a leadership playbook; available in Hungarian and English.
- Example initiative: Montenegro’s “Customer Live Voice” workshops to capture direct feedback from targeted groups (youth, retirees, sailors).
- No regular cooperation with consumer organizations or representatives.
- Regulatory context and references: EU and national rules on prudential requirements, consumer credit, APR disclosure, deposit interest/returns, and payment account fee information (PAD Directive).
- Notes: definitions for NPS and SQM; details on representativeness criteria for sampling (age, gender, education, settlement type, region).

nodes.title: Processes to remediate negative impacts and channels for consumers and end-users to raise concerns
nodes.heading: Processes to remediate negative impacts and channels for consumers and end -users to raise concerns
nodes.start_phrase: The Banking Group members provide a wide range of complaint channels for their customers.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: ESRS S4-2 and S4-3 disclosures on customer engagement, remediation of impacts, and complaint handling across OTP Group.
- Customer feedback and satisfaction: Groupwide, standardized measurement using TRI*M, supplemented by NPS and SQM in some subsidiaries; analysis by customer segments; annual, country-level surveys with representative samples; benchmarking against competitors.
- Engagement channels: Complaint handling used as a key engagement tool; no regular cooperation with consumer organizations.
- Customer-centric product development: 2024 launch of a group-level Service Design Framework (portal, tools, training, templates, playbook, and expert support) to embed research- and data-driven design across products, services, and processes.
- Local initiatives: Montenegro’s “Customer Live Voice” workshops gather direct feedback from specific customer groups (youth, retirees, sailors).
- Complaint channels and access: Multiple non-discriminatory, human-rights-aligned channels (ethics line, website, phone, branches, mail; social media forwarded to handlers; any email in Slovenia). In Hungary and Bulgaria, customers may also complain to the National Bank and financial arbitration bodies.
- Transparency and confidentiality: Clear communication of channels and processes via multiple media; data handled confidentially per law and Code of Ethics.
- Monitoring and effectiveness: Use of dedicated IT systems and identifiers to track cases; designated owners; customer notifications; regular (monthly/quarterly/annual) reporting on volume, status, and resolution times; analysis of recurring issues, channel usage, and response times; customer satisfaction with complaint handling measured in several countries.
- Remediation: Aim to restore original state or provide fair compensation for justified complaints; cross-department collaboration on systemic errors.
- 2024 improvements: OTP Bank developing a new complaint handling interface to automate processes and enhance reporting; DSK Bank overhauled complaint handling (process analysis, KPIs, standard workflows, updated policies, staff training, improved customer status communications), with a CEO-chaired Customer Experience Committee reviewing complaints monthly.

nodes.title: Channels Available to Customers for Submitting Complaints
nodes.heading: Channels Available to Customers for Submitting Complaints
nodes.start_phrase: Customers can submit complaints through the ethical reporting system (see @G1 -1) and complaint reporting channels (website, telephone customer service, in person at branches, by postal mail).
nodes.summary:
- Overview of OTP Group’s customer complaint channels, including ethical reporting, website, call centers, branches, postal mail, and forwarding from social media; Slovenia allows complaints to any bank email with mandatory logging by employees.
- Additional external complaint options in Hungary and Bulgaria via the National Bank and EU financial arbitration bodies.
- Customer communication on complaint channels and processes through websites, publications, branch regulations, written notices, and social media; channels designed for general users.
- Implicit trust in channels inferred from usage; no formal trust measurement conducted.
- Confidential handling and storage of complaints and related data per law and the Code of Ethics.
- Complaint tracking across the group using dedicated systems (e.g., OTP Bank, DSK Bank, Slovenian, Croatian, CKB) or other IT tools (Ipoteka, Ukraine, Albania); where systems are absent, operational processes ensure effectiveness.
- Unique identifiers for each case, assigned responsibility to specific employees or teams, and proactive customer updates on process and required actions.
- Regular monthly, quarterly, and annual reporting on complaint volumes, statuses, and resolution times to monitor effectiveness and drive improvements.
- Data analysis to identify recurring issues, systemic weaknesses, channel usage patterns, and response-time gaps.
- Customer feedback mechanisms: satisfaction surveys in Bulgaria, phone interviews in Slovenia, and feedback collection in Serbia, Albania, Montenegro, and Moldova to enhance complaint handling.
- Cross-department collaboration to correct errors impacting multiple customers or causing significant financial loss.
- 2024 improvements: OTP Bank developing a new complaint handling interface to automate workflows, control processes, and speed processing and reporting.
- DSK Bank’s end-to-end enhancement: process and KPI analysis, standardized workflows with clear roles, policy updates, staff development and communication training, improved customer transparency on status, and monthly CEO-led Customer Experience Committee reviews.

nodes.title: Ensuring the Effectiveness of Complaint Handling, Tracking Issue
nodes.heading: Ensuring the Effectiveness of Complaint Handling, Tracking Issue
nodes.start_phrase: The tracking of raised and handled complaints at OTP Bank and several subsidiaries (DSK Bank, Slovenian, Croatian subsidiaries, and CKB Bank) is done in dedicated complaint handling systems or other IT systems (Ipoteka Bank, Ukrainian and Albanian subsidia ries).
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: OTP Group’s complaint management framework within the Integrated Annual Report 2024 (Management Report, Consolidated).
- Complaint submission channels: ethical reporting system, website, phone service, branch visits, postal mail, and forwarded social media inquiries; in Slovenia, any bank email triggers a formal complaint entry; in Hungary and Bulgaria, customers may also apply to the National Bank and EU financial arbitration bodies.
- Customer communication and access: channels and processes are publicized via websites, publications, written notices, in-branch regulations, and social media; channels are open and usable for the general public; trust is inferred from actual use.
- Data protection: complaint content and related data are handled confidentially in line with laws and the Group’s Code of Ethics.
- Tracking and governance: dedicated complaint systems in OTP Bank, DSK Bank, Slovenian and Croatian subsidiaries, and CKB Bank; other IT solutions at Ipoteka Bank, and Ukrainian and Albanian subsidiaries; where systems are absent, processes ensure effectiveness. Complaints get unique IDs, assigned owners, and customers are kept informed.
- Performance management: monthly/quarterly/annual reporting on volumes, status, and resolution times; analysis of aggregated data to find recurring issues and systemic weaknesses; monitoring of channel usage and response times to identify bottlenecks or deficiencies.
- Customer feedback: satisfaction with complaint handling measured via surveys (Bulgaria) and phone interviews (Slovenia); feedback also collected in Serbia, Albania, Montenegro, and Moldova; cross-functional follow-up for multi-customer or high-loss errors.
- 2024 improvements: OTP Bank developing a new interface to automate workflows, strengthen process control, and speed processing/reporting; DSK Bank’s end-to-end enhancement with process/KPI analysis, standard workflows, updated policies, staff and communication training, improved status transparency to customers, and monthly CEO-led Customer Experience Committee reviews.

nodes.title: Improving Complaint Handling
nodes.heading: Improving Complaint Handling
nodes.start_phrase: OTP Group pays special attention to continuously improving its services, based on information and experiences revealed during complaint investigations.
nodes.summary:
- Customer complaint channels: OTP Group accepts complaints via an ethical reporting system, website, phone, branches, and mail; other inbound points (e.g., social media) are forwarded to complaint handling. In Slovenia, any bank email can receive complaints, which staff must log. In Hungary and Bulgaria, customers may also complain to the National Bank and EU financial arbitration bodies. Customers are informed about channels and processes via websites, publications, branch materials, communications, and social media. All reports are handled confidentially per law and the Code of Ethics.

- Complaint handling effectiveness and tracking: Subsidiaries use dedicated complaint systems or IT solutions; where unavailable, processes ensure effective handling. Each case has a unique ID and a responsible handler/group; customers are kept informed. Regular monthly/quarterly/annual reports track volumes, status, and resolution times. Data analysis identifies recurring/systemic issues, monitors channel usage and response times. Customer satisfaction with complaint handling is measured in Bulgaria (surveys), Slovenia (phone interviews), and feedback is also gathered in Serbia, Albania, Montenegro, and Moldova. Cross-functional cooperation addresses errors affecting many customers or causing significant losses.

- 2024 improvements: OTP Bank began developing a new complaint handling interface to automate workflows, control processes, and speed processing/reporting. DSK Bank overhauled its processes and KPIs, standardized workflows, updated policies, trained staff (incl. communication skills), improved transparency for customers, and established monthly CEO-led reviews via the Customer Experience Committee. Slovenia enhanced complaint software for data protection, file handling, and type visibility, and trained departments. Croatia improved interdepartmental communication. CKB implemented new software that auto-routes complaints to expert teams, accelerating resolution.

- Complaint volumes (2024): ~581,000 closed complaints; ~308,000 substantiated. 612 ethical reports (106 from employees; remainder from customers/other stakeholders; anonymity limits breakdown). 7,811 reports via other channels, largely from Ukraine and Moldova (Ukraine includes non-customer and non-complaint reports; some subsidiaries could not provide data). Approximate total customer complaints: ~589,000. No serious customer-related human rights incidents. Business partners are not required to operate complaint channels. The Group may recommend terminating customer relationships after considering all facts, including potential impacts on other customers.

- Information security and data protection – Anti-fraud Policy (ESRS S4-1): Defines evaluation of current practices, future fraud trend mapping, response measures, goals, and tasks. Commits to prevention, detection, and investigation in line with legal and supervisory guidance. Sets principles, concepts, and the fraud function’s role within the three lines of defense. Details tasks such as detection criteria, efficient information flow, real-time transaction monitoring, investigation of suspicious events, actions to confirm/exclude internal involvement, staff education, prevention forums, feedback mechanisms, and fraud risk self-assessment. Describes the Fraud Competence Center’s responsibilities and cooperation with internal control functions. Supported by a Group Fraud Prevention Strategy and related procedures.

nodes.title: Number of Customer Complaints
nodes.heading: Number of Customer Complaints
nodes.start_phrase: OTP Group handles a large number of complaints year after year.
nodes.summary:
- Subsidiaries strengthened customer complaint management:
  - Slovenia: enhanced complaint software for better data protection, clearer file handling, improved complaint-type visibility; conducted cross-department trainings.
  - Croatia: improved interdepartmental communication to speed responses.
  - CKB: deployed new software auto-routing complaints to expert teams, significantly accelerating handling.
- Complaint volumes and reporting (2024):
