  - 612 ethical reports via the Ethical Reporting System (106 from employees; remainder from customers/other stakeholders; customer share not identifiable due to anonymity).
  - 7,811 reports via other channels, mainly from Ukraine and Moldova; Ukrainian figures include various non-customer and non-complaint reports; data unavailable for Albania and Russia.
  - Combined customer complaints across channels: ~589,000.
  - Note on data: procedures are being harmonized, but cultural/financial literacy differences limit cross-country comparability.
- No serious customer-related human rights incidents in 2024.
- Business partner expectations: OTP Group does not require partners to maintain complaint channels; decisions to recommend terminating customer relationships consider all available facts and potential impacts on other customers.
- Information Security and Data Protection – Anti-fraud Policy (ESRS S4-1):
  - Defines fraud prevention/detection/investigation aligned with legal and supervisory guidance; maps fraud trends, sets goals and tasks, emphasizes employee roles and integration within internal defense lines.

nodes.title: Information Security and Data Protection
nodes.heading: 3.3.1. Information Security and Data Protection
nodes.start_phrase: The policy covers the evaluation of current fraud prevention and management practices, mapping future fraud trends, assessing the financial organization's involvement, responding to trends, and defining related goals and tasks.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on customer complaint management across OTP Group subsidiaries:
  - Slovenia enhanced complaint software for stronger data protection, clearer file handling, better complaint-type visibility, and trained staff across departments.
  - Croatia improved interdepartmental communication to speed responses.
  - CKB deployed new software that auto-routes complaints to relevant expert groups, accelerating processing.
  - Group-level harmonization of procedures and definitions is advancing, but cultural and financial literacy differences limit cross-country comparability.

- 2024 complaint and reporting metrics:
  - ~581,000 closed complaints; ~308,000 substantiated.
  - 612 ethical reports via the Ethical Reporting System (106 from employees; remainder from customers/other stakeholders; customer share not identifiable due to anonymity).
  - 7,811 reports via other channels, mostly from Ukraine and Moldova; Ukrainian figure includes all report types; no data from Albania and Russia.

nodes.title: Policies
nodes.heading: Policies
nodes.start_phrase: The policy covers the evaluation of current fraud prevention and management practices, mapping future fraud trends, assessing the financial organization's involvement, responding to trends, and defining related goals and tasks.
nodes.summary:
- Customer complaint management
  - Subsidiary improvements: Slovenia upgraded complaint software (better data protection, clearer file storage, improved type overview) and trained multiple bank departments; Croatia enhanced interdepartmental communication for faster responses; CKB introduced new software that auto-routes complaints to expert groups, speeding resolution.
  - Group harmonization of procedures and definitions continues, though cultural and financial literacy differences across countries limit data comparability.
  - 2024 volumes: ~581,000 closed complaints; ~308,000 substantiated; 612 ethical reports via the Ethical Reporting System (106 from employees, remainder anonymous from customers/others); 7,811 reports via other channels (mostly Ukraine and Moldova; Ukraine includes non-customer and non-complaint reports; Albania and Russia no data). Combined customer complaints approx. 589,000.
  - No serious customer-related human rights incidents in 2024.
  - Business partners are not required to maintain complaint channels; OTP may recommend terminating business relationships based on comprehensive facts and potential impacts on other customers.

- Information security and data protection policies (ESRS S4-1)
  - Anti-fraud Policy: Defines prevention, detection, investigation, trend mapping, goals, and tasks; emphasizes employee role, real-time monitoring, efficient information flow, investigation, education, forums, feedback, and fraud risk self-assessment. Establishes the Fraud Competence Center’s tasks and cooperation with internal control functions. Group-wide scope via subsidiary transposition; ESC accountable for implementation; excerpt available publicly; supplier compliance declarations required; aligned with legal and supervisory guidance (incl. MNB). 2024: most subsidiaries implementing policy, strategy, and a second wave of detailed procedures (fraud process, investigation dept procedures, Fraud Forum rules).
  - Security Policy: Sets group security principles and directions to ensure lawful, safe, prudent operations; group-level, mandatory in Hungary and abroad; implemented by the Security Directorate reporting annually to the ESC; available internally. Group adoption of ICT and information security policy underway.
  - Data Protection Policy: Part of the Compliance Policy; commits to fundamental rights and data protection principles for personal/banking data and third-party transfers; group-wide minimum standards aligned to local laws; coordinated by the Data and Consumer Protection Department; DPO accountable and independent where appointed; policies published on websites. 2024: no significant policy changes; supervisory recommendations integrated into procedures.

- Actions on information security and fraud management (ESRS S4-4)
  - Governance and coordination: Fraud topics regularly addressed by the Executive Steering Committee; tiered committee decision-making for suspicious events with cross-functional participation (business, governance, internal control, operational risk).
  - Continuous analysis and feedback loops inform decisions, capability development, and organizational adjustments. Core principles include customer/bank protection, zero tolerance, prevention first, completeness, speed, objectivity/proportionality, integrity/employee ethics, cooperation, and innovation.
  - Dynamic adaptation to evolving fraud behaviors; strict adherence to time-bound regulatory tasks (e.g., MNB rules).
  - Technology and education: Ongoing tech enhancements with exploration of AI; alignment with market best practices; customer-informed design via surveys (latest security awareness survey completed Dec 2023, evaluated 2024).
  - Cyber Defense Center delivers continuous, high-quality employee training supported by globally recognized certifications (e.g., CompTIA, Blue Team Level 1, Microsoft Cybersecurity, ITILv4, GIAC Forensic).
  - Measures broadly apply across all activities and customer groups unless otherwise specified.

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: Actions
nodes.start_phrase: This section first provides information on the measures related to information security and fraud management, followed by a presentation of the measures grouped by their nature.
nodes.summary:
- Focus and governance: Details OTP Bank Group’s approach to information security and fraud management, overseen by the Executive Steering Committee with cross-functional committees, continuous inter-unit communication, and feedback-driven decision-making. Principles include customer and bank protection, zero tolerance, prevention-first, completeness, speed, proportionality, integrity/ethics, cooperation, and innovation.
- Adaptive, technology-led defense: Continuous updating of measures to match evolving fraud patterns; development of technologies including AI exploration; ongoing employee education via the Cyber Defense Center with globally recognized certifications; customer security awareness survey concluded in Dec 2023.
- Organizational strengthening: 2024 restructuring within the Security Directorate (e.g., Investigation Department, Fraud Management Support Department, Fraud Competence Center) to speed reporting and recovery.
- Group-wide support: Parent bank supports subsidiaries in building/strengthening anti-fraud units and systems; feasibility and implementation of comprehensive or e-channel monitoring underway in several countries; best-practice sharing via a Fraud Information Sharing platform with regular utilization feedback; group-level indicator sharing and incident management for cross-border fraud.
- Product risk management: Risk-based protective measures embedded into new and existing products and services, with emphasis on secure e-channels.
- Key developments and tools:
  - Brand protection and takedowns: Rapid detection and takedown of phishing/misuse; 23,664 social media posts and 127 accounts removed; reduction of Foxpost-type phishing.
  - Caller verification: In-app verification for InternetBank/MobileBank users to combat phone fraud.
  - Integration with national systems: Technical readiness to join Hungary’s Central Fraud Filtering System (KVR) and adherence to CyberShield communication recommendations.
  - Subsidiary initiatives: Slovenia’s project to reduce customer losses and a dedicated fraud information website; Ukraine’s certifications (ISO/IEC 27001:2015 ISMS, PCI DSS 4.0, SWIFT CSP).
- Customer education: Segmented, ongoing multi-channel campaigns (web, internet banking, social media, radio/TV/print), immediate reporting contacts to Fraud Management, 150,000 branch leaflets and 200,000 rural brochures; participation in national CyberShield initiatives; local campaigns in Slovenia and Ukraine.
- External collaborations: Active role in Hungarian Banking Association working committees; ELTE Cyberlab for applied cybersecurity research; 24/7 cooperation with National Police; leadership and knowledge-sharing through EIVOK.
- Monitoring damages and remediation: Continuous analysis and tuning of real-time monitoring rules (>100 adjustments in 2024); group-level trend tracking and targeted measures; regulated correction, follow-up effectiveness checks, and management reporting; customer compensation when bank at fault, per local regulations.
- Data protection framework: Law-compliant, purpose-limited processing; compliance controls and audits; mandatory data protection training group-wide and consumer protection training for relevant staff; designated data protection officers with annual professional training; complaint and ethics reporting mechanisms; corrective actions communicated via newsletters; periodic risk analyses.
- Data protection incidents and GRI 418-1 (2024): 39 substantiated external complaints; 17 regulatory complaints; 37 privacy breaches; 0 data theft; 0 data loss. Noted incident clusters: 130 at OTP Faktoring (misaddressing), 21 in Slovenia (administrative errors), 12 in Croatia (misaddressing).
- Targets and performance management:
  - ISO 27001 certification for Cyber Defense Center’s incident management by Dec 31, 2025.
  - Business-side implementation and use of Hungary’s KVR for monitoring by July 1, 2025.
  - Cameras on 200 ATMs by end-2025 to aid identification.
  - Goals mix absolute/relative and measure both frequency and damages; monitored daily to quarterly with governance reporting; goals set annually and not revised until achieved; terminology standardized via Anti-Fraud Policy and Strategy to ensure consistent group-wide communication.

nodes.title: Targets
nodes.heading: Targets
nodes.start_phrase: The Fraud Prevention Strategy includes goals directly and indirectly related to information security and data protection:
nodes.summary:
- Customer privacy and data protection performance (GRI 418-1): reports 39 substantiated external complaints, 17 regulatory complaints, 37 privacy breaches, and zero data theft or data loss incidents in 2024; references separate disclosure for related legal proceedings.
- Fraud Prevention Strategy targets (ESRS S4-5): obtain ISO 27001 certification for the Cyber Defense Center’s incident management by 31 Dec 2025; implement the MNB Central Fraud Filtering System with operational data use from 1 Jul 2025; install cameras on 200 ATMs by end-2025. Goals mix absolute/relative measures, focus on reducing fraud frequency and damage, and are tracked via daily to quarterly trend analyses with rapid intervention and reporting to governance bodies.
- Goal-setting approach: grounded in evaluations and risk analyses; involves customer input (forums, surveys, feedback) and collaboration with affected organizational units; standardizes anti-fraud terminology across policies to ensure effective communication.
- Frameworks and references used: internal Anti-Fraud Policy and Fraud Risk Self-Assessment; EU PSD2 SCA RTS (2018/389), DORA (2022/2554), ISO 27001; Hungarian National Bank (MNB) Recommendations 12/2022 and 5/2023.
- Access to Quality Information (ESRS S4-1) – Responsible Marketing Policy: commits to fair, accurate, clear communication; avoids promoting irresponsible borrowing or overconsumption; helps customers manage finances sustainably. Applies to OTP Bank and recommended to subsidiaries; overseen by the Head of Marketing and Communications; published on the website and internally; aligned with the Hungarian Advertising Code based on the ICC Code. Supported by a group Tone of Voice handbook and ongoing staff training to ensure plain, consistent language across channels.
- Financial Education Strategy: aims to boost customers’ financial confidence and conscious money management with suitable product portfolios; applied at OTP Bank in 2024, extending to subsidiaries in 2025; adopted by the ESG Committee and led by the Head of Marketing and Communications; aligned with UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking and MNB expectations on financial awareness.

nodes.title: Access to Quality Information
nodes.heading: 3.3.2. Access to Quality Information
nodes.start_phrase: Key content: The policy states that OTP Bank is committed to responsible marketing of its products, prioritizing fair commercial communication, accurate information, and product recommendations.
nodes.summary:

- Under “Access to Quality Information” (ESRS S4-1), it details:
  - Responsible Marketing Policy: OTP Bank’s commitment to clear, fair, and accurate customer communications; avoidance of promoting overconsumption or irresponsible borrowing; support for reasonable, sustainability-aware financial management; scope covering OTP Bank with recommendation to subsidiaries; accountability with the Head of Marketing & Communications; policy availability on the website and internal repository; alignment with the Hungarian Advertising Code based on the ICC Code; implementation supported by a group Tone of Voice handbook and regular staff training on clear communication.
  - Financial Education Strategy: Objective to increase financially confident and conscious customers with suitable product portfolios; applied to OTP Bank in 2024 with extension to subsidiaries in 2025; adopted by the ESG Committee with implementation by the Head of Marketing & Communications; motivated by the UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking and aligned with MNB expectations on developing financial awareness.

nodes.title: Policies
nodes.heading: Policies
nodes.start_phrase: Key content: The policy states that OTP Bank is committed to responsible marketing of its products, prioritizing fair commercial communication, accurate information, and product recommendations.
nodes.summary:
- The section outlines the regulatory and standards framework guiding goal setting, including OTP Group’s Anti-Fraud Policy, fraud risk self-assessment and action plan, EU PSD2 SCA RTS (2018/389), DORA (2022/2554), ISO 27001, and MNB recommendations on internal defenses and payment fraud.
- Under “Access to Quality Information” (ESRS S4-1), it details a Responsible Marketing Policy committing to fair, accurate, and clear communication, avoiding promotion of overconsumption or easy debt repayment, and supporting sustainable, responsible borrowing. It applies to OTP Bank (recommended to subsidiaries), is overseen by the Head of Marketing and Communications, aligns with the Hungarian Advertising Code/ICC standards, and is operationalized through a Tone of Voice handbook and regular staff training.
- A Financial Education Strategy seeks to boost customers’ confident, conscious financial decision-making with suitable product portfolios; it was in effect at OTP Bank in 2024, to be extended to subsidiaries in 2025, adopted by the ESG Committee, led by the Head of Marketing and Communications, and aligned with UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking and MNB expectations.
- “Actions” (ESRS S4-4) emphasize customer education across the Group: branch staff teach self-service channels (ATMs, InternetBank, MobileBank), highlight responsible borrowing, and share Hungarian National Bank financial awareness materials. OTP Bank ran media campaigns focusing on children’s financial education and family money discussions, continued the “Finance Made Simple” video series with partners, expanded to Instagram and TikTok with content on everyday banking and data security, enhanced the online branch locator (including accessibility details), and plans to set quantified education goals by 2025.
- Subsidiary initiatives include DSK Bank’s articles, trainings, videos, and targeted campaigns for elderly customers (with guides on ATMs, card payments, savings); the Slovenian subsidiary’s video series and resources, including materials for vulnerable groups; and OTP Bank Croatia’s participation in national initiatives promoting responsible financial behavior and safe online shopping.

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: Actions
nodes.start_phrase: OTP Group places great emphasis on educating customers about various financial products and using digital channels and tools.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on customer financial education and digital literacy across OTP Group, aligned with ESRS S4-4:
  - OTP Bank (parent) integrates education into branch roles, promotes responsible borrowing, shares national regulator materials, runs media campaigns emphasizing children’s financial education, and partners on the “Finance Made Simple” video series. Expanded social media (incl. Instagram, TikTok) with content on everyday banking and data security. Upgraded website branch locator. Plans to implement and quantify a Financial Education Strategy by 2025.

    - Croatia: Participation in national association initiatives; tips for safe online shopping.
    - Serbia: Branch-led education on products and digital channels; special in-branch events leveraging administrative staff.
    - Uzbekistan (Ipoteka Bank): Social media video education; participation in Global Money Week and Cybersecurity Awareness Month; pilot with Meeter Greeter toolkits to shift less digitally skilled customers to digital.
    - Ukraine: Shared central bank consumer info; supported a public lecture series on Ukrainian financial history.
    - Montenegro: Ongoing educational materials; introduced Meeter Greeter in branches to demo digital products for older customers; campaigns with incentives; multilingual digital platforms with tutorials.
    - Albania: Participation in national financial education campaigns; year-long literacy initiative.
    - Russia: In-app “stories” to inform customers about new offers and changes.

- Enhancing clarity and accessibility of information:
  - OTP Bank: Service Design Group rewrites customer texts for clarity and Tone of Voice alignment.
  - Croatia: New CMS; removal of jargon; workshops with an external clarity specialist.
  - Serbia: Simplified communications of complex legal topics; visual aids; personal financial manager in app; more video content.
  - Uzbekistan (Ipoteka): Plain language, transparent benefits/risks; dialogue scripts for front-office staff.
  - Montenegro: Branch visits by customer experience team; continuous feedback loop; SQM system to track satisfaction; expanded service channels (video calls, live chat, phone, email).
  - Russia: Staff training to explain complex topics; simplified documents; clear presentation of key conditions; feedback-driven adjustments.
  - Note to legal proceedings related to marketing/information rules referenced elsewhere.

- Targets (ESRS S4-5):
  - Commitment to set measurable, group-wide goals based on the Financial Education Strategy focused on:
    - Increasing customers’ confident, conscious financial navigation.
    - Aligning customer product portfolios with individual goals.
    - Strengthening OTP Bank’s positive brand impact and perception.
  - Quantification/operationalization pending; 2024 effectiveness not measured.

- Access to financial products and services (ESRS S4-1):
  - Compliance Policy mandates ethical, consumer-protective product development and accessible, fair, high-quality services.

- Accessibility Strategy (for customers with disabilities):
  - Defines needs assessment methodology, measures taken since 2007, and two-year goals; last reviewed in 2023.
  - Scope: OTP Bank, with a Group Recommendation guiding subsidiaries.
  - Governance: Adopted by Management Committee; Deputy CEO, Retail Division accountable.
  - Training: Mandatory for branch staff; voluntary for non-customer-facing roles.
  - Stakeholder focus: Built on needs assessments of customers with disabilities.

nodes.title: Targets
nodes.heading: Targets
nodes.start_phrase: We will set comprehensive, measurable goals for quality information based on the Financial Education Strategy, first at the parent bank and then extending to the group level, focusing on:

nodes.summary:
- Focus on clear, customer-friendly information and communication across OTP Group:
  - Uzbekistan: plain-language materials, clear product benefits/risks, front-office dialogue scripts.
  - Montenegro: branch coaching by customer experience team, active feedback use, 2024 rollout of SQM system to track satisfaction by branch/product/employee; expanded channels to video calls and live chat alongside phone and email.
  - Russia: staff training to explain complex finance, simplification of documents and terms, clear presentation of key conditions with references, feedback-driven communication.
  - Reference to legal proceedings on marketing/communications noted elsewhere (@G1-4).

- Targets (ESRS S4-5):
  - Group to set measurable, comprehensive goals under the Financial Education Strategy, aiming to increase financially confident customers, ensure portfolios fit individual goals, and improve brand perception.
  - Quantification/operationalization to follow; no 2024 effectiveness measurement yet.

- Access to Financial Products and Services (ESRS S4-1):
  - Compliance Policy embeds ethical and consumer-protection principles in product development and service accessibility.
  - Accessibility Strategy for customers with disabilities:
    - Covers OTP Bank; Group Recommendation guides subsidiaries.
    - Governance: adopted by Management Committee; Retail Division Deputy CEO accountable.
    - Training: mandatory for branch staff; voluntary for others.
    - Stakeholder basis: needs assessments among customers with disabilities.
    - Alignment with Hungarian acts and decrees; consistent with EU requirements.

- Actions on accessibility (ESRS S4-4), progressing toward EU Accessibility Directive compliance by 2025, in physical and digital domains:
  - Mobility impairments:
    - 1,110 branches accessible (all in Hungary except one heritage site; >70% in Bulgaria, Slovenia, Croatia, Ukraine, Montenegro; >25% in Serbia, Uzbekistan, Moldova, Russia). Disability bells installed where only mobile ramps are possible in Hungary.
    - 2,730 ATMs accessible (all in Croatia and Russia; some in Hungary, Slovenia, Serbia, Ukraine, Albania, Moldova).
  - Visual impairments:
    - 386 branches with tactile guide paths (some in Hungary and Russia; one in Croatia).
    - 444 branches with Braille-button call devices (some in Hungary, Bulgaria, Croatia).
    - 3,361 ATMs with Braille labels (Hungary, Slovenia, Serbia, Uzbekistan, Ukraine, Moldova, Russia); 1,411 ATMs in Hungary fully accessible with audio via headphones and screen darkening.
  - Deaf and hard-of-hearing:
    - 342 branches with induction loops (all in Hungary and Croatia).
    - 341 branches with sign-language interpreter tablets (all in Hungary; some in Serbia), supported by SINOSZ.
    - 64 branches with sign-language-speaking staff (some in Hungary and Serbia).
  - Note: relevant national legislation for the EU Directive not yet adopted in Bulgaria and Croatia.

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: Actions
nodes.start_phrase: OTP Group continuously improves the accessibility of its infrastructure.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and standards: Describes OTP Group’s approach to accessibility and inclusion under ESRS S4 (Actions and Targets), aligned with EU Directive 2019/882, national accessibility laws and decrees, and GRI (FS13, 418-1). Includes reporting definitions for branches/ATMs and specific accessibility terms.
- Physical accessibility progress:
  - Mobility: By end-2024, 1,110 accessible branches and 2,730 accessible ATMs across the Group; group-level accessibility proportions—branches 76%, ATMs 49%.
  - Visual: 386 branches with tactile guide paths; 444 branches with Braille-labeled call devices; 3,361 ATMs with Braille labels, including 1,411 in Hungary with audio guidance via headphones and optional screen darkening; group-level proportions—branches 27%, ATMs 25%.
  - Hearing: 342 branches with induction loops; 341 branches with sign language interpreter tablets; 64 branches with sign-language-speaking staff; group-level branch proportion 22%.
- Partnerships and customer information: Collaboration with SINOSZ and MVGYOSZ; accessibility details disclosed on OTP Bank’s website and branch locator.
- 2024 developments by entity:
  - OTP Bank (Hungary): Installed 151 tactile paths, 171 interpreter tablets, induction loops in all branches; >100 accessible ATMs added; refreshed mandatory staff training completed by Sep 2024.
  - DSK Bank (Bulgaria): New ATMs support external headphones (~30 in 2024).
  - Slovenia: Full branch assessments, renovations begun; ATM keyboard highlighting; Bankart ATM text-to-speech planned for 2025; staff guidelines for vulnerable customers.
  - Croatia: 13 new induction loops; loops to be standard in renovations.
  - Startup collaboration: Inclusio app to notify staff of arriving customers with disabilities and their support needs.
  - Ukraine: Physical accessibility assessments in 21 branches.
  - Montenegro (CKB): Staff training and improved signage.
  - Russia: Ramps, tactile/visual markings; updated staff training materials.
- Digital accessibility:
  - By end-2024, selected subsidiaries’ websites, internet and mobile banking are partially accessible.
  - OTP Bank and Hungarian subsidiaries follow WCAG 2.1 A (some AA) during design; comprehensive testing planned H1 2025; full internet/mobile banking accessibility targeted for 2025.
  - Slovenia launched WCAG 2.2 project.
  - Browser tools and simplified content introduced for users with cognitive/mental disabilities.
- Access in disadvantaged/low-population areas (GRI FS13):
  - OTP provides broad coverage; density lower in disadvantaged areas; competitor data limited in some markets.
  - Country snapshots include counts, changes, and shares of branches/ATMs in disadvantaged areas for Hungary, Bulgaria, Croatia, Serbia, Albania, Montenegro, Uzbekistan, Russia, Ukraine; disadvantaged areas not defined for Slovenia and Moldova.
- Mobile Bank: Launch of mobile branch buses in Hungary (3 buses by end-2024) offering live-system retail services in towns without branches.
- Social Lab initiative: New Group program aligned with UN PRB Financial Health & Inclusion; standardized four-stage methodology (challenge identification, problem definition, solution prototyping with stakeholders, scaling); 2024 focused on problem definition and solution selection; test projects for disadvantaged groups and youth to start in 2025.
- Housing loans and inclusion:
  - ~510,000 active housing loan contracts Group-wide at end-2024, ~59,000 new; ~42% in Hungary; strong portfolios in Bulgaria, Slovenia, Croatia, Serbia, Uzbekistan, and CKB.
  - Significant state-supported schemes: ~91,000 Hungarian “Home Creation” contracts; 5,000+ in Croatia; nearly 15,000 at Ipoteka Bank; Russia doesn’t offer mortgages; limited in Ukraine.
- Preventing over-indebtedness: Lending policy and regulation ensure transparent, prudent conditions; risks monitored via IFRS Stage 3 ratio; proactive condition changes to prevent deterioration; no separate tracking for disadvantaged-customer loans.
- Targets and governance (ESRS S4-5):
  - Goal to meet EU accessibility requirements across physical (branches, ATMs, contact center) and digital (web, internet and mobile banking) channels by 2025.
  - Branches to be fully equipped by June 2025 (tactile paths, call systems, interpreter tablets, induction loops, mobile ramps, disability bells).
  - ATMs to feature screen reader software and large-font options across all functions.
  - Websites/digital channels to meet WCAG 2.1 Level A.
  - Accessibility strategy in place since 2007; continuous review; ongoing engagement with advocacy groups.
  - Central tracking via Branch Unified Master Database; mandatory staff sensitivity training monitored; Ukraine to make 5 more branches accessible in 2025.
- Reporting notes: Clarifies S4-3 compensation scope (excludes transaction refunds); GRI 418-1 counting method for confirmed misuse of personal information; definitions of branch/ATM and accessibility measurement scope; terms for guide lanes, Braille push buttons, and induction loops.

nodes.title: Targets
nodes.heading: Targets
nodes.start_phrase: We will define goals related to the availability and accessibility of products and services – beyond legal compliance – through the @Social Lab , and have already set goals for accessibility.
nodes.summary:
- Section outlines ESRS S4-5 targets focused on improving availability and accessibility of products and services beyond legal requirements, with goal-setting coordinated through the Social Lab.
- Compliance context: EU Directive 2019/882 applies to OTP Group EU subsidiaries, covering branches, ATMs, and digital platforms (web, internet banking, mobile banking).
- Strategic aim: design physical (branches, contact centers, ATMs) and digital channels (Mobile and InternetBank) so customers with disabilities can access all services/products in line with legal requirements.
- 2025 targets for branches: install tactile guide paths, customer call systems, sign language interpreter tablets, induction loops, mobile ramps, and disability bells.
- 2025 targets for ATMs and digital channels: equip all ATMs with screen reader software and font-size increase options, expand screen reader functions to all features; ensure website and digital channels meet WCAG 2.1 Level A.
- Governance and engagement: Accessibility Strategy in place since 2007, regularly reviewed and aligned with regulatory changes; continuous dialogue with advocacy organizations to refine service processes.
- Monitoring and training: ongoing tracking of accessibility tool deployment in the Branch Unified Master Database; continuous staff sensitivity and preparedness training; Ukrainian subsidiary plans to make 5 additional branches accessible in 2025.
- Reporting policy and definitions (S4):
  - S4-3 AR23 clarifies compensation figures exclude transaction refunds.
  - GRI 418-1: counts confirmed misuse of customer personal information without overlap across types.
  - Definitions provided for bank branch, ATM, and scope of accessibility data (S4-4 31a).
  - Clarifications of accessibility-related terms: accessible public areas (“drawers”), guide lanes for visually impaired, Braille-labeled physical call-ticket buttons, and induction loop systems for hearing-impaired users.

nodes.title: Reporting policy for heading S4
nodes.heading: 3.4. Reporting policy for heading S4
nodes.start_phrase: S4-3 AR23: The amount of compensation does not include refunds for transactions.
nodes.summary:
- ESRS S4 targets: OTP Group will set goals on product and service availability and accessibility beyond legal compliance via the Social Lab; accessibility goals are already defined.
- Regulatory scope: EU Directive 2019/882 on accessibility applies to OTP’s EU subsidiaries covering branches, ATMs, and digital platforms (web, internet banking, mobile banking).
- Accessibility commitments and 2025 targets: design physical (branches, contact center, ATMs) and digital (Mobile, InternetBank) channels for customers with disabilities; equip all branches by June 2025 with tactile guide paths, call systems, sign language interpreter tablets, induction loops, mobile ramps, and disability bells; ensure ATMs have screen readers and large-font options, with expanded screen-reader functionality; ensure website and digital channels meet WCAG 2.1 Level A.
- Ongoing approach: Accessibility Strategy in place since 2007; regular reviews aligned with legal changes; continuous engagement with advocacy organizations; tracking of supportive tools in a master database; ongoing staff sensitivity and preparedness training; Ukraine aims to make 5 more branches accessible in 2025.
- Reporting and definitions (S4/G1/GRI): clarifies S4-3 compensation scope; GRI 418-1 reporting on confirmed misuse of customer personal data; definitions of bank branch, ATM, accessibility scope (S4-4), accessible areas, guide lanes, Braille call buttons, induction loops, sign interpreters and sign language associates; definitions for “total accessible accounts” and hearing-impaired accessible accounts; ATM accessibility criteria.
- Access in underserved areas (GRI G4: FS13): reports total and percentage of branches/ATMs in sparsely populated or economically disadvantaged areas, with country-specific definitions provided for Hungary, Bulgaria, Croatia, Serbia, Uzbekistan, Ukraine, Montenegro, Albania, and Russia.
- Governance focus: emphasizes transparency, ethical conduct, compliance, and internal controls; balances sustainability and ethical norms with legal obligations to ensure profitable operations for depositors, shareholders, and investors.
- Employee engagement on compliance: dissemination via intranet, knowledge management, conferences, e-learning, and a network of compliance officers.
- Material impacts, risks, and opportunities: positive societal impact from ethical conduct and AML; residual risks of non-conformities; financial and reputational risks from non-compliance; anti-corruption efforts yield social benefits though abuses can still occur; cross-referenced to SBM-3 for details.
- Policies underpinning corporate culture (ESRS G1-1): Code of Ethics (incl. Gift Policy) and Compliance Policy (incl. Sanctions, Anti-Corruption, AML/CTF) publicly available; Code of Ethics sets behavioral expectations, ethical commitments, and reporting channels for violations; all employees and partners must be familiar with and track updates.

structure.title: Governance Information
structure.heading: 4. Governance Information
structure.start_phrase: For OTP Group, transparent operations and ethical business conduct are of paramount importance.
structure.summary:
- Part of the Integrated Annual Report 2024 covering Governance Information, specifically Corporate Governance at OTP Group.
- Highlights commitment to transparency, ethical business conduct, legal compliance, risk reduction, and strong internal controls; balances long-term sustainability with the legal duty to ensure profitability for depositors, shareholders, and investors.
- Emphasizes clear internal responsibilities and compliance with environmental, social, and regulatory expectations across the entire Group.
- Details employee engagement and compliance awareness via intranet communications, knowledge management, international conferences, e-learning, and a network of compliance officers.
- Defines the locus of impacts and risks as Group-wide operations, with anti–money laundering (AML) as a critical focus for Group banks.
- Presents material topics and related impacts/risks:
  - Corporate culture, compliance, AML: positive societal impact from ethical conduct and AML; residual non-conformity risk; financial and reputational risks from non-compliance and AML breaches.

- Points to further detail in SBM-3 and subsequent sections.

- Notes that key policies or extracts are publicly available on OTP Bank’s website under Due Diligence information.

nodes.title: Corporate Governance
nodes.heading: 4.1. Corporate Governance
nodes.start_phrase: Ensuring legal compliance, reducing risks, and effectively enforcing business, ethical, and internal controls are key objectives.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on OTP Group’s corporate governance emphasizing transparency, ethical conduct, legal compliance, risk reduction, and robust internal controls.
- Balance between long-term, sustainable corporate culture and legal duty to ensure profitability for depositors, shareholders, and investors.
- Group-wide commitment to meeting environmental, social, and regulatory expectations through clear internal responsibilities and regulation.
- Employee awareness and engagement via intranet content, knowledge management, international conferences, e-learning, and a network of compliance officers.
- Scope of impacts and risks spans the entire OTP Group’s operations; anti–money laundering (AML) is highlighted as essential for Group banks.
- Material topics and impacts:
  - Corporate culture, compliance, and AML: positive societal impact of ethical conduct and AML; residual risk of non-conformities; financial and reputational risks from non-compliance, especially AML breaches.
  - Corruption and bribery: social benefits of effective prevention; acknowledgment that abuses may still occur.
- Policy framework (ESRS G1-1):
  - Code of Ethics (including Gift Policy): group-level since 2006, continuously updated; sets behavioral expectations, ethical commitments, and reporting channels for violations; mandatory familiarity and adherence for all employees and business partners.
  - Compliance Policy: includes Sanctions Policy, Anti-Corruption Policy, and AML/Counter-Terrorism Financing Policy.
  - Key policies or extracts are publicly available on OTP Bank’s website.
- Reference to further details on impacts, risks, opportunities, and their management (SBM-3 and subsequent sections).
- Note on G1-1: promotion of corporate culture considered as measures and objectives under ESRS.

nodes.title: Policies on Corporate Culture and Business Conduct
nodes.heading: Policies on Corporate Culture and Business Conduct135
nodes.start_phrase: The two most defining policies of OTP Group regarding corporate culture and business conduct are the Code of Ethics and the Compliance Policy.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on corporate governance: Transparent operations, ethical conduct, legal compliance, risk reduction, and robust internal controls; balancing long-term sustainability with profitability obligations to depositors, shareholders, and investors.
- Group-wide scope and culture: Transparency, clear internal responsibilities, and compliance with environmental, social, and regulatory expectations; employee awareness via intranet, knowledge management, conferences, e-learning, and a network of compliance officers.
- Material topics, impacts, and risks: 
  - Corporate culture, compliance, and AML: Positive societal impact from ethical conduct and preventing money laundering; residual non-conformity risks; financial and reputational risks from non-compliance, especially AML.
  - Corruption and bribery: Social benefits from prevention; residual abuse risk remains.
- Policy framework (aligned with ESRS G1-1):
  - Code of Ethics (incl. Gift Policy): Group-level since 2006; clear behavioral expectations, reporting channels, anti-corruption and gift rules, commitment to environmental sustainability; mandatory training; applies to executives, employees, and agents; based on UN, OECD, ILO, and UNGPs; minimal changes in 2024.
  - Partner Code of Ethics: Extends ethical requirements to suppliers and partners via GTCs/contract clauses; public availability; otherwise mirrors the Code of Ethics.
  - Compliance Policy: Principles for an independent compliance function; group-wide guidance with local adaptation; embeds responsible corporate governance, transparency, and public disclosure; includes a sanctions compliance policy and a public defense-industry financing policy; aligned with MNB recommendations and EU/international supervisory guidance; Board and Supervisory Board oversight.
  - Sanctions Compliance: Adherence to EU, UN, UK, US, and applicable national sanctions; prohibits activities that violate or circumvent sanctions; customer and transaction screening; enhanced reviews for sensitive transactions; group-level minimum requirements.
  - AML/CFT Policy: Group-level annual risk assessment; risk-based customer categorization, KYC, transaction monitoring, and FIU reporting; mandatory group-wide standards with deviations only under parent bank approval to meet local laws.
  - Anti-Corruption Policy: Zero tolerance for bribery and illicit advantages; identifies higher-risk areas; applies to employees and partners; broad availability, contractual anti-corruption clauses, and mandatory training; aligned with UN/EU instruments and Wolfsberg ABC guidance.
- Governance, accountability, and availability: Board of Directors and Supervisory Board responsible for policy implementation; policies available in internal repositories and many publicly on the website; internal stakeholders contributed to policy development.
- Actions and targets: Ethical Reporting System/whistleblowing—employees must report illegal practices or Code violations via supervisors or compliance contact points; anti-corruption and compliance training integrated into programs.
- Standards and disclosures: References to ESRS requirements (e.g., G1-1) and cross-references to broader impact/risk management (SBM-3).

nodes.title: Actions and targets
nodes.heading: Actions and targets
nodes.start_phrase: According to the expectations of the Code of Ethics, OTP Group employees are required to draw attention to any illegal practices, violations of the rules and values outlined in the Code of Ethics, or any practices that may lead to abuse, by notifying the affected parties o r their immediate supervisor.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of group-level compliance policies: AML/CFT and Anti-Corruption frameworks set by OTP Bank for the entire Group, aligned with the Group’s Compliance Policy and applicable internal regulations and General Business Rules.
- AML/CFT policy: defines group-wide requirements, procedures, and workflows; available in internal repository and on the Bank’s website; designed to comply with EU and UN Security Council financial and asset restrictive measures.
- Anti-Corruption Policy: zero tolerance for bribery and illicit advantage; identifies high-risk areas and guides development of related regulations and employee conduct; applies to all employees, contractual partners, and others involved with Group members; governed by the Board of Directors and Supervisory Board; accessible internally and publicly with an anti-corruption clause expectation for partners; training integrated into the Compliance training program; aligned with domestic/international laws and Wolfsberg ABC Guidance.
- Actions and targets on culture and compliance: emphasis on ethical conduct, awareness, and application of the Code of Ethics and Partner Code of Ethics.
- Ethical Reporting System: mandatory reporting by employees of illegal practices or Code violations; external parties can report or inquire on Partner Code issues; multiple channels (in person, mail, phone, email, local compliance contacts, online system), including anonymous reporting; continuous operation with confidentiality and whistleblower protection.
- Reporting procedures and timelines: acknowledgment within 7 days for written online reports; investigations within 30 days, extendable with notice up to a 3-month maximum; outcomes communicated to whistleblowers; fair process with impartiality and right of the reported person to present a defense and provide evidence.
- Case handling and governance: Ethics Department head closes first-instance procedures, determines violations, and proposes remedial/preventive measures; appeals allowed within 15 days to the Ethics Committee (second instance); referrals to authorities when legally required; criminal matters coordinated with the Security Directorate; immediate notification to the President-CEO organization and Supervisory Board for reports involving senior executives, subsidiary heads, or the Compliance Directorate; ethical cases may be initiated and investigated outside the reporting system, with mandatory referral from complaint handling to the Ethics Department for classification and handling.
- Ethical training: annual mandatory training for all employees; mandatory completion for sales agents shortly after onboarding; content covers ethical foundations, conflicts of interest, conduct inside/outside the bank, political involvement, workplace finances, corruption/undue influence, mutual respect, and cooperation; regular review and monitoring of understanding and adherence; annual leadership-specific ethics training to support role-model behavior and issue handling.
- Note on organizational change: from January 1, 2025, the Ethics Department at OTP Bank will be named the Integrity Department (naming may differ across Group members).

nodes.title: Ethical Reporting System
nodes.heading: Ethical Reporting System
nodes.start_phrase: According to the expectations of the Code of Ethics, OTP Group employees are required to draw attention to any illegal practices, violations of the rules and values outlined in the Code of Ethics, or any practices that may lead to abuse, by notifying the affected parties o r their immediate supervisor.
nodes.summary:
- Describes OTP Group’s ethical/violation reporting system, open to employees and external parties via multiple channels (in person, letter, phone, email, compliance contacts, and an online Reporting System), with 24/7 availability, option for anonymity, confidentiality, and whistleblower protection per law.
- Acknowledgment of written reports submitted through the Reporting System within seven days, including procedural and data processing information under the Whistleblower Act.
- Investigations start promptly and conclude within 30 days; extensions are allowed in justified cases with notice, but total duration cannot exceed three months. Whistleblowers are informed of outcomes or reasons for non-investigation.
- Ensures fair process: all participants act independently and impartially per the Code of Ethics; reported persons may present their position personally or via legal representative and submit evidence.
- First-instance decisions are made by the Head of the Ethics Department (renamed Integrity Department at OTP Bank from Jan 1, 2025), determining legal/ethical breaches and recommending remedial and preventive measures.
- Appeals: whistleblowers or reported parties may appeal to the Ethics Committee (second instance) within 15 days via the reporting channels.
- Regulatory and criminal matters: the Ethics Department initiates procedures with competent authorities when required; criminal complaints are coordinated with the Security Directorate.
- Escalation: immediate notification to the head of the President-CEO organization and the Supervisory Board when reports involve senior executives, first executives of subsidiaries (domestic or foreign), or the Compliance Directorate’s activities.
- Ethical cases, including corruption and bribery, may be investigated immediately and independently outside the standard reporting system; complaints units must forward such cases to the Ethics Department for classification and handling.
- Ethical training: annual mandatory training for all employees (sales agents must complete shortly after onboarding), covering ethical foundations, conflicts of interest, conduct inside/outside the bank, political involvement, workplace finances, corruption/undue influence, and mutual respect/cooperation, with practical guidance; regular monitoring of understanding and adherence.
- Leadership development: separate annual ethical training for leaders to equip them to address ethical issues effectively.

nodes.title: Ethical training
nodes.heading: Ethical training
nodes.start_phrase: OTP Group considers it particularly important to familiarize employees with ethical norms and the ethical reporting system, and to raise awareness among them.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of OTP Group’s ethics and compliance framework, focusing on the whistleblowing system, ethical leadership and staff training, and AML/CFT awareness.
- Whistleblowing system: open to employees and external parties; reports accepted via in-person, letter, phone, email, compliance contacts, and an online Reporting System; anonymous reporting allowed; continuous operation; confidentiality and whistleblower protection ensured.
- Procedural timelines: acknowledgment within 7 days for online reports; investigation within 30 days, extendable with notice but capped at 3 months; outcomes and reasons communicated to the whistleblower.
- Fair process safeguards: independence and impartiality required; reported individuals can present their position and evidence.
- Governance of cases: Head of the Ethics Department closes first-instance cases, determines violations of law/Code, and proposes remedial/preventive measures; affected parties may appeal to the Ethics Committee within 15 days.
- Escalation to authorities: Ethics Department initiates proceedings when legally required; potential criminal matters coordinated with the Security Directorate; immediate notification to the President-CEO organization and Supervisory Board when senior executives or the Compliance Directorate are implicated.
- Intake and triage: ethical incidents, including corruption/bribery, may be investigated outside the reporting system; complaint-handling units must promptly refer such cases to the Ethics Department.
- Ethical training: annual mandatory training for all employees; sales agents must complete training shortly after starting; topics include ethical foundations, conflicts of interest, conduct inside/outside the bank, political involvement, workplace finances, corruption/undue influence, and mutual respect; understanding and adherence are monitored.
- Leadership ethics: annual training for leaders on leading by example, creating a proper work environment, equal treatment, and managing conflicts of interest; leaders must foster a safe speak-up culture, model appropriate behavior, and ensure compliance with the Code of Ethics.
- Compliance training program: risk-based and tailored; includes onboarding orientation and ad-hoc/annual refreshers; materials and tests prepared by compliance units; participation criteria set by function; content reviewed at least annually and plans adjusted per risk assessments and development needs.
- AML/CFT awareness: training and whistleblowing are key measures; at least annual mandatory training, typically online (some in-person), covering regulations, updates, and case studies; training concludes with a test.
- Entity coverage: training mandatory for all employees at DSK Bank, OTP Bank Slovenia, Ipoteka Bank, OTP Bank Ukraine, OTP Bank Albania, OTP Bank Moldova, and OTP Bank Russia; in Hungary (OTP Bank and Merkantil Bank) training targets AML/CFT-involved and customer-facing staff and their managers, with annual general and specialized modules and written/online exams.
- Organizational note: From January 1, 2025, the Ethics Department at OTP Bank will be renamed the Integrity Department (naming may vary among Group members).

nodes.title: Taking action against Money Laundering
nodes.heading: Taking action against Money Laundering
nodes.start_phrase: The main measures related to combating money laundering include the training program and the operation of the whistleblowing system.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on ethical leadership and culture: Leaders must model the Code of Ethics, ensure equal treatment, create a safe, comfortable environment for raising ethical concerns without retaliation, and maintain appropriate tone, language, and behavior. They are responsible for fostering an ethical culture and monitoring compliance with lawful tools. The Code guides conduct but cannot prescribe actions for every situation.
- Ethics and compliance training framework: OTP Group provides tailored training with adequate time, budget, and resources, including orientation for new hires and ad-hoc or annual refresher mandatory courses. The compliance function monitors participation, addresses knowledge gaps, and bases the annual training plan on compliance risk assessments, legal requirements, and internal expectations. Compliance units develop and test materials, review them at least annually, and adjust plans as needed.
- Key leadership training topics: leading by example; creating an appropriate work environment; ensuring equal treatment; managing conflicts of interest.
- AML/CFT measures: Focus on regular (at least annual) mandatory training and an operational whistleblowing system to combat money laundering and terrorist financing.
- AML/CFT training approach: Delivered mainly online with some in-person sessions; includes regulatory overviews, current updates, case studies; concludes with testing. Two models across banks—mandatory for all staff in some subsidiaries, and targeted to AML/CFT-involved and customer-facing roles (and their managers) in others.
- Banks with AML/CFT training mandatory for all employees: DSK Bank, OTP Bank Slovenia, Ipoteka Bank, OTP Bank Ukraine, OTP Bank Albania, OTP Bank Moldova, OTP Bank Russia.
- Hungary-specific details (OTP Bank and Merkantil Bank): Training aligned with the AML/CFT Act and MNB regulations. Managers and AML/CFT-involved staff receive annual general training with written/electronic exams; customer-facing employees receive more detailed annual specialized training. Merkantil Bank’s annual training is e-learning with an online exam.

nodes.title: Enhancing AML/CFT Awareness
nodes.heading: Enhancing AML/CFT Awareness
nodes.start_phrase: To increase the AML/CFT awareness of the Banking Group's affected employees, regular (at least annual) mandatory training sessions are held.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on ethical leadership: leaders must model the Code of Ethics, foster a safe, respectful work environment, enable good-faith reporting without retaliation, set the right tone and behavior, and monitor ethical compliance using lawful tools.
- Group-wide compliance training: risk-based, legally aligned programs with orientation for new hires and annual/ad‑hoc refreshers; compliance prepares materials and tests, monitors completion, addresses gaps, and reviews content at least annually.
- AML/CFT awareness and training: at least annual mandatory training delivered online or in person; scope varies by subsidiary (some train all employees; others focus on AML/KYC, customer-facing roles, and managers). Content covers regulations, updates, case studies, and ends with testing.
  - All-employee mandatory AML/CFT training at DSK Bank, OTP Bank Slovenia, Ipoteka Bank, OTP Bank Ukraine, OTP Bank Albania, OTP Bank Moldova, OTP Bank Russia.
  - Hungary (OTP Bank, Merkantil Bank): training for AML/CFT-involved and customer-facing staff and managers; annual refreshers with exams; specialized training for customer-facing roles; Merkantil via e‑learning with online exam.
  - Serbia: training per national AML law for staff establishing relationships and executing transactions.
  - Croatia: training for customer-facing staff and senior management per legal requirements.
  - Montenegro (CKB): training for identified risk-exposed roles, including senior management and Supervisory Board.
  - Romania: mandatory training for staff involved in AML/CFT or KYC.
  - Ongoing internal communications share AML red flags and good practices via intranet/newsletters.
- AML whistleblowing system: anonymous reporting channel for AML/CFT violations; investigations completed within 30 days by designated compliance roles; reports include actions, deadlines, responsibilities; Compliance Director ensures implementation and escalates to authorities when warranted; operates continuously.
- Anti-corruption framework: anti-corruption training embedded in ethical training; risk assessments and investigations support ESRS G1‑3 requirements.
- Contractual safeguards: Anti-corruption and Compliance Policies require inclusion of an anti-corruption clause in all contracts and regulatory documents; deviations allowed only exceptionally with documented justification and risk acceptance, and must be reported to compliance; phased extension to all group members planned for 2025.
- Corruption risk areas identified: gifts and representation, charity and sponsorship, partner interactions, contracting, investments and asset management/maintenance, hiring, and real estate purchase/management/sale; vigilance expected across all activities with potential corruption risk.

nodes.title: AML Whistleblowing System
nodes.heading: AML Whistleblowing System
nodes.start_phrase: OTP Bank operates a whistleblowing system for reporting illegal activities related to the prevention and combating of money laundering and terrorism financing.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on OTP Group’s Anti-Money Laundering/Counter-Terrorism Financing (AML/CFT) training and controls across subsidiaries.
- Country-specific training coverage:
  - Serbia: Mandatory AML training for staff establishing customer relationships and executing transactions.
  - Croatia: Training for customer-facing employees and senior management per legal requirements.
  - Montenegro (CKB): Identified AML/CFT-exposed roles (customer-facing, transaction executors, compliance, internal audit, security, operational risk management, senior management, Supervisory Board) receive training.
  - Romania: Mandatory training for employees responsible for or involved in AML/CFT and KYC processes.
- Ongoing AML knowledge sharing via internal forums (intranet, professional newsletter) on customer due diligence, thorough customer understanding, and red flags (e.g., strawman arrangements, unjustified cash usage).
- AML whistleblowing system:
  - Anonymous reporting of suspected AML/CFT law breaches.
  - Investigations completed within 30 days by designated personnel (Compliance Directorate or AML/CFT Department leadership, depending on the case).
  - Formal investigation reports include actions, deadlines, and responsible persons; approved by the head of the Compliance Directorate with oversight of implementation.
  - Immediate notification to authorities when justified; system operates continuously.
- Anti-corruption framework:
  - Anti-corruption training integrated into Ethical training; supported by risk assessments and investigations aligned with ESRS G1-3.
- Policy requirements for anti-corruption clauses:
  - Anti-Corruption and Compliance Policies require inclusion of anti-corruption clauses in all contracts and regulatory documents, emphasizing risk minimization—especially in tenders and preparation phases.
  - Deviations allowed only exceptionally with documented justification; contracting department assumes risk and must notify compliance.
  - Gradual extension of clause application to all group members planned for 2025.
- Key activities identified as high corruption risk: gifts and representation, charity and sponsorship, interactions with contractual partners, entering contractual obligations, investments and asset lifecycle management/maintenance, hiring, and real estate transactions; vigilance mandated for any other risk-bearing activities.

nodes.title: Taking action against Corruption
nodes.heading: Taking action against Corruption
nodes.start_phrase: OTP Group's anti -corruption measures include the anti -corruption training system, which is part of the Ethical training (see the same disclosure requirement above).
nodes.summary:
- AML/CFT training across subsidiaries:
  - Serbia: Mandatory for staff establishing customer relationships and executing transactions.
  - Croatia: Legally required training for customer-facing employees and senior management.
  - CKB Montenegro: Identifies and trains all roles exposed to AML/CFT risks (customer-facing, transaction executors, compliance, internal audit, security, operational risk, senior management, Supervisory Board).
  - Romania: Mandatory for employees responsible for or involved in AML/CFT and KYC processes.
  - Group-wide knowledge sharing via intranet/newsletters on customer due diligence, thorough customer knowledge, and red flags (e.g., strawman use, unjustified cash).

- AML whistleblowing system:
  - Enables anonymous reporting of AML/CTF-related illegal activities.
  - Investigations completed within 30 days by designated personnel (Compliance Directorate designee for cases involving the AML/CTF Department; otherwise by the AML/CTF Department lead or designee).
  - Investigation report includes actions, deadlines, and responsible persons; approved by the head of Compliance, who ensures implementation.
  - Immediate notification to authorities if warranted; system operates continuously.

- Anti-corruption framework:
  - Anti-corruption training integrated into Ethical training; supported by risk assessments and investigations (ESRS G1-3).
  - Anti-corruption and Compliance Policies aim to include an anti-corruption clause in all contracts and regulatory documents, emphasizing risk minimization, especially in tendering and preparation.
  - Deviations from the clause allowed only in exceptional cases with documented justification; contracting department assumes risk and must notify compliance.
  - Planned gradual extension of the clause to all group members in 2025.

- Corruption risk areas identified:
  - Gifts and representation; charity and sponsorship; interactions with contractual partners; undertaking contractual obligations; investments and asset purchases/management/maintenance; hiring; purchasing/managing/selling real estate.
  - Attention required for any other activities carrying corruption risks.

- Note: The “Prevention and Detection of Corruption and Bribery” disclosure is treated as an ESRS action.

nodes.title: Prevention and Detection of Corruption and Bribery
nodes.heading: Prevention and Detection of Corruption and Bribery141 ESRS G1 -3
nodes.start_phrase: The @Anti -corruption Policy and the @Compliance Policy stipulate that OTP Bank must strive to include an anti-corruption clause in all contractual relationships and regulatory documents.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: Anti–Money Laundering/Counter-Terrorist Financing (AML/CFT) training, whistleblowing, and anti-corruption governance across OTP Group.
- AML/CFT training:
  - Serbia: Mandatory training for staff establishing customer relationships and executing transactions, in line with national law.
  - Croatia: Training for customer-facing employees and senior management per legal requirements.
  - Montenegro (CKB): Identifies and trains roles exposed to AML/CFT risk (customer-facing, transaction execution, compliance, internal audit, security, operational risk, senior management, Supervisory Board).
  - Romania: Mandatory training for staff involved in AML/CFT and KYC processes.
  - Group-wide knowledge sharing via intranet and newsletters on customer due diligence, red flags (e.g., strawmen, unjustified cash use), and emerging trends.
- AML whistleblowing system:
  - Anonymous reporting channel for suspected breaches of AML/CFT laws.
  - Investigations completed within 30 days by a designated investigator (Compliance Directorate head assigns depending on whether the AML/CFT department is implicated).
  - Outcome report includes actions, deadlines, and accountabilities; approved by the head of Compliance, with escalation to authorities when warranted.
  - System operates continuously.
- Anti-corruption framework (ESRS G1-3):
  - Anti-Corruption Policy and Compliance Policy require inclusion of an anti-corruption clause in contracts and regulatory documents; deviations allowed only exceptionally with documented justification and notification to Compliance. Gradual extension to all group members planned in 2025.
  - Risk-based annual assessments determine priority units/activities; Compliance conducts ongoing, recurring anti-corruption investigations, focusing on higher-risk areas (e.g., suppliers/agents).
  - Group members must adopt detailed rules, contractual provisions, and procedures to enforce the policy.
  - Training: Annual ethical training (includes anti-corruption) is mandatory for all employees; 100% coverage of functions exposed to corruption/bribery risks.
  - Monitoring and remediation: Compliance monitors policy implementation and legal alignment; anomalies trigger review and policy updates with reporting to governing bodies. Annual reports inform governing bodies on implementation status.
  - Reporting channels: Violations can be reported under the Code of Ethics/Partner Code of Ethics; investigations follow the ethical reporting system. Conflict of Interest Policy ensures separation between investigator and subject and safeguards against personal interest conflicts.
- Corruption and bribery cases (ESRS G1-4):
  - No convictions across OTP Group for violations of anti-corruption/bribery laws.
  - 2024: Two confirmed internal cases at Uzbek Ipoteka Bank; both became public locally but were closed through internal investigations without official authority decisions.
    - Case 1: Branch financial adviser accepted money to assist a mortgage application before formal submission; employment terminated.
    - Case 2: Two branch employees attempted to falsify documents to aid a third party for a mortgage before application; employment terminated.
  - No business partner contract terminations required.
- Cross-references indicate alignment with ESRS disclosures and integration with the group’s ethical training and reporting systems.

nodes.title: Corruption and Bribery Cases
nodes.heading: Corruption and Bribery Cases ESRS G1-4
nodes.start_phrase: No convictions of guilty of violating anti -corruption and anti -bribery laws have been made against members of OTP Group.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and governance of anti-corruption: OTP Group applies annual, risk-based assessments to identify units/activities at higher corruption risk and runs continuous, periodic compliance-led investigations, with particular focus on suppliers and agents. Group-wide anti-corruption rules and contractual clauses are implemented and monitored by local compliance functions, which review anomalies, adjust provisions, and report annually to governing bodies. Whistleblowing/reporting channels follow the Code of Ethics and Partner Code of Ethics, and conflicts of interest are managed by separating investigators from subjects.

- Training and awareness: Annual ethics training, including anti-corruption and anti-bribery, is mandatory for all employees, covering 100% of functions exposed to such risks.

- Incidents (ESRS G1-4): No members were convicted of violating anti-corruption or anti-bribery laws. Two internally confirmed cases at Ipoteka Bank (Uzbekistan) in 2024—one bribe accepted for mortgage assistance and one attempt to falsify documents before loan application—were investigated internally; involved employees were dismissed. No business partner contracts were terminated; no official body decisions were issued.

- Legal and regulatory procedures (GRI 2-27, 2024): 440 closed cases across OTP Group; 4 significant; 135 closed with fines. Total fines: HUF 879.4 million (HUF 617.4m for 2024 practices; HUF 262.0m for earlier practices). No fines for anti-corruption/anti-bribery rule violations. Key categories:
  - Supervisory procedures: HUF 584.7m (HUF 572.5m tied to 2024 practices)
  - Data protection: HUF 215.0m (HUF 6.5m for 2024 practices; HUF 208.5m earlier)
  - Consumer protection: HUF 69.3m (HUF 28.5m for 2024 practices; HUF 40.8m earlier)
  - Smaller fines in information provision, taxation, environment, marketing, health and safety
  - Country regulatory practices differ, driving variation in procedure numbers

- Competition law matters: Three ongoing cases (OTP Bank, Ipoteka Bank Uzbekistan, OTP Bank Russia). Three closed cases with minor fines: Ipoteka Bank (HUF 0.6m for microloan advertising non-compliance) and two cases at the Russian subsidiary (total HUF 1.5m). The “Interchange” case against OTP Bank is a repeated GVH procedure reopened in 2021 after the 2009 fine (HUF 281m) was annulled and refunded; still ongoing in 2024.

- Other notable proceedings:
  - Hungary (MNB): HUF 102m fine for payment services violations; remedial measures required
  - Bulgaria (CPDP): HUF 209m fine against DSK Bank for a 2019 data protection case (final in 2024)
  - Montenegro (Central Bank): HUF 424m fine for internal control and operational risk deficiencies after a branch fraud (paid post-period)
  - Albania (National Bank): Required practice modifications; no fine

nodes.title: Legal Procedures
nodes.heading: Legal Procedures
nodes.start_phrase: Above is a summary of the closed regulatory procedures and the amounts of fines paid by OTP Group members.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: OTP Group’s 2024 legal and regulatory proceedings, fines, notable cases, and the Group’s reporting policy under G1/GRI/ESRS.
- Groupwide outcomes (GRI 2-27):
  - 440 cases closed; 4 significant; 135 closed with fines.
  - Total fines: HUF 879.4 million (HUF 617.4m for practices applied in 2024; HUF 262.0m for earlier practices).
  - Largest fine categories: supervisory procedures (HUF 584.7m; 138 cases, 3 significant, 64 with fines) and data protection (HUF 215.0m; 19 cases, 1 significant, 3 with fines).
  - Other categories: consumer protection (HUF 69.3m), information provision (HUF 6.6m); minimal or no fines in competition (HUF 2.1m), taxation (HUF 0.2m), environment (HUF 0.4m), marketing communication (HUF 0.5m), health and safety (HUF 0.3m). No fines in IT/cybersecurity, anti-corruption/bribery, equal opportunity (own or non-own workforce), accessibility, labor law, or combined marketing/info rules.
  - Note: Country regulatory practices differ, influencing case volumes.
- Competition law:
  - 3 ongoing cases (OTP Bank, Ipoteka Bank Uzbekistan, OTP Bank Russia).
  - 3 closed cases with total fines HUF 2.1m (Ipoteka: HUF 0.6m for marketing non-compliance in microloan ads; Russia: HUF 1.5m across two cases).
  - Significant ongoing “Interchange” case against OTP Bank: original 2009 GVH fine of HUF 281m annulled on appeal; fine refunded; new GVH procedure re-initiated in 2021, ongoing in 2024.
- Other significant procedures:
  - Hungary (MNB): HUF 102m fine on OTP Bank for payment services violations; corrective measures required.
  - Bulgaria (CPDP): HUF 209m fine on DSK Bank for 2019 data protection breach (final in 2024).
  - Montenegro (Central Bank): HUF 424m fine for internal control/operational risk deficiencies post-branch fraud (paid after reporting period).
  - Albania (National Bank): required practice changes; no fine.
- Voluntary codes: No 2024 non-compliance related to product/service information or marketing communication.
- Equal opportunity and discrimination:
  - Two equal opportunity legal proceedings closed at OTP Bank Serbia; no fines.
  - 14 discrimination-related reports across the Group (9 OTP Bank, 2 OTP Bank Romania, 1 each at DSK Bulgaria, CKB Montenegro, OTP Factoring); none substantiated.
- Reporting policy (G1/GRI/ESRS):
  - Anti-corruption/bribery training coverage counts employees who completed or were assigned during the period.
  - Publishes number of convictions and total fines for anti-corruption/bribery; excludes cases under appeal or pending.
  - Discloses non-compliance by topic without overlap; reports total closed cases, cases with fines, and fines split by current vs earlier practice.
  - Significant non-compliance: single fine ≥ HUF 10m, or multiple fines for the same practice totaling ≥ HUF 10m; non-fine cases generally not significant unless designated by experts.
  - Discrimination defined per ESRS (including harassment); reports total cases, cases involving own workforce (S1-17), and substantiated cases.

nodes.title: Reporting policy for heading G1
nodes.heading: 4.2. Reporting policy for heading G1
nodes.start_phrase: G1-3 21. b: In the case of anti -corruption and bribery training programs for employees in risky functions, when calculating the percentage of employees working in vulnerable functions covered by these programs, the group takes into account employees who completed the training program during the reporting period and those who were a ssigned to complete the program, whether or not they completed it by the reporting date.
nodes.summary:
- 2024 compliance outcomes: no non-compliance with voluntary codes on product/service information or marketing communication.
- Equal opportunity cases: two legal proceedings closed at OTP Bank Serbia; none of the cases resulted in fines.
- Discrimination reports: 14 across OTP Group (9 OTP Bank, 2 OTP Bank Romania, 1 each at DSK Bank Bulgaria, CKB Montenegro, and OTP Factoring); none substantiated.
- Reporting policy (G1):
  - G1-3: Anti-corruption/bribery training coverage for vulnerable roles counts both employees who completed training during the period and those assigned to complete it, even if not finished by the reporting date.
  - G1-4: The Group discloses the number of convictions for anti-corruption/bribery and total fines in the period, excluding cases under appeal or still pending.
  - Alignment with ESRS and GRI 2-27: Non-compliance disclosures are presented together; topic-based reporting avoids double counting; the Group reports closed cases, cases with fines, and amounts, distinguishing fines for current-period practices vs. earlier-period practices.
- Definition of significant non-compliance: any single fine ≥ HUF 10 million; aggregated fines for the same practice totaling ≥ HUF 10 million; cases without fines are generally not significant unless deemed otherwise by experts.
- Discrimination definition and reporting: follows ESRS (including harassment; bases such as gender identity, race/ethnicity, nationality, religion/belief, disability, age, sexual orientation). The Group reports total discrimination cases, separately highlights cases involving its own workforce (S1-17), and reports the number of substantiated cases.
